en: Śrīḥ!
Composed by Ācārya Daṇḍin, *Avantisundarī*:
[He worshipped] Hiraṇyagarbha, Īśāna, the primordial Puruṣa, and Hari.
I bow to the three who are without falsehood or diversity, whose bodies are the universe. || 1 ||

Salutations to that sage who, in former times, bestowed the consciousness of the *Mahābhārata* upon the mechanical bodies of mortals— that stream of honey which flows from his mouth as the heart-pleasing *Rāmāyaṇa*. || 3 ||
I bow to that [Lord] by whose grace there arose for the poets the expressive power of speech, so that they might be instructors of words. || 4 ||
...supreme, whose mental walls are variegated by the paintings of the three worlds. || 5 ||
It is said that Subandhu, having escaped from the imprisonment of Bindusāra,
bound the very heart of that same king, the Vatsarāja.
Just as with the *Tāmraśāsana*, what kind of genre (*jāti*) has been abandoned by the *Bṛhatkathā* when it is accompanied by the *Gomukha*? (5)
This work, which was granted by Nārāyaṇa and rests upon Devadatta, [was composed] by Mūladeva...
Having repeatedly conquered with his keen-edged sword, Śūdraka once again held the world in check by means of his speech that fulfilled its own purpose.
Even transcending the world, [her] speech [proceeds] along the path of revelation...
With his facial features and limbs well-proportioned, and with his characteristic marks and postures clearly manifest,
Bhāsa stood even after death as if through his dramatic compositions embodied in physical forms.
By King Śrī-Sarvasena...
[for the sake of] the victory of Hari. || 12 ||
Standing as a bridge in this world for those who perceive the Reality, our preeminent poets have attained the status of fifty-six authorities. (13)
I myself am intoxicated...
[how great a burden is there for one who understands? || 14 ||
By him whose speech was once rendered helpless, being smeared with the flowing honey [of the Vaidarbhī style], this path of the Vaidarbha has been cleared by Kālidāsa. (15)
The eye is damaged... [O Lord], he who is capable of pervading even the three worlds with but three steps—would not the mind of that Nārāyaṇa be capable of pervading the three poems? 17.
Who that is not mad would not praise him today—the primordial poet who faces every direction, the sovereign emperor of poets? (18)
Though pierced by a sharp-pointed arrow, the peacock remained unpained; remarkably, he did not abandon his playful grace even during his cries. || 19 ||
...this strikes me as marvelous:
though she was born without caste, she has become the abode of the excellence of noble birth. (20)
Born from Dhavala, that Manovatī spreads passion through these poets who are like scent-elephants. || 21 ||
...not born of the lineage of Dāmodara;
for even in winning over animals, it possesses a sound that is as if pleasing to the heart. || 22 ||
Fie upon that crow-like poet who, having beheld her face, spreads [his wings]... || 23 ||
...Indeed, it is difficult to speak ill [of him].
Who shall wash away the blackness of the twice-born enemy of Kauśika? (24)
Even if licked by the mouths of crows from a threshing floor, the goddess Sarasvatī remains stainless;
therefore, that something... || 25 ||
Through mutual favor toward one another, may they flourish in prosperity and fame, being devoted to each other. || 26 ||
May the Asuras be defeated; may the gods be victorious; may Sarasvatī be victorious;
may the assembly of great poets be victorious... || 27 ||

...resting upon the face of the lady of the [western] direction like a leaf-adorned finger, shining with a completely radiant complexion; a cluster of chowrie-flowers fixed upon her ear through the abundance of fragrance produced by an unceasing stream of gifts; like a branch of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) capable of yielding the offerings for the birth of desire, bestowed by the Fortune of the Universal Monarch’s realm upon that noble woman; [a place] where the bees were drawn to the fragrance of the treasure-chests filled with gold and jewels, and where the waters were deep and white as lotuses, capable of bearing perfumes.

Having disregarded Vasvokasārā as one who abandons her many dwellings for the gods and lacks the city of Avāsavatī, he—having performed his duties at Vegavatī, whose banks resounded with the sweet, intoxicated warbling of swans and whose waves were stirred by the glances of young women—embraced all that was produced from rivers, oceans, islands, and cities; and having cast off his watery nature, he stood, more firmly girded than even the immovable mountains, like the Ocean of Milk itself, white with lime-plaster during the cold season.

It was encircled by a ring of ramparts that mimicked the garland of peaks on Mount Kailāsa, as if swallowing the entire expanse of Airāvata along with all its clusters of planets of sovereignty; it was endowed with four gate-towers that resembled the elephants of the quarters stationed at the ends of the horizon, their frontal globes washed by the river of the sky; and it possessed vast oceans of space colored by the rays from the clusters of jewels shimmering upon the great surfaces of the gate-towers—oceans bearing many-folded expanses and producing supernatural splendors through the arrival of numerous Naga women.

It was adorned with great highways like Bhogavatī, lined with excellent palanquins resembling the kings of serpents; because its entire surface was made of jewels, it gave rise to the suspicion that it was another sky; and it was graced by great palaces such as Nalinaka and others, which were inhabited by hosts of immortals like divine chariots, and by other [residences] fit for great men, like the Great Men themselves.

Adorned with feet, knees, arms, necks, noses, foreheads, and heads endowed with the [auspicious] marks; with firm forearms, shoulders, and crowns; with unloosened joints and eyes; with fourfold, rounded, and noble breeds; with excellent and fierce power; adorned by those who know the [essence of] horses (*kutavedin*); with non-vulgar ornaments; marked with *tilaka* spots; possessing fragrant [traces of] elephants; bearing the passion of the *aśoka*; great and auspicious; with blossoming *palāśa* flowers; like lions; charming as Arjuna; captivating as Mādhavī vines; like chariots of desire for the beloved—[such were the horses].

[The groves were] like circles of artisans with their lathe-wheels; like palaces of joy, endowed with beautiful pigeons; like cities of Rati, surrounded by *sāla* trees; like the inner apartments of the God of Love, possessing the splendor of pure jasmine; like playful painters, encircled by creepers of various colors; like oceans of passion, with clusters of shimmering young shoots; like the children of Dharma, attended by nursemaids; like lovers, adorned with lovely tresses; like pleasure-grounds, containing abodes of mango trees; and like the Kauravas...

With *damanaka* flowers that rose with a pale-white luster; charming with an abundance of blossoms like the life-stories of Gaurī, which captivate Śrīkaṇṭha; where the thick *karavīra* trees—uprooted by the force of battle as if they were the Kauravas in the Mahābhārata war—roamed about; beautiful with lovely *campaka* trees like the limbs of the body; beloved by the people of the flower-city of Kāntapura like the Magadha kingdom; adorned with betel vines and areca palms like the limbs of Lord Śiva; and delightful with unfading *karamaṇīya* flowers like the company of the virtuous.

With pleasure gardens both external and internal—where the joy of the women was increased by groves of blooming white lotuses that resembled mountains, as if the Nandana groves had been gathered together out of a desire to conquer Indra’s city—she seemed to be protecting the cool season, which had sought refuge there out of fear of the summer heat; she was like a court of justice where the entire host of gods, acting as householders in their own abodes, had simultaneously brought before it the moon, whose beauty had been drained by the labor of churning the ocean and whose broad rays had increased, as if for the audacious purpose of forcibly seizing the nectar.

The region was characterized by clusters of ponds that served as a vast expanse for the sky, appearing as if they had come forth from the ocean to engage in worldly activity; they were embraced by groves of lotuses that seemed to blaze like the submarine fire (Vaḍavāgni); they bore flocks of water-birds with sweet warbling and intoxicated, graceful movements, which raised a great clamor as if distressed by the heavy burden of the sun’s rays; and through the sporting of various flocks of birds, they displayed a mass of clouds bent down by their greed for water. Thus, the surrounding countryside was filled with the preparations for the harvest.

The capital city named Kāñcīpuram was like a female royal swan resting upon the green lotus leaves of emerald terraces; it possessed rows of white palace halls like a flight of birds, and its beautiful tinkling girdle-bands hung from the orb-like hips of a multitude of women whose gait was graceful and slow.

With her, Amarāvatī seemed to hover above as if out of sheer lightness, being raised up by the Grandfather (Brahmā). And in that city, rows of palaces—fitted with earthly nectar yet longing for the taste of divine ambrosia—brush against the moon during the nights with their girdles of fluttering silken banners. And in that city, swarms of bees upon the crest-ornaments of sweet-voiced women, having been surpassed by the shadow of the wings of their curled hair, seem to cry out incessantly as if in terror.

The blue lotuses of her ears, surpassed by the playful side-glances [of her lover], appear to manifest a darkening hue as if from grief; the leaf-patterns of her teeth lie curled up, covering her ears as if out of embarrassment at her smiles that are moons; the reddish garments covering her breasts bear a pallor as if from sorrow, being eclipsed by the luster of her lips; and the lotuses of her graceful movements wither slowly, as if from the heat, imitated by the sprout-like hands of her lover.

The flowers of her playful charms heave again and again, as if sighing from exhaustion, surpassed by the clusters of rays from the jewels upon her nails. Her upper garments, their excellence of color eclipsed by the loveliness of the orb of her hips, assume a final state, as if out of despondency. And the juices of the thick lac-dye, cast aside at every step by the natural redness of her lotus-feet, fall down as if from pain.

Upon the surfaces of moonstones, it was as if devoured by the sun; upon the courtyards of sapphires, as if swallowed by darkness; upon the floors of rubies, as if entering the fire out of shame at being thus disparaged; and upon the sections of crystal walls, as if plunging into water due to the agony of that burning—thus the orb of the reflected sun wandered with extreme restlessness throughout the entire day.

And she was like another grammarian, yet not one of words: she was pure with the warmth of her passion; she was capable of assuming the role of a consort for hundreds of men through manifold modes of embrace; she was independent of external instruction; she was skilled in all the case-endings (*kāraka-vibhakti*) of the object (*sampradāna-karma*) of giving; she was adept at the untroubled path of approach; she was ignorant of the occurrence of grammatical *vikāra* (modification) or *āgama* (augment); she knew no *upasarga* (prefixes); she was expert in the practice of unprecedented application; she possessed all the phonemes (*varṇa*) as the objects of *guṇa* (strengthening) and *vṛddhi* (vowel-increment) operations; she spoke in fourfold ways; and she never refused [her services], even when the time was inappropriate.

With courtesans moving about like deities of dalliance, who had rendered the celestial women depicted in the murals of the divine palace motionless—as if deprived of consciousness by grief—by utterly eclipsing their own beauty, grace, wit, and elegance; he beheld that host of divine women.

Because of its vastness, there was no space for the world; because of the height of its palaces, mountains were like mere clods of earth; because of the abundance of jewels in its marketplaces, the oceans were as if empty; because of the cleverness of its citizens, the god of love appeared rustic; because of the depth of its ponds, the bed of the ocean seemed shallow; because of the excellence of its artisans, Viśvakarman appeared ignorant of nothing; and because of the intellectual power of its scholars, even Kāvya, Aṅgiras, and Rauhineya seemed unripe in their knowledge.

Her husband was like another Indra, yet he was not the protector of the gods, nor the destroyer of rival kings, nor the one who shattered the strength of mountain ranges, nor the bringer of calamities through rain, nor one who pursued the inclination of those fond of sin, nor one who desired the undertaking of long ascetic penances, nor the consecrator of Janārdana; rather, he possessed a body as radiant as the sun, was as skilled in the use of the axe as Hara, was the lord of the stars like the moon, and had a voice as melodious as Keśava.

Like a king of the *yakṣas*, his teeth were ever-sharp; like the break of dawn, he bore the luster of a ruby; like the expanse of the earth, he had a broad forehead; like the father of Umā (Śiva), his arms were as long as the coils of a serpent; like the one whose banner is the monkey (Kṛṣṇa), his eyes reached to his ears; like a *sāla* tree, his shoulders were exceedingly thick; like a palace, his nose was praised for its lofty height; like one intent on battle, he was always engaged in close combat; like a desert region, his chest was level and even; like a lover, his waist was slender; like a mountain of frogs... [he was] like a mountain of frogs.

With his garments dyed by the jewels of his thick, high, broad, and massive thighs, bearing firm pillar-like legs like the lord of servants (Yama), possessing auspicious marks on his hands and feet like the Sāmavedic tradition, and having drawn away the entire wealth of his beloved [the Earth] out of indignation at the title "King" as if from the Moon, he was a lion-king among all the deer-like kings; thus, there was a king named Siṃhaviṣṇu (or Varma) in the regions of Pallava, who was a source of great esteem for his statesmanship.

He was embraced by Śrī as he ascended the throne with impetuous joy—she who had been made grey by contact with the pollen stirred up from the navel-lotus of Nārāyaṇa when it quivered in agitation, and who now seemed to have her body turned tawny by the mass of dust from the *piṣṭātaka* powder used to increase the auspiciousness of his royal consecration.

And he, whose [body] was as if repeatedly split open by the fire of his own majesty within the waters of his consecration—those waters which were sought for the purpose of practicing swimming across the entire circle of the ocean’s depths; and whose thick, hard sword-blade, having drunk its fill of water, repeatedly struck against the surfaces of the pearl-stones, as if heated by the intense torment of swallowing the boiling life-breaths of his enemies consumed by the fire of his wrath.

And by him, whose shoulders were filled with the fresh bloom of youth, [he was] like a refuge for another who had been scorched in battle; and while that king ruled the earth with the pillar of his arm, there was the destruction of the enjoyments of serpents, yet no serpents [were harmed]; ...there was the breaking of pots, yet no pots [were broken]; there was the mutual falling of balls, yet no balls [were lost]; there was the transgression of well-spoken verses by night-stalkers, yet no night-stalkers [were harmed].

There was the spreading of darkness, yet no transgressions; there were [the qualities of] virtues, yet no cruel men; there was the crushing of feet by thorns, yet no thorns; there was the devouring of double-tongued serpents by winds, yet no destructive storms; there was the destruction of the beauty of hunters, yet no hunters—such was the wonderful state of the subjects.

Now that king, though devoted to the propitiation of all the gods and possessed of supreme intellect, took delight in the qualities of poets which generate divine joy. Though not a god himself, he somehow tasted the nectar-essence enveloped in the arts.
Once, when he had entered the assembly hall, a certain young Gandharva, like Tumburu, played the lute for him as follows:

"May the man-lion form of Viṣṇu—the cause of the world's origin—protect you; his thunderbolt-like claws, whose power was recognized by the shattering of the mountain that was the heart of the Lord of the Danujas."

Having heard this noble verse, he, being curious about its excellence, asked him: “Good sir! Whose are these syllables that appear so powerfully composed with grandeur, and whose is this arrangement of letters, so sweet and clear, which produces joy for the ears like a sprout of the moon’s rays?”

Having prostrated himself, he made this request: "O King! I am most highly favored; may this person be further graced by granting me a moment of your attention. In the northwestern direction, there is a great abode of Brahmins named Ānandapura, the crest-jewel of the noble lands."

From him issued forth Sarasvatī, like [the river] from the world of Brahmā, or like the form of Agastya who has drunk and then disgorged the deep-sounding ocean; she favored the southern direction. For the sake of his friend Acala, Mūladeva—having uprooted the entire expansion of the doctrines of gamblers—established a city named Acalapura on ground that was not merely laborious for its fields of rice-scratching forests fragrant with the water and flowers of *gavākṣa* trees. It was like another heavenly realm upon the surface of the earth, a no small abode for those of meritorious deeds.

There dwells one who increases the lineage of Kuśika, whose fortitude is sustained by the extensive expansion of secluded mantras; she is hospitable to all, yet accepts no gifts; she is of great and noble form, a mass of Brahman, and the very continuity of Brahman.

Therein was born a son named Dāmodarasvāmin, composed of splendor, who was like the navel-lotus of the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself—the embodiment of all the seven sacrificial threads (saptatantu)—and who is the sole abode of Brahman.

At the very onset of his youth, he—who possessed an exceedingly beautiful form—was affectionately united by Sarasvatī herself, who approached him like a maiden choosing her own husband; she was one whose true nature as merit was revealed through her unartificial speech, who was enchanting in every limb, skilled in all the arts, proficient in all languages, endowed with proper proportions, graceful in the arrangement of her words, charming and pleasing to the heart through her ornaments, and pure in both lineage and conduct.

For who indeed can accomplish their purpose by following a path as they desire, transcending the power of destiny? Since even the prince Kauśika bound his affection for the sake of meritorious deeds upon the son of the king named Viṣṇuvardhana—a great devotee of Śiva, possessed of great majesty, the source of cattle, and radiant in splendor—just as the moon, seeing its own likeness, fixes its love upon the sun-like Bhāravi.

Once, while out on a hunt, he was led by that man against his will to eat meat unfit for his family, being the remains of an offering; out of sheer shame, he approached his parents and, under the pretext of going on a pilgrimage, wandered through various regions. He came within the range of Durvinīta—the banner of the Gāṅgeya clan whose fame rests upon his habit of wandering, who bears the contrary name [of Vinīta], and who is a treasure-house of virtues like the moon is a mine of lilies.

And by this [person], who displayed such goodness as self-surrender and so forth—rooted merely in the transgression of the virtuous—he has been captivated. This noble lady and this other... [are] the play of the intellect of that young brahmin; indeed, his knowledge of what is existent and non-existent in the worlds is well known.

"And as for his age, he is about twenty years old. Having thus prostrated himself with his head touching the ground, the King—[having performed the customary] salutations—and filled with curiosity, honored him like the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) honoring the sacred bathing places of the Sarasvatī, and brought him under his own influence, drawn by the continuous stream of his many auspicious qualities.

...having manifested his supreme favor by adopting as his own son the son of that best of the twice-born, the primordial poet Caturānana—who, through his majesty, had displayed extraordinary qualities and propitiated [the deity]—and having previously revealed the various categories of Prakrit objects, he granted him a land-measure equal to a *brahmadeya*, accompanied by a [not small] measure of modesty appropriate thereto.

On one occasion, having heard some popular songs sent by him, the lord of the earth was exceedingly pleased. He filled a golden vessel with fragrant... and sent it, saying: "This is the breast-milk of your mothers, overflowing with love for your virtues. Because of its great abundance, there would be the burden of effort for you to drink from each breast individually; therefore, we have collected it all together in one place. And the king continued to bestow such honors upon him every month, every fortnight, and indeed every day.

Being thus favored, and by means of the excellent compositions produced on Mount Gandhamādana and elsewhere, as well as the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of poetry in both Sanskrit and Prakrit, he brought glory to the Deccan.

And, having married against the king’s will, he begot three sons—named Siṃha, Viṣṇu, and Manorathātilobha—who were composed of *brahman*, who served as the foundation for the entire range of speech, whose roots were infinite, whose established dwellings were fixed upon the stability of mountain ranges, who were as profound as the ocean, and whose radiant splendor shone forth through the patronage of illustrious royal swans; they were like the three worlds themselves.

In whose houses there resounds the clear sound of Vedic chanting by those well-versed in recitation; the sound of all the scriptures being expounded according to their respective positions; the clamor of the swans in the domestic ponds drawn forth by the chatter of anklets on the lotus-feet of the womenfolk; the tumultuous noise of satisfying the multitude of all guests; the ornamentation of the humming of swarms of bees wandering in pursuit of fragrant scents; and the sound of various festivals commenced by circles of matrons worshipping the household deities—a sound like a drum proclaiming the power to bestow gifts of tender leaves.

The middle son, slow with the sound of the ornaments of Sarasvatī as she moved through the fourfold compositions of his words day and night, attained after a long time—like a long-cherished desire—the four sons of Dāmodara, Bhavadāsa, Siṃha, and Viṣṇudatta, who were presided over by Brahmā; who were like great oceans for the world, filled with a multitude of honored and mighty sounds, revered by kings, fit for the protection of boundaries, possessing heaps of jewels of great virtues, and endowed with great courage. Dharmapāla had three sons: Śaṅkaragaṇa, Vidyādharagaṇa, and Mahādevagaṇa. Of these, the middle one, Śaṅkaragaṇa, was born after a long interval, like the fulfillment of a desire for the majestic Dharma seeking to conquer the Kali age. He obtained four sons from his wife, who were like great oceans: Dāmodara, Bhavadāsa, Siṃha, and Viṣṇudatta, who were established in the Brahman. Dharmapāla had three sons: Śaṅkaragaṇa, Vidyādharagaṇa, and Mahādevagaṇa. Of these, the middle one, Śaṅkaragaṇa, was born after a long interval, like the fulfillment of a desire for the majestic Dharma seeking to conquer the Kali age. Among them, the youngest was Vīradattaśarman, whose conduct was pure by nature; his wife was a Brāhmaṇī named Gaurī of the Māṭhara lineage, who occupied the station of housewife as Arundhatī does for the Brahmarṣi Vasiṣṭha. To quell the anxiety born from the birth of many daughters, he obtained from her a single son named Daṇḍin. Free from jealousy because he was the son of a co-wife rather than the son of his father’s favorite, that noble lady nurtured Daṇḍin from the seventh year onward, as serene as the goddess Sarasvatī herself.

And when that [text] was brought forward, his teacher recited it with a voice as if out of a desire to see his own preceptor. Meanwhile, while the Draviḍas, Coḷas, and Pāṇḍyas were agitated by the oppression of a foreign army; while noble women were being violated; while the maintenance of sacred fires had ceased; while heaps of grain were plundered; while householders were fleeing; while [the people] were yawning in despair; while boundaries were broken down and rows of groves were cut away; while assembly halls and water-stations were destroyed; while almshouses were overturned; while the wealthy were slain; and while [the people] were being struck down...

When the Draviḍas had been devoured by the Kāpathas... in the Kali age, Kauśikadāraka Daṇḍin—having lost his circle of kinsmen, with his attendants mostly fled, his means of livelihood ruined, and his treasury exhausted by famine—wandered through various regions. He resided for a long time in well-known teacher’s households and acquired irreproachable learning.

And in assemblies of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas of the highest rank, [he was] the architect named Māndhātṛ—the praised builder of the palace for that one who, like the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), amazed the invincible [opponents] with his craftsmanship; who was skilled in the expansion of the systems of application revealed by the complete synthesis of the essence of the meaning of the treatises; who was an expert in the sixty-nine types of temple construction; who was adept in the various designs for vehicles, seats, beds, and so forth; and [who possessed knowledge] of the sixfold [classifications] known as the *sthitacara*, *dhāra*, *dvīpa*, *jvara*, *vyāmiśra*, and *saṃjñā*.

Then the master builder named Lalitālaya—a third among those who employ mechanical devices, adorned with the thirty-six qualities of a master craftsman, the upholder of all architectural rules, a carpenter and woodworker esteemed by the ranks of artisans, and refined by the Kṣatriyas—approached, and with palms joined in reverence and eyes moist with emotion, sat down upon the ground that had been pointed out for him.

Even upon seeing him, the people were struck with wonder, saying: "This man, they say, has displayed a door-battle with mechanical men; by him, it is said, the sky was made jagged with a mass of water from false clouds; he, they say, created a mechanical conjurer; he, they say, simultaneously pierces the frontal globes of countless enemy elephants in battle with arrows as thick as pestles; and by him, they say, in the Dravidian tongue—"

Composed by Śūdraka and bound together, it is said that his father, having surpassed even the Yavanas, was told by a machine, "This one is hungry," to which [the father] replied, "He is indeed superior even to him. Thus there were such outpourings of words from those whose curiosity had blossomed.

When the clamor had completely subsided, he said to Daṇḍin: “There is something I wish to inform you. All your extraordinary artistic skills have indeed been exhausted by constant negligence and laxity; for even this slight display today is enough to cause wonder among the common people. But as for those like you, who know the heart of the scriptures composed by Brahmā, Indra, Parāśara, and others—how insignificant is this proficiency of yours before them?”

For the sole purpose of favoring him alone, the right hand of the Blessed One—the wielder of the Śārṅga bow—who out of compassion for the great city of Anumahāpura has favored the mountain that possesses a garland of waves and whose lotus feet are carried by the hands of massive billows, was broken at the wrist for some reason. It has been reassembled by me. You should examine whether it is worthy of that divine form fashioned by the exceedingly great former masters, or not.
"For it is not possible for those like us to remain without fulfilling the request made by you, which is unique to this occasion."

Then, seated right nearby—like the very abode of all virtuous qualities, possessing a power of renunciation that was never satiated even by the vow of giving away all his possessions, the assembly hall for the constant union with the Goddess of Fortune, whose grace and elegance in play were worthy of imitation by all citizens, the foremost of all heroes and another name for the "valorous" themselves, the prince Raṇamalla, the commander-in-chief, who was a mass of affection accumulated from playing in the dust together [with the King]—spoke: “Noble sir, this request of the preeminent artisan is indeed worthy of honor.”

The mountains, oceans, and forests are full of many wonders; and this friend of yours is the son of the Brahman-sage named Bhavabhūti—a mass of universal Brahma-knowledge, author of the *Kalpasūtra-ṭīkā*, an ocean overflowing with the rivers of all sciences, who has manifested the splendor of the thirty-three gods through thirty sacrifices, and who is capable of both cursing and bestowing grace. Among his sons, who possess equal intelligence and every other excellence, he is the second; he is peerless in the three Vedas, the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*), history, the arts, and poetry, and his heart is given unalterably to the opinions of his friends.

Devoted to the service of his guru, a supreme devotee of Maheśvara, a helmsman who has mastered the sciences, one who never transgresses even against Karṇa, surpassed by none in the power of renunciation, skilled in explaining the true meaning of the mantras, a knower of the four Vedas, whose conduct is characterized by compassion toward all people as if they were his own mother—this is Mātṛdatta. And at that time, this Sahajakīrtti, the repository of tradition belonging to Karasvāmin, a crest-jewel among the multitude of Brahmins, Devaśarmā, came from Kerala for the sake of seeing you; what [can be said] of these others as well?

This undertaking was in accordance with his resolve; without hesitation... on the following day, together with his circle of friends, including Śrī Jayantanārāyaṇa, Bhajana, Ānanda, and others... [he beheld] the host of the enemies of the gods, who were capable of tearing apart the wings of the mountains yet were themselves unable to withstand the thousand-eyed Indra... like a forest grove agitated by the young elephants of the god of love, like a false witness for the emergence of wonders from the Kālakūṭa poison and other such things, [rising] from the sky...

He gazed at the ocean, that mass of fortune made manifest by the frequent visits of the river-women, formidable with its circle of jewel-lit hoods of the radiant serpent-king; he beheld it as the royal mountain Kailāsa being touched at its base by the surging waves of the sea, which were as terrifying as the coils of venomous serpents or the staff-like arms of Rāvaṇa; and he saw it with its sands variegated by fragments of pearls released from the interiors of oysters shattered by the breaking of restless waves, and with its garlands fragrant with cool scents.

Having traveled some distance along the coastal path of the ocean—which was marked by clusters of *bakula* and *cakra* flowers in bud, filled with the abundant fragrance of mangoes, and perfumed by the pervasive scent of blooming, fragrant *campaka*, *aśoka*, *utpala*, *puṃnāga*, *tilaka*, *sāla*, and *sinduvāra* trees, and lined with *kramuka* and coconut groves—he beheld [the mountain] whose body was being lashed by the rows of waves of the salt sea, which were dark like garlands of full-blown blue water-lilies and resembled the glances of the Goddess Lakṣmī; and which possessed a mass of copper-colored eyes flashing from its thousand hoods raised high.

Once again, as if to dispel the apprehension of an assault by the Dānavas Madhu and Kaiṭabha, he beheld with wide-open eyes the Blessed One being supported by Śeṣa—who remained motionless like a pillar—while his lotus-throne was graced by a thousand-wondrous-petaled lotus issuing from the aperture of his navel, its flow of radiance arising from his eyes which were half-closed and languid in yogic sleep.

With his own pair of hands folded effortlessly like buds, his head bowed by the weight of devotion to his guru, and his inner stains as if washed away by the purifying spray from contact with the Master’s body—like droplets of water from the ocean’s shore—he gazed intently with focused eyes at the body of that image. Finding no distinction in its construction or proportions anywhere, he looked at the architect himself and said: “This is wood for a mere book-cover; what artifice have you employed here?”
But that preeminent artisan, his fatigue dispelled and his purpose accomplished, thought "this much is enough for me," and bowed with palms joined in reverence.

And at that very moment, there suddenly approached from all sides swarms of bees from the groves on the shore, their wings whirling with great agitation; they caused the delusion that the lotus-dwelling of the Lord’s navel had reappeared, and gave rise to the suspicion that another *pārijāta* tree had blossomed; they brought to mind the fragrance of the sighs of Lakṣmī, who was longing for the festival of love long suppressed by her yogic sleep; they acted like the perfume of the celestial damsels being enjoyed by Indra, and, wafting toward him, they smeared his very nose.

A certain divine and extraordinary fragrance arrived. With their eyes cast out by intense wonder, asking "What is this?", they all beheld that region of the ocean as it turned crimson at twilight—reddened as if by some indescribable, shimmering circle of young sprout-creeper tendrils; as if smeared with the luster of the jewels on the hoods of emerging serpents; as if colored by the flames of the submarine fire (Dāruṇa-vahni); and as if copper-red with the clusters of Kalpavṛkṣa trees visible upon the peaks of winged mountains flying upward.

In an instant, as they watched, there appeared a lotus flower—slightly larger than the wheels of the chariot, with its rows of filaments raised high, tossed up and then sinking again by the surging garlands of restless waves.

And again, by the mere touch of the lotus-feet of Acyuta... [by that very means, adorned with divine garlands, unguents, and ornaments], he appeared as some Vidyādhara, his single arm radiant with clusters of rays from the edge of his sword, while his other hand held a shield variegated with jewels; as if striking away the splendor of the sun with his own brilliance, he circumambulated the Blessed One and offered a salutation with palms joined in a gesture pregnant with meaning.

Carrying a cloud of sword-blade radiance as thick as a mass of water, with its long hanging pearl-strings tossed by the force of his upward leap and its swaying crest-garland, the world was suddenly struck with such extreme astonishment that it forgot its inner self; and [the king], enveloped in a dense cluster of rising and high-flying raiment, fell into deep reflection.

Now, there was a childhood friend named Rāmaśarman, whose mind was captivated by wonder; who was a connoisseur of the savor of stories and histories; who spoke with a smile; who was distinguished in the arts (*kalāsu*), being uniquely skilled (*vilakṣaṇaḥ*) and possessing a ready wit that found its openings in fruitful speech; who was disciplined in the sciences (*vidyāsu*), confident among friends, and averse to evil; who was fortunate, delicate, clever, generous, compassionate, virtuous, noble-minded, and delighted in truth; and who was of the *Ulābhija* lineage, belonging to the *Viśvāmitra* clan, accomplished, and known as Rāmaśarman.

In matters of following the mind, in warding off evil courses, in confidential trusts, and in that beloved state which is desirable even at the cost of one's life, he indeed spoke to Daṇḍin: "Is this not manifest even to the son of Gaurī?"

Even by those who perceive it directly, this most wonderful manifestation is difficult to believe; for instance, here before us, after the lotus-eyed Lord set foot upon this lotus, there arose from the sky—adorned with armlets, crowns, and bracelets, and leading a host—a red lotus that, though emerging from a flower yet to fully blossom, imitates the orb of the sun, and which is now the very transformation of that very lotus.

Nowadays, because such beings as these are so rarely encountered, our hearts are oppressed by the weight of a vast and spreading wonder; indeed, it is impossible for you to fathom this distance through the process of inference alone. Therefore, how can your honorable mind conceive of this?

He replied to him: "Friend! Is it not the case that our views are all the same? This can be inferred here and understood thus: 'This is some lord of the sky-dwellers who, having incurred the displeasure of a certain wrathful great seer due to an offense involving flowers, was cursed and attained the state of a lotus; fallen from the sky into the ocean, he has been carried by the currents from the land and wanders for a long time, nearly as vast as an eon, within the salt waters of the sea.'"
His heart was already overcome by a desire to know this matter of wonder; therefore, saying "Come, let us go," he returned toward Kāñcī together with his companions.

Urged again and again by his dear friends—Mātṛdatta, Rāmaśarman, Vimata, and others—their minds drawn by the passion of hearing that marvel, he, having adorned himself for a series of nights and being unwearied in the yoga of devotion, performed the worship of Viṣṇu according to the ritual prescribed in the Kalpa and lay down upon a bed of *darbha* grass. As he lay thus, the incorporeal Sarasvatī favored him in a dream.

“My child! Your desire has been fulfilled. May the Teacher of gods and asuras, whose body is the Triple Veda, the Lord of the three worlds, the dweller in the three abodes—be well-pleased with you. May this wondrous work appear before you: a teacher of instruction for all human goals, possessing the manifold flavors of the histories of all continents, profound with the essence of the entire collection of arts, esteemed for its synthesis of the sentiments of all philosophical systems, enchanting with its narration of the lineages of all primordial kings, and marvelous in its celebration of the deeds of all gods and asuras.”

[Having reached the further shore of... the lord of all men, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas, named Rājavāhana... [the night came to an end]. Awakened by wonder, and having bathed in the divine waters, he performed the morning twilight rites after a long interval; he duly worshipped the Blessed Lord, gratified the most excellent of the twice-born with delicious food consisting of the four tastes, and himself partook of sacrificial food (haviṣya). Then, dressed in auspicious and praiseworthy attire, for his circle of friends who were eager to listen—

Kathāpavaṇtisundarī spoke thus: "By means of the effort undertaken at your request, I have beheld a most wonderful and exceedingly great narrative, culminating in the attainment of the power to move through the sky by a lotus born from the ocean, through the grace of the lotus-eyed Lord—the sole auspiciousness of the three worlds, the destroyer of Madhu, Naraka, Ariṣṭa, Keśin, and Kaṃsa, and who is expert in the rite of removing the fears of his devotees. If you have curiosity, I shall tell it; let it be heard:"

[The people there were] those whose castes and stages of life were nearby, intermingled, and distinct; who were not visible to the sun; who possessed beautiful women; whose households were heavy with their own undertakings; whose houses were lofty with limbs joined in the theater-ring (*raṅgodraṅga*); whose people were simple yet possessed the grace of actors; who were hospitable to all people; who were noble and fearless; who were free from the occurrence of mental anguish and physical disease; who had elephants that made the ground firm and green with grass; who were fragrant with the spreading scent of lotuses; and whose river currents were navigable.

The regions were made beautiful by fields of barley and *ṣaṣṭika* rice; there were plots of land for *śāli* rice, sections of wheat-fields, and vast stretches of sesame grounds. There were excellent tracts of *kaulastha* (black gram), lands devoted to esteemed *māṣya* beans, fertile soils for *udgīna* (lentils), and choice plots for *māsurī* (peas). Abounding in *mañjīraka* (a type of bean) and *pariṣa* (?), they were rich in *rājamāṣa* (kidney beans), variegated with clusters of *niṣpāva* (mung beans), and surrounded by heaps of white mustard seeds. In some places, the ground was reddened by the blooming buds of mature safflower.

The country named Magadha is characterized by villages where the inhabitants rear cattle, goats, sheep, and buffaloes; where various streets are carpeted with young grass cut for fodder; where rows of forests provide timber for the construction of palaces and other buildings; where the boundaries of the villages are dominated by trees bearing abundant fruit; where there are circles of vast lakes adorned with cranes and swans; where there are pleasant rows of water-stalls providing cool shade; where the ground is smooth and naturally beautiful; where charming rest-houses are established near every well; and which is garlanded with sacred groves.

In that realm, even the name of treason against the king was not heard; even a report of calamities did not circulate; even a mention of strife was not made; even the memory of a commoner’s wife [being unfaithful] did not arise; even a thought of theft did not exist; and even the occasion for insults never occurred. Furthermore, in that place, mud served only as a benefit to mud—for indeed, there was no other kind of mud, such as saffron-paste, upon the slopes of the breasts of women; there were only stones on the surfaces of the pleasure-mountains.

The thorn was seen only in the stalks of lotuses, yet it was seen again in the embraces of beloved women. A flight [of steps] was obtained only for ascending the pinnacles of palaces. This [time] was difficult to discern, and as the water-birds sported nearby, it seemed as if—out of fear of the exertion required to leap over thousands of closely packed mountain peaks filled with wealth and grain—the [city] was unable to admit them; and as if driven away by the continuous sound of drums raised for auspicious occasions, it was mocked with loud laughter by thousands of lakes blooming with white and red lotuses.

I suspect that in this place, the Ocean of Milk has hidden itself for fear of being drunk by the one born from a jar (Agastya); the mountain ranges have concealed themselves, having become like celestial abodes out of fear of the thunderbolt of Hari; the nectar-essence has been cast by the Moon into the sugarcanes of Puṇḍra out of dread of the pollution caused by the infusion of poison from Rāhu’s mouth; and the circles of clouds, having abandoned the path of the wind, cling to the earth under the guise of groves of trees, as if terrified by the agitation of a powerful gale.

And for such a person as he, this was the ornament of the Magadha realm, the means for the earth to conquer heaven, the cause of the disparagement of the bliss of liberation, and the very life-breath of living beings. It was encircled by a great moat—like the Ganges, turbid with waves, provoked by the passion of its own enjoyment—and it stood within high, white ramparts. Because it was situated in the midst of those walls, it appeared as if it had been carved out from the lunar orb and cast down for the sake of providing beauty to the young and lovely women of the city; and because its reflection was cast into the interior of the floor of pure jewels, [it seemed as if it were the moon itself].

It was adorned with great palaces made of choice timber, which, with their wings of spreading nets of jewel-rays, seemed like Garuḍas entering the netherworld (rasātala) for the purpose of uprooting the serpents; it was illuminated by jeweled archways set within moats, which resembled the vine-like arms of the city goddesses raised up out of curiosity at the sight of the rising ocean; and it was endowed with market-streets that, encircled by the luster of many emerging gems, were like the girdle-strings of Lakṣmī, broken during her impetuous dalliance in love.

It was resplendent with lakes whose waters were indistinguishable from the net of rays of their jeweled pavements, appearing like portions of the sky gathered together—where the darkness was pierced by the light of emerging clusters of stars, and the glow of twilight was intensified by rows of lotuses shaken by flocks of intoxicated swans. It bore the marks of sovereignty over the entire city, like turbans fixed upon its head, in the form of the many-colored, pale-pink cloths of flower-pollen from the groves; as if to ward off the pride of ascending to the heights of the planets.

There was a city named Kusumapura, which, with its fluttering banners raised high, appeared like the single flower upon the creeper of the entire splendor of Jambudvīpa; it resembled an ocean from which the essence of all jewels of men and women had arisen.

There, the divine sun-god, though his path is obstructed by thousands of cloud-scraping palaces, appears as if still possessing the luster of childhood even while stationed in the midst of the sky—his body reddened by the surging streams of light from rising ruby jewels, as if burning with indignation. Furthermore, the earth, the supporter of all beings, though exhausted by the terrible blows of the massed waves of the seven oceans, never wavers, as if out of respect for its essential strength.

And while dwelling there, he honors the city of Alakā with thousands of lords of wealth, mocks the abode of the gods with his imperishable treasures, and surpasses Bhogavatī with his infinite serpents.

In that city, the citizens were not drinkers of honey-wine yet were fond of giving gifts; they did not follow after the emaciated (or fire) yet were manifestly prosperous; they were not of fickle enjoyment yet were possessors of wealth; they were not talkative yet were addicted to the *Bṛhatkathā*; they were not reservoirs of water yet were attached to building bridges; they were not touched by intoxication yet were insatiable for the flavor of the *Kādambarī*; they were not enemies of the gods yet were devoted to the vision of poetry; they were not dull-sighted yet possessed keen insight, and they were renowned for their great learning and were knowers of the *Rāmāyaṇa*.

There dwell those who are ignorant of the misfortunes that befell Rāma, yet who have seen the Mahābhārata and are bewildered by the news of Bhīma’s blows with his mace; those who are experts in logic (*pramāṇa*) yet are skilled in the practice of sophistry (*chala*); they inhabit a place that is the sole abode of all contradictions, yet they practice meritorious deeds that are delightful for their lack of conflict.
And in that lake, on its beautiful bank, the Mandākinī descended from the world of the gods in part for the purpose of the consecration of the venerable Kātyāyana, the son of Fire (*Hutāśana*).

And in that city of many wonders, where the *saptacchada* tree possesses the pale hue of the cheeks of longing women and the *madhūka* flower [shines], there is the city of Puṣpapura. It is like Puṣkara, possessing infinite enjoyments; like Indra, the rider of the best of steeds, it is the abode of the virtuous and has severed the wings of those who have committed transgressions; like Kubera, the lord of treasures, it is the refuge of meritorious beings; like the Sun, it is the place of rising for the feet of the great-splendored Ṛṣis worthy of worship; and like the Wind, it is the destruction of dense [darkness] and the complete exhaustion [of all things].

There was a king named Rājahaṃsa, who destroyed the transformations of the dust of passion (*parāga-vikāra*); like the Himālaya, he possessed unbroken wings [or: an unimpaired sovereignty] over the ocean of jewels; like Śeṣa, he supported the entire world while being the abode of serpents [or: the refuge of those seeking enjoyment]; like the flower-armed god of love, he possessed a radiant pleasure-grove [or: a brilliant army] whose splendor surpassed that of Phālguna (Arjuna) through his own virtues; and like a *cakravāka* bird, he dwelt with his lotus-abiding consort, moving solely within his own circle [of dominion]. He was the sole royal swan sporting in the lake of the world, which was adorned by the white water-lilies of his own fame.

The people regarded him as if he were the God of Love reborn, having surpassed the superhuman perfection of Yama’s form and his unbearable prowess, and having extinguished the heat born from the lingering flames of the fire from Śiva’s eye; and they saw that he constantly bore a pair of mountain-like arms, which had taken upon themselves the burden of the world to humble the pride of the exultant Dāmodara when he lifted Mount Govardhana, and which surpassed even the majesty of Mount Meru.

And he, with the radiance of his eyes, lips, hands, and feet—which were as pale-red as fresh *bandhūjīva* flowers—seemed to torment the groves of lotuses, which had been forgotten by Lakṣmī once she had attained the bliss of dwelling upon his own chest.

And his staff-like arm—darkened by the mass of his sword-blade and clad in armor—having been employed in splitting the high frontal globes of rutting elephants, in shattering the broad door-panel chests of circles of great warriors, in turning back the surging waves of the ocean of destruction caused by the force of excellent horses, and in breaking the diamond-cages of multitudes of chariots, became as if thirsting from that exertion; thus, upon the battlefields, he drank up the entire milk-ocean of his enemy’s fame, which was white with the pollen of *ketakī* buds.

He who, though possessing the four castes properly established, made the entire world white—even as the milk-ocean at the time of universal dissolution; from whom the seekers received all their wealth, his enemies received fearlessness, his senses defeat, the Kali age humiliation, Sarasvatī his mouth, the circle of friends his heart, and even his entire body was marked with the characteristics of a Great Man, while the skin of his neck was scarred by the rubbing of the ropes of the multitude of rutting elephants.

I believe that even when they were in the throes of extreme agony, the trees of the coastal forest did not forget the monkeys—the elephants of the rutting season whose thick roots were shattered by their temples, whose sprouts and young shoots were severed by their massive trunks, who crushed flower buds and tender leaves, whose humming was joined by the rustling of creepers as they were torn apart, and who, in their frenzy to dispel the heat of intoxication, broke the trees with blows from their heads, causing them to shriek as their trunks were shattered. Even in such a state of intense suffering, those trees could not forget the monkeys.

And he, the son of Vena—who was proud of having attained the status of a *gotra* from the very earth (*bhūmivala*)—was of exalted intent; with qualities as cooling as the rays of the moon, he made the heavens, the earth, and all the quarters fragrant... [There was] no transgression of the *ācāryas*, nor any confusion of castes (*varṇavyatikara*), nor any confusion of castes, nor any suspicion of royal impropriety, nor any suspicion of royal impropriety, nor any thought of destruction, nor any thought of destruction among the subjects.
And while he reigned, even Indra (*pākaśāsana*) was unable to bring about drought, much less others.

And that king [was endowed with] a tongue like Rāhu swallowing the entire circle of kings; a streak of smoke from the mass of fire born of his fury; a flow of ichor from the temples of elephants intoxicated by pride; a line of forest on the shore shattered by the impetuous assault of rival forces; a swarm of bees for sucking the honey of his enemies' lives; a serpent-maiden for guarding the world’s great treasure; the dark hue of the first emergence of the *kālakūṭa* poison during the churning of the nectar of battle; and a mass of clouds resting upon the mountain peaks of his own arms.

Having adorned the entire earth—whose girdle is the four oceans, whose mountain slopes are thick with forests, whose tresses are the wild woods laden with every kind of flower, and who wears the dark blue sky as her upper garment—just as the messenger of Kāma might adorn the Fortune of Victory when she goes to meet her lover; and having done so by means of a sword-streak as terrifying in form as the horns of Yama’s buffalo, he rested among his ancestors and grandfathers, who were full of affection for him and possessed intellects refined by the expansion of all the sciences.

Among those who possessed mastery through immersion in all arts; who were goads for restraining the female elephant of the wicked royal fortune; who were skilled in the application of the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*); who, like the feet of the Great Boar, caused the world of serpents to tremble at their tread; who, like waves, were the source of a multitude of jewels of excellent virtues; who, like the staff-like arms of the slayer of Nisumbha, supported the circle of kings that had become the cause for seizing the jewel of sovereignty; and who, like the tusks of Airāvata, were of great stature.

Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his chief ministers named Sumati, Sumitra, Suśruta, and Sumantra, he—possessing a beauty like that of the god of love—delighted in the inner apartments, following the path of passion as taught by his fresh youth.

And that monarch had [a daughter] who was like a goddess to the entire host of women; she surpassed even a girdle of jasmine flower-garlands with her mutually corresponding delicacies of limb, and possessed a mind endowed with an incomparable softness. Thus, with her eyebrows alone she was a bow, with the luster of her face alone the moon, and with her very breath she surpassed the Malaya breeze in its fragrant scent, while shaking it as it were.

With her lower lip, which was like the red glow of the morning sun, she seemed to coil up the mass of darkness out of fear; and with her naturally fragrant breath, which kissed her broad hips adorned with a jeweled girdle like a cluster of fresh clouds, she displayed, as it were, a stormy day for her husband’s secret tryst—a storm that was like the trunk of the elephant of Love. She shone with her vine-like arms, tender as a wreath of *śirīṣa* flowers and resembling two lotus stalks drawn forth by force from the beauty of the white lotuses of her moon-like face.

She was radiant with two breasts that seemed as if they had been fashioned from the very essence of all the beauty distributed throughout her entire body; which appeared like the repositories of the pride of the God of Love after he had been consumed by Śiva; which served such a purpose as to be worthy of being plastered with sandalwood paste and white lime by the Creator; which were like two jars for the dwelling of passion; which seemed filled to the brim with the overflowing sweetness of a pure mind; and which, being exceedingly heavy, shared the same nature as the massive, firm, and swelling frontal globes of an elephant.

She possessed a waist-stalk that was firm and unyielding; she shone with a pair of shanks that had become exceedingly slender, as if they were the very remnants of her body employed to steady her thighs which were exhausted by the weight of her exceedingly full hips; and she seemed to drink up the entire mass of luster from the groves of lotuses in all the worlds with the rays of the ten moons of her toenails, as if those rays were smeared with the passion ignited in the hearts of her beloveds when struck during a lovers’ quarrel.

Under the guise of their stainless passion and loveliness, which were constantly nourished by their rosy hue, she seemed to gather from the red *aśoka* trees clusters of blossoms to bestow as gifts during the beatings that fulfilled her longing; she bore, as it were, the delicacy of all sprouts granted by the hand of Spring, who had been vanquished by the fragrance of her lotus-face; and with the pair of her lotus-feet, she made the Sindhu women appear as if born far away, while her two banner-like eyebrows were composed of waves, her pair of eyes of blue lotuses, and her lips of red lotuses.

She was composed of white water-lilies in her slight smiles, of fragrant lotuses in her breaths, of nectar in her speech, of serenity in her mind, of ruddy geese in her breasts, of whirlpools in the hollow of her navel, of sandbanks upon the slopes of her hips, and of lotuses on the soles of her feet; she was like the Mandākinī descended from the abode of the gods for the enjoyment of the royal swan, as if fashioned by assigning the five qualities of grace, artistry, loveliness, passion, and cleverness to the five elements.

Like Prajāpati, she was delightful with deep, resonant laughter like the thundering of the rainy season; like autumn, she bore the splendor of lakes; like the state of winter, she was adorned with garlands of hanging pearl necklaces; like the beauty of the cool season, she possessed fresh jasmine flowers; like the power of spring, her slender body was graced by the play of beautiful vine-like arms; like the perfection of dharma, her lower lip was soft and pale-red; by virtue of her conduct being consistent with all seasons, she possessed the very nature of the Nandana grove; she was the foremost among all the women of the harem, like Rati to Kandarpa, or like Śacī.

There was a queen named Vasumatī, who was dearer even than life to her husband; she was like Śailasutā to Śatamakha, like Lakṣmī to Puṣkarekṣaṇa, like Buddhi to Dhanādhipa, like Devasenā to Senāpati, like Gaurī to Pracetas, and like Rohiṇī to Budhabhavana, or Arundhatī to Śaktiguṛu.

And while that sovereign was enjoying the pleasure born of union with that lotus-eyed woman—and with others as well who possessed every art—as they engaged in various unopposed pursuits of dharma and artha, the season of the Goddess of Flowers arrived, as if to consecrate him for the conquest of the quarters, bringing with it thousands of jars in the form of flower-buds filled with floods of honey from trees and creepers. The frosty water melted away, as if shaken off by the force of the descent of spring.

When the sun-garment had departed, disregarding even the southern quarter, the northern direction attained a supreme beauty as if it were a bridegroom approaching his bride. As the day-maker was absent, the Malaya breeze, scorching the weary travelers, crept forth very slowly like the long-drawn sigh of the quarter that had been seized by him.

When the three worlds were being set ablaze—like a single dwelling—by the fire of Love fanned by the Malaya breezes, the host of lovers, seeking a refuge capable of counteracting that burning, sought shelter in the jar-like breasts of the assembly of beloved women. As if desiring to make the hearts of those away from home drink from the flood of warm tears arising in their minds from the presence of their lovers, the mass of Love’s flames discharged arrows that blazed with intense heat.

Upon the vital parts of the amorous women—who were reclining on beds of fresh shoots spread beneath the mango trees—the spreading sweetness of the honey fell like a sprinkling of caustic salt upon their bodies already wounded by love, as it issued forth from the hearts of buds torn open by the claws and beaks of cuckoos.

And at that time, while the red kurava, aśoka, śalmali, palāśa, vādibhadra, pomegranate, and japārāja flowers were blooming—acting like the surging waves of the ocean of passion that was overflowing to submerge the entire world; appearing like the flickering tongues of flame from the lustration fire of the camp of the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāma), who is skilled in the rites of the battle of love; serving as the upper garments of fine silk for the royal ladies; and possessing the splendor of the gathered digits of the moon brought forth by all the groves, which had been incited to anger by the lotus-feet of beautiful women striking the aśoka trees.

In these [forests], where the firm bonds of white bears—the bodies of various trees in the yakṣa groves—were shattered by the continuous flight of a multitude of stone-tipped arrows; where the Karīra blossoms and filaments were smiling and radiant with the ashes from the mass of the fire of heart-born passion, extinguished by the flames of the eyes kindled by the wrath of the Destroyer of Andhaka; and where there were white Sinduvāra, Vakula, Sāla, Tilaka, Navamālikā, and other trees, as if they were the yellow garments of Lalitamādhava.

In groves of *madhūka* trees, amidst clusters of *diṣṭivṛddhi*, *piṣṭātaka*, *prakaraiḥ*, *sudantī*, *kaṭa*, *kiṅkirāta*, *karṇikāra*, and *campaka* flowers, that elephant—surrounded by beautiful women like rutting female elephants—plunged into pleasure gardens whose expanses were blinded by the darkness of swarms of bees intoxicated with honey.

And there he beheld circles of drinking assemblies where pairs of *cakravāka* birds were distressed by the arrival of twilight—the flush upon the cheeks of amorous women intoxicated with wine; where clouds, red as liquid lac, hung like foliage as if out of curiosity or desire to gaze at the beautiful interior of the celestial realm; where the sky remained fixed as if in wonder, and where the birds’ own heroic exploits were being sung amidst the swirling of their dark, cloud-like locks of hair.

The ornaments of the women of the inner apartments—consisting of tinkling jeweled girdles, anklets, and armlets—were set against canopies of tender flowers and sprouts swaying on mechanical swings; their silken lower garments were shimmering within the interiors of vine-cottages where the wind entered through trembling shoots, while the workmanship of their fine cloths was animated by the lattice of rays from their jeweled girdles mingled with the light from the gems of their fingernails.

Partaking of amorous delights that were like those of a royal bull—delights in which the slopes of the breasts were moistened with perspiration from fatigue as they released camphor powder amidst the radiance of swaying pearl necklaces; in which tender, playful kisses were exchanged to restore the broken connection of lips parted by sweet disputes; in which the garlands of blue lily eyes belonging to the beloveds served as substitutes for throat-ropes crushed during firm embraces; in which the force of the battle of love was intensified by the melodies of charming birds; and in which the excellence of passion was brought about by a perfect balance of mutual desire—the king experienced the seasonal splendor of the pleasure groves.

And when the months of Caitra and Vaiśākha had arrived—variegated with diverse flowers; possessing a realm of Daityas as it were, consisting of the pure month of Śukra; possessing a realm of Yama as it were, with the world daily rendered resonant by the rays of the sun turning crimson; possessing a realm of Rākṣasas as it were, with the waters of the low-lying rivers being leaped over by swift monkeys; possessing a realm of Kiṃpuruṣas as it were, with Kiṃpuruṣas intoxicated by passion and the exuberance of the forest thick with the heavy heat of groves of trees; and like a realm of Manmatha...

Desiring to experience the fierce heat that blocked the celestial abodes with circles of leaves whirled by the hosts of Maruts, he entered the lakes together with women whose bellies were like the palms of their hands—lakes where blooming lotuses and red water-lilies seemed as if set ablaze by the fire of Kandarpa who had entered out of fear of the summer heat; lakes where the coolness of the water beneath lattices provided a refreshing surface, resembling cool winter dungeons for one fallen into the terrible summer season, and whose depths were darkened by the dense black shadows of swarms of bees.

As the affectionate beloved friends entered, the ponds rose up to meet them, embracing them firmly with the hands of their outstretched waves; meanwhile, the bees—held back by the lotuses, which were like fortresses in the water acting as a rampart against the onslaught of powerful adversaries, yet now raising their stalks as if by force—fell with a soft sound upon the faces of the beautiful women, those very enemies of the lotuses.

The waves of the multitude of boats, which were eager for the means of their own immersion and were intent on casting men into the water, surged upward like the side-long glances of long-lashed women lying within the womb of the Jambū river, desiring to see the confusion. The exceedingly restless ripples of the lake, kissing the bimba-like lips of the king’s ladies, did not recognize them; rather, sporting with the minds of those whose pride was being crushed, they carried away the spreading passion.

The eyes of the passionate women became exceedingly restless, as if out of anger at the blue water-lilies standing face-to-face before them. Even when the waters were turbid from being churned by the circle of breasts upon the high mounds of the cakora-eyed women, their innate nature—that is, their essence as water—was proclaimed without words. Disregarding even the elders, the force of the water struck down the heavy burdens of the broad hips of the fair-thighed women; for there is no discernment in that which is agitated. The clusters of girdles, observing silence within the midst of the water, justified their status as "virtues" (guṇatva) only in that sense.

Even though they were devoid of red lac, their bud-like lips surpassed groves of red water-lilies by their very color; for these lips had repeatedly rendered assistance in the victory over rivals during the battles of love that had arisen there.

And so, while the excellent pavements were being covered with water poured from the mouths of beautiful young women, and while the riddles (*prahelikā*)—in which the waves were scattered and the bees were made to sport by the sprinkling of water from cupped hands—were being played, the Lord of the Earth, like the Great Boar (*Mahāvarāha*), moved forward carrying the Goddess Earth upon his chest as she was utterly agitated; he sported in the waters up to the region of his hair and shoulders through a water-game that followed eight paths, distinguished by the various activities of diving, leaping, and searching for objects fallen on the ground during their movements in the shallow riverbeds.

And while he was delighting in the primary musical instruments—played with a voice distinguished by clarity, faltering tones, and depth, characterized as both restrained and unrestrained, and rendered charming through many sweet modulations—certain beautiful women sprinkled him with streams of water released from the hollows of their bud-like hands, as if with the liquid essence of the sprouts of their affection. Others drenched him with streams of saffron water poured from the mouths of conch-shells and horn-tips, which were like the crest-flames of the fire-breathing serpent of the God of Love.

Others, inflamed by the passion of amorous play manifested through their rivals, impetuously dragged him toward themselves with the side-glances from their reddened eyes—glances known as "crooked" (jihya)—which were like rushing streams of safflower-dyed water. Others, whose movements were as difficult to discern as those of darkness upon the water, approached him by resting their lotus-hands against his palms; their prostrations and supplications could only be inferred from the intensity of their touch, as they performed these humble acts at his feet by mere chance.

The king, agitating the proud, delivering the bewildered, consoling the frightened, appeasing the angry, encouraging the joyful, and restraining those who had set out, made the hopes of some bear fruit like a creeper with its blossoms; he brought about the ruby-like jewels of some; he snatched away the silken garments of others with an imperceptible gait, as if they were intense longing; and under the pretext of shaking off the pollen of lotuses, he rendered the pupils of some women’s eyes exceedingly smooth, copper-hued, and free from collyrium.

Kissing their eyes and bellies, he pressed his nails—like invisible arrows of Kāma—into the breasts of some, as if they were the very abodes of desire. Clad in a *caṇḍātaka* garment, possessed of dense grace, with his eyes directed toward the outer corners of his brows and his hair tied back, his limbs drenched in a flood of saffron-red dye, he terrified the entire flock of royal swans. Having sported there as if from a lake after a battle, he departed together with his beloveds, who were like the goddesses of victory, and went forth.

Having performed the auspicious rites of the appropriate ablution immediately after his bath, and having worshipped the sun according to the prescribed rules, having paid homage to the Lord Agni, and having propitiated the God who is the son of Devakī, he—along with his friends, having anointed himself with fragrant sandalwood paste following the [king’s] command, and [using] food prepared by skillful cooks...

Having established his fortitude with food that was refined through thirteen types of processing—namely, cleansing, preparation, washing, solidifying, softening, cooling, clarifying, oiling, coloring, and the addition of fragrance—which were accomplished by a hexad of operations involving various sub-varieties; and having partaken of a drink whose flavor surpassed nectar, which emitted a sharp, pale-red fragrance, whose presence was inferred by its touch, and which was suited to his own person, he rinsed his mouth with a wick of incense smoke.

Having consumed pieces of betel nut that exhaled the intense fragrance of *pārijāta* flowers, along with a roll of betel leaf as pale as the cheek of Indra’s bride, and conch powder as pink as the interior of a ripe *pāṭalī* bud—these three substances being bitter, pungent, and clean, yet warming from the friction and lightening the mouth—he, his lips reddened by the betel, proceeded along a path of jeweled mosaic to the decorated dining pavilion, where he sat upon a very soft, white linen seat provided with a Chinese silk cushion.

Having taken a moment’s rest upon the surface of a couch provided with a footstool, its legs adorned with excellent jewels and set upon golden slippers of affection, fragrant with flower-scented garments, and equipped with a nearby golden water-vessel; and having dismissed his beloved vassals who had entertained him for a long time with varied conversation; he proceeded gradually as the chariot—driven swiftly, trailing a luster like the filaments of a *kadamba* bud, and longing to kiss the face of twilight—moved forward.

He spent his time in the palace courtyards, which were cooled by the sprinkling of sandalwood water and adorned with offerings of blooming jasmine; these courtyards were made lovely by the women, who were as beautiful as hanging upper garments of long garlands of unfolding jasmine buds, and who were delightful in their attire that wafted a fragrance secluded from worldly pleasures, as if they were the very light of the jewel-peak that dispels the darkness of the fading heat. Accompanied by his dear, clever friends, he passed the evening in musical gatherings and song-circles. For the remaining two watches of the night, he spent his time under the influence of the hearts of those women who spoke so sweetly and intoxicatingly.

And thus, when summer had concluded, the clouds—having stolen the splendor of every *śirīṣa* flower, having exhausted the luster of the *karañja* blossoms, having manifested the command to destroy the *jambhakā* demons who had begun to mock the radiant orb of the moon, possessing curved and tender lightning-flashes, perfuming the quarters with the fragrance of opening *kuṭaca* buds, making the sky fragrant with *kesara* pollen, and resounding with the cries of peacocks [and cranes] against the rainbow... [and the moonlight]—[appeared].

In that vast expanse, the *upaguptā* flowers were as numerous as the sun, the cows, the hosts of serpents, and the lunar days; the *dṛptātakas* were like garlands; the well-born *jāti* flowers bloomed in abundance; the *mudita* and charming *yūthikā* vines rained down their blossoms; the new *vārṣikī* creepers and the buds of the graceful *lāṅgalī* swayed; the rows of pure *jambū* trees were laden with fruit; the bees hummed loudly as they kissed the blooming *kadamba* flowers; gentle breezes dripped with droplets of water; and the deep night was made resonant by the drum-like croaking of frogs.

The nights were distinguished by the breaking of the year’s gloomy days; the beloveds of the swift-minded *manoharis* (lovers) hastened to their dwellings; the earth was embraced by flocks of cranes spreading out; the bonds of the *śilindhra* trees were loosened; the clouds thundered with deep, resonant roars like the breasts of women; the exhaustion within the hearts of the *ketakī* flowers was relieved by the sprinkling of fresh rain; the forest floors became dark-green meadows fit for walking; the peacocks indulged in the playful grace of their dances; the families of serpents sank down in relief; and hundreds of rivers surged with waves of water that breached their banks.

The days of the rainy season appeared as if composed of pure bliss, bestowing the happiness of the yogic sleep (yoganidrā) brought about by the water poured upon the demons; they were like a fresh youth, possessing a sapful body grown from the charcoal of the earth—the hips of the forest-land girdled with the coral-belt of the rows of clouds protecting Indra—and granting the gift of tranquility.

And during those rainy seasons—which served as cooling pavilions for the Fortune of the Three Worlds weary from the heat of summer—there wandered deer and dancing peacocks, accompanied by beautiful women who had assumed the graceful attire and charms of Kirāta maidens; they wore garlands of *kuṭaja* buds, long girdles of *kadamba* flowers, their ears adorned with *ketaka* and *barha* feathers, their foreheads marked with the auspicious sign of intoxication, their sprout-like feet stained with moist red ochre, and their hair coiled in curls.

He sported upon pleasure-mountains where the *nīpa* trees were bursting into bloom, where waterfalls were roaring, and where the surfaces of jeweled stones were washed by showers of rain. And, accompanied solely by his intoxicated beloved, he took delight in the jeweled bowers, which were warmed by the diffusion of the finest black aloe incense and whose paths were covered by the creepers, shrubs, and clusters of seasonal trees and vines, while his passion was doubled by the sound of the falling rain.

In circular, square, and oblong pleasure-pools within jeweled pavilions, which were filled with pleasantly warm water and adorned with hundreds of golden lotuses, he sported playfully like the summer heat alongside women whose gait was like that of fragrant elephants.

And as the nights grew dense, while the garments of those women whose fortitude was shaken by the god of love were distressed by the offense of the driving rain during their secret trysts on cloudy days, and as they were heard rehearsing with care the ornaments for their bodies and their skill in deceiving their kinsmen under various pretexts, he—placing within himself the pride of being a man—proposed to assist the mass of darkness as it approached, veiled in its playful blue silk garment, as if out of sheer joy.

In some places, the path was revealed by the successive touch of palace walls; in others, the foreground was illuminated by streaks of flickering lightning; in others, there were moments of total confusion caused by deep thundering like the beat of city drums; and in others, the courtyards of the mansions and the trunks of trees along the paths were embraced in a state of panic by the downpour of a thick shower of arrows from the first clouds that seemed to seize the very sky as if they were enemies—[all this] while he proceeded with compassion toward those who, impelled by passion, had rashly undertaken the adventure of going to meet their lovers.
She performed in many ways the dance of amorous play, a flavor consisting of extraordinary courtesy, consolation, and dalliance, characterized by exceedingly noble and agitated charms.

He emerged from the cage of clouds as if from the depths of a prison cell, into a world that had once again begun to breathe; while the interiors of the great lakes and clouds, their waters exhausted, seemed like faces pained by indignation at being long confined; and while the *stokaka* birds were mute, having ceased their own clamor, and the clouds—having shed the garments of their water—seemed to have vanished somewhere out of shame.

When the lakes of the atmosphere—whose floods of rainwater had been sucked up by the great clouds of the thundering ocean—were becoming visible like emerald pavilions; when the quarters of the sky, dark as the throat of Śiva, were tinged with the hue of Indra’s bow; when the peacock feathers, once brilliant as the rainbow, were withered; and when the lotus groves began to expand in every direction as if to dispel the fear of the clouds, which now resembled harmless serpents emerging from the clouds and flying through the air with total fearlessness; ... [the text continues].

While the days and nights for travelers were passing; while the rivers—turbid throughout the entire year, their waters once swollen by the downpour of rain from many directions—were now gradually approaching the ocean with very slow currents, as if out of shame for their long persistence in agitation, their garlands of foam thinning; while the autumn season, skilled and proficient in the scent of rut that binds bees to intoxication, was rending the hearts of the prideful elephants of the god of love in the *saptaparṇa* forests, [the trees] whose forms were white with blossoms...

While rows of swans were falling everywhere like the flights of arrows from the flower-arrowed god, piercing the hearts of those separated from their lovers; while the forest glades—whose beauty was enhanced by the fresh pollen of the *āsana* trees, which resembled golden dust scattered by the earth’s grace—became like quivers for the mind-born Cupid; and while [the birds], fearing a depletion of their own [store], avoided the earth as if it were the quiver of the Mind-Born, they captured the sweet whistling sounds repeatedly uttered by their own mouths.
