While the female guardians of the *kalama* rice were permitted to break off the ears of grain by the gentle rustling sounds fearlessly emitted by rows of parrots; while the lord of the luminaries, his brilliance redoubled, was wielding a dark sword-edge that caused the entire host of lovers to tremble; and while the night-lilies were laughing—as it were out of pride—filled with the sweet humming of intoxicated female bees upon seeing the masses of clouds, which had ceased their thundering, were taking refuge in the shadows of the moonbeams, and were as light as the cotton of the *śalmali* tree; [The original text continues here.]

In the clear autumn, while the rows of mansions—cool with sprays of frost-water and white as sandalwood paste brightened by the rays of the autumnal moon, and smiling with offerings of blooming *śephālikā* flowers—were in full bloom; and while the wine was sweet as honey and the jeweled goblets were filled with the influence of the month of Mādhava, the charming young women stood for a moment without desire to drink, thinking the cups were empty because they were reddened by the shadows of their own palms resting upon them as supports. They were then restrained by their laughing lovers.

As if with the desire to kiss the lotus-face of the intoxicated woman, the moon, in the form of a reflection, fell upon the rows of waves. Having been drunk by those fair-faced women along with the wine, the moons reflected in their mirrors seemed to weep out of intoxication under the pretext of providing flavor. Thus, although they were so affectionate, the stars—the pupils of their eyes—did not refuse to reflect the image of the Moon within themselves; nor did the moon-like faces of those fawn-eyed women, from which drops of perspiration were trickling, reject his presence.

For whom, indeed, do pleasures not exist on account of women? Even that Moon, following them as they fell, sank right there; yet he was unable to draw them back. For even by those lotus-faces of the broad-hipped women, which were slow-moving due to their transition between other stars, that friend of the night-lotuses was eclipsed. Indeed, the sin of one who violates the Guru’s bed must bear fruit in that very body.

The eyebrows of the fair-browed women, taking on the form of darkness as if they had entered into a state of defeat by the sea-monster [of the moon], began to dance. Even a man of great fortitude might be moved by joy at the misfortune of an enemy; how much more so those who are naturally fickle? Upon the cheeks of the lovely-faced women, a smile emerged like the rising of the moon—a nectar-like smile that, like the moon’s ascent, causes the groves of night-lilies to bloom and intoxicates all.

Even the sweet-voiced female bees, intoxicated with honey and piteously lamenting as they cast their gaze—mistaking the moon-marked face for their long-lost mates—into the dancing ripples of the wine’s waves, likewise mourned.

And being awakened by their laughing lovers through the application of knowledge of reality, those women—whose deer-marked moons (faces) were already observed—covered even him with the mass of radiance from their own eyes, which mocked a forest of blossoming *bandhujīva* flowers; thus, with their curved brows and hips, they deceived us deceivers by placing blue-lotus earrings upon the shoulders of their beloveds, so that no deer-marks could be seen there either.

He too, his cheeks reddened by drinking mouthfuls of wine from the lotus-faces of his beloveds—his cheeks appearing like silver lotuses clinging to his temples—bore the stainless reflection of the moon upon his ear-ornaments as they swayed like chowries; with a body white as sandalwood paste, he sported like Indra’s elephant in the waters of the Mandākinī amidst a lattice of moonlight.

And as his fatigue was dispelled by drops of nectar sprinkled from the hollowed palms of the deer-eyed women, he spread through the night the sounds of his own limbs, which were resonant with the soft jingling of his bracelets, the charming tinkling of his anklets, and the girdle-string, while his chest thundered like a cloud.

Thereafter, as if to avoid the fault of redundancy with his own lotus-like hands and face, he withdrew the forests of day-lotuses; crushing the groves of blue water-lilies that were arrogant in their lingering under the radiance of the women’s eyes; dispersing the masses of clouds—which had been melted by the fierce heat of autumn and turned to water—under the guise of scattering frost-sprays; bestowing dignity upon all medicinal herbs as if they were now held in the grasp of the moon; and concealing the forest trees that were perpetually embraced by fire, as if out of enmity toward the mist.

As if out of wrath at the growth of his enemy—the lotus-born Brahmā—he caused the waters to steam with vapor; as if desiring to favor those with wings [the mountains], he caused the naturally cool pearl-ornaments to rest; as if initiated in the fierce task of subduing the plunderers who had prematurely ravaged the heavy fruit-bearing groves of the entire world of living beings, he caused the circles of kings to contract; and in the sky, he obstructed the sun—that thief boastfully intent on forcibly seizing the essence of the three worlds—while increasing the affection of those who bowed before him.

The winter season unfolded, naturally cool, bringing forth the crackling heat of the day’s end, its limits over which all living beings were restrained, and wherein almost all worldly undertakings were brought to a close.

At that time also, within great palatial interiors—which, as if to dispel the heat induced by the youth of the nearby courtesans, were filled with thousands of iron braziers whose sandalwood fuel was being devoured by tongues of flame and which, having dispersed the masses of snow, seemed to have caused the vault of heaven to cower in fear of their excessive weight; and which, due to the darkness of the heavy clouds of smoke from incessantly burning black agallochum, appeared as if they had become unable to behold the faces of the women of the quarters who were now soiled—[the sun shone].

Surrounded by his attendants—who, with their hands holding lamps fragrant from the pouring of scented oil, sought out the winter nights as they were being shortened by the closing of the world, while the rows of palaces looked on through windows wide and open—he, dressed in attire suited to the season, ascended a costly couch together with his queen.

And while he was being covered, as it were, by the mass of light from the half-glance of his beloved—possessing a luster red, blue, and white like a variegated cloak; while the sprout of his lower lip was being anointed with a passion appropriate for that moment, resembling a saffron unguent that was an outburst of the fire of love swelling within his heart; and while his ear-ornament was being fashioned, as it were, by the clusters of rays of his smile consisting of jasmine buds, which served as the secret whispers of love to be told at the ear—he waited for a moment.

When the female attendants had departed, having provided the necessary implements for the festival of love through their amorous conversations, he—his passion intensified by the commencement of sweet kisses, his teeth falling helplessly and visibly upon her, his play of sharp nails employed in the struggle to seize her jewel-like lower lip which was throbbing with pain and bitten by him, and his grasp doubled in its pressure—acted with graceful charm.

Threatened by the knitting of eyebrows playful as a stone blocking the path of her garment—a garment obstructed by the exit of her deceptive departure; with the opposition of her breasts hidden by the intense confusion ignited by the disarray of her loosened tresses during the impetuous seizing of her hair; deepened by the pressure of his heavy hips which intensified her cries as she moved on the scales; and with the slender stalk of her waist trembling from the dense pain of his elevated bosom.

He engaged in an exceedingly extensive act of love, which was rendered charming by the playful confusion of unrefined imaginings; it was characterized by the tremulous eyes of the girl, bewildered by the sudden bite on her lower lip; by her cheeks being scratched by his curved fingernails; and by her face, agitated with cries and moans. His hair was disheveled as it was crushed during kisses, and his body was marked by lines of sweat that glistened like the rubbed-away aloe-wood paste. The young woman displayed a manly vigor born of intense passion, while the upper coverlet rippled with waves reddened by the trail of lac-dye from his feet. His dangling locks of hair were scattered about, and the pillow at the foot of the couch was greyed by the spreading powder of *mala-kavaasa* (sandalwood paste), creating a delightful scene of amorous sport.

The winter had passed, and [the season] beyond winter arrived; in that time when the hundreds of hollows were abandoned by birds whose cold was stilled by the heat, when the midday sun was awaited by the world for its coolness, when it was suited for the cultivation of the stores of ascetic penance, when it was capable of enduring the entire fire of merit ignited to protect the lives of travelers whose faces were grim with hostility toward the frost, amidst thousands of beautiful and radiant *hasantikā* fires, upon the stone slabs cooled by the rays of the thousand-rayed sun, upon the deerskin with its praiseworthy fur, which is the cause of delighting in garlands—[in such a place].

In this place where there is a longing for the abundant and thickly growing *pravāra* flowers; where the groves of *kuñja* are filled with clusters of *vakula* trees submerged in passion, like those born from beloved *priyaṅgu* vines; where the interior of the lotus-like belly of the Himalayan cloud is made eloquent by the dense entreaties of female cranes (*ārīpuṭa*) within their cages; where the abundance of *rodhra* trees resounds with the trumpeting of elephants; where the young deer find comfort in their stillness as they rest upon the slopes of mountain caves; where the *akuṇḍyaka* plants have eyes searching for rabbits; where pairs of lovers are unable to leave the surface of their beds; and where the *mādhavī* creepers are heavy with the weight of new fruit—[in such a place...]

In the cold season, when the leaves of the *talapatri* trees are ripening from being easily drawn by the gentle breeze, when the morning mist is thick with the smoke from the agitated, naked women submerged in the waters of other ponds, when the moon of the unbearable night is devoid of fortune, and when the world is closing its eyes during that winter time—abounding in many pieces of crystal-like ice, dense camphor, green lotuses, and deer and fish—the [sage] has his face veiled by a woolen blanket and his lotus-feet encased in soft protective leather boots.

Eager to taste the flavor of fresh passion, he approached the young maidens of the inner apartments—who had made appointments on the terraces of the palace pavilions in the pleasure groves that were shaken by the fear of the winter wind—and who, having transgressed their bounds, were overcome with fear of their ladies-in-waiting; he went to them as they sat upon the laps of their beloveds, who were offering sweet consolation, within the pleasure-pavilions where the windows were fitted with closed shutters and the attendants were skilled in song, so that they might hear [his words] from their laps.

With her lower lip partially concealed by her sprout-like hands, which were agitated and momentarily flustered; with her slender body turned aside in the passion of a kiss that had been interrupted; with her firm bud-like breasts quivering as they emerged from her pale, hard skin mottled with a network of bristling horripilation; with her garment slipping slightly from her rounded hips; and with the string of her coral girdle jingling loudly.

He proceeded, his path shown by the girl whose forehead-mark was spoiled by the incessant rain of perspiration; he tasted the garment of her compassionate teeth; his thighs were sluggish with the agitation of the first-frayed restraint; the rhythm of the dance was broken by sudden twists; his inner body was paralyzed and exhausted, granting breaths of relief only at intervals; he caused compassion through the wandering of eyes whose pupils trembled with tears; he ended with a request made by joining tender palms in a pitiable supplication; he experienced the true essence of love as it was seized by passion; and he attained satisfaction through secret amorous dalliance.

He, who was beloved by women skilled in the arts of love and well-acquainted with the nuances of passion, experienced a fear rarely found even on the battlefield. Seized by the principal ladies of the harem in their agitation, his feet were bound by the girdle-strings that had no room left upon their hips; as if struck by their creeper-like eyebrows knitted in a lover’s pique, he felt his heart tremble. His chest was beaten by their sprout-like feet—which, like the tender leaves of the red Ashoka tree, seemed to drip the blood flowing from the arrows of Love—as they were washed by the water of their indignant perspiration.

Her body was smeared with saffron paste moistened by the liquid lac from their feet; she caused him to carry away her many-layered garments. When her limbs were agitated by the touch of the favorable cool breeze, she was consoled and led back to the bedchamber by those dark-eyed women. Even though he had committed no offense, he was gazed upon by the long-eyed women with side-long glances crooked by the knitting of their brows, as if they were suffering from the pain of wounds on their lips made harsh by the caress of the cold wind.

Thus, enjoying at his pleasure objects of desire acquired through the strength of his own arms—objects that were delightful and free from all obstacles—he once heard from the attendants in the inner quarters of his chief queen, Vasumatī, that she was pregnant. Overcome with joy and having distributed gifts of full vessels (*pūrṇapātra*), he questioned Yaśovatī, the remaining [queen], regarding her pregnancy longings (*doḥlā*) and other matters.

She, however, made this representation: "O King, during the month of Caitra, when the Queen had bathed well and was dressed in pure silk garments, she was indeed consecrated in a dream with waters drawn from golden jars and attracted by the fragrance of the *surabhi* flower. Furthermore, her gaze—longing for a face like a dark-blue cloud and falling with affection upon the edges of swords as if they were [gentle] breezes—is fixed in passion."

Having heard of her divine nature and perceiving that she was pregnant, he fulfilled her longing for a celestial stroll upon the floors of crystal palaces in the sky—floors which, being as white as a mass of snow, could only be discerned by touch—as if with a rain of nectar.

And when the *Vardhamāna* musical performance had been duly employed following the festival, and while the Queen’s pregnancy was gradually increasing as the time for delivery drew near, the King—his joy swelling day by day—was once seated in the assembly hall after his meal, accompanied by a few trusted friends and ministers; then the Great Chamberlain approached and, having prostrated himself, addressed him thus:

"Your Majesty! A certain wandering mendicant stands at the entrance, saying, 'I desire an audience with Your Majesty. Permitted by the king, he was ushered in; the monarch beheld the wandering ascetic, his body emaciated by vows and observances, his form soiled by the dust of the road and by hardships, bearing as his personal requisites wooden sandals, a small book, a rosary, a water-pot, a triple staff, and other such implements; he had a prominent nose, small ears, sunken eyes, and thin cheeks."

Having performed the appropriate courtesies, he, together with his ministers, questioned him in private as he sat upon a cane seat with his attendants cleared away: "How is it that you have come here alone? He replied: "Your Majesty is already aware that I, wearing such a disguise, dwell in the city of Mālava among the Mālavas, surrounded by a multitude of many disciples, at your command."

And there, the lord of Mālava, a king named Mānasāra, who had been uprooted and re-established by you, bore his head—covered with the mass of pollen from your lotus-feet—with extreme sorrow as if it were a heavy burden. Having lost his appetite for the pleasures of sovereignty due to the fever of indignation, he abandoned his harem of beautiful women—who surpassed celestial nymphs in beauty, who were skilled in the expansion of charming tales, and who possessed soft voices, laughter, and modesty—and devoted himself to a most rigorous asceticism.

Furthermore, considering that the fruit of this world is difficult to achieve through asceticism—which is otherwise fit for bestowing the rewards of other births—he sold his own great flesh to Mahākāla. Satisfied by his extraordinary valor, the Lord Āmardaka bestowed upon him a certain sword for the sake of your victory.

He spits out flames like a venomous serpent, and he falls through the path of the sun like the king of birds; yet, like a great warrior acting on his master’s command, he does not turn back until he has taken the lives of those who stand within his range of vision. Having secured him as an ally, his suspicion regarding your power is diminished, and he considers even the supreme sovereignty residing in Śaṅkara as something already within his grasp. Thus, he mobilizes his forces for an attack upon you.
However, Your Majesty is the final authority in this matter.

The king, though filled with dejection, restrained his agitation through his natural fortitude: "Surely his word has been heard, for he is one whose soul is unfailing. For intolerance toward the humiliation of an enemy is indeed appropriate to the hearts of kings, which are composed of pride. And the reckless deeds of the noble, performed regardless of their own lives, are capable of astonishing even the gods. Moreover, the gods, whose satisfaction is never in vain, would grant even those desires that are difficult to attain."

Therefore, let this matter—which is conducive to that [goal] and which does not fall within the scope of immortals—be reflected upon; for an intellect that proceeds in accordance with the scriptures finds scope everywhere.

They traverse even the sky, they cross over even the lord of waters, they enter even the netherworld (pātāla), they dwell even in the caverns of the asuras, they ascend even the peak of Mount Meru, they sport even with venomous serpents, they deal even with base men, they bring even elephants under their control, they bind even the lords of beasts, and they win over even the hearts of playful women... indeed, men who exert effort following skillful means surely achieve success.

"For one who lacks means, even that which is already in the palm of one's hand is impossible to employ; thus, remaining undisturbed, with a firm bond and immovable, like the roar of a lion in its cave...

Then Sumati, whose mind had long reflected upon their path, spoke: "Your Majesty, that which was stated by the authors of the treatises on statecraft—that destiny is inconceivable—has now arrived. The grace of Āmardaka is unattainable through all human efforts. This being the case, to appease an enemy whose power has arisen from the strength of his own forces by surrendering oneself is fraught with uncertainty; the other alternative is utterly opposed to worldly enjoyment."

Nevertheless, this very point has been illustrated in the treatise by the following example: "In the event of certain defeat, because of the destruction of both the people and the kingdom through unrighteousness, we shall take our treasury, vehicles, and whatever else is essential, and seek refuge in some inaccessible forest. There, we shall await our time, or we shall propitiate the goddess Caṇḍikā—who dwells in the caves of the Vindhya mountains, who is pleased by offerings of human flesh from men sacrificed by the Śabaras, and who is skilled in granting desired boons."
And other ministers, while [his] life still remained, supported this very view of Bhadra with various arguments of great and small weight.

Having heard this, the lord of the people, as if perceiving the very essence of virtue, revealed it under the guise of the moonlight of his pure smile; and with a voice suited to Rāma’s remorse, he spoke these words: "There exists this earth, encircled by the ocean-girdle and garlanded with provinces and cities, intended for the protection of one's own body. Yet, this extraordinary gravity of yours—permitted by those who have mastered themselves as an instrument for achieving the three goals of life—is something quite unique; otherwise, it would belong to an unfortunate man like me."

Of that which arises from the soil of the womb, whose self is accumulated through the division of many branches; which is nourished by the pouring of clouds [of food]; which is dense with the spreading creepers of sinews and veins; which is thickly strewn with the stumps of hundreds of bones; which is frequented by the herds of deer that are the fickle senses; whose hollow heart is terrifying due to the dwelling of the venomous serpent of the flower-arrowed god [Kāma]; which is shaken by the force of the wind [of age]; which is possessed by the ogress of burgeoning thirst; whose sprouts are the masses of blood; and from which the flowers of grey hair are born.

What essence is there, and what use, in this body-perception—a desolate wilderness to be withered by the heat of transformation and to be shattered by the forest-elephant of Death? Behold, for a moment, this mechanical body: it consists of three hundred bone-pins, six hundred and seventy or seven hundred sinew-ropes, fifty smears of flesh-muscles, twenty-four channels and conduits carrying the vital fluids, seven constituent elements (dhātus), and three humors (doṣas).

By means of the five winds (*marut*), the eleven sense-faculties (*indriya*), the seven layers of skin, and other such manifold complications, the artisan of karma—expert in mental construction—has fashioned this body, whose beauty is established only through lack of inquiry. It is said that with one hundred and seven vital points (*marman*), whatever part is struck anywhere, being incapable of resisting the blow, perishes at that very instant.

This machine of the Dharma may be designated by one or another of these names: a cage of bones, a thicket of sinews, a pool of blood, a heap of flesh, a jar of fat, a mire of filth, or a nest of diseases. Herein dwells the wicked moon of misfortune, a man impoverished in wisdom. Herein, within this grove of existence, the great serpent of craving—with its many mouths—brings forth the transformations of enjoyment. Herein, upon this poisonous tree, the greedy birds of the five senses devour the fruits of birth.

In this lake, the impenetrable veil of the clouds of ignorance covers the waters of wisdom; here in this cremation ground, the host of ancestors consisting of the six internal enemies, made harsh by their rising power, grants its presence.

Alas, how painful! The power of this sinful king is unstable; his realms are averse to him and beset by suffering. His journey is inevitably fraught with great toil; manifold diseases are his adversaries. He has but one mouth, yet many openings for his vulnerabilities. His complexion is inconsistent; his vision is fixed solely upon his treasury; his disposition is prone to perceiving faults. He shows contempt for those who are devoted, while destructive winds rage within him.

With his head... not ceasing from the play of the senses, he maintains the staff of the path for one who is yet unmarried; for this very reason, the flame of the lamp is eternally perishable, the fresh flood of water is motionless, and even the most stable waters... yet this state of the Lord of the Sun (Ravisthātṛ) does not endure.

And for the sake of this very same evil-souled, ungrateful man, people endure being seized by the throat while standing at the door of another’s house; they compose [their bodies] with their patience cast away by the brandishing of swords; they contract their limbs; they smooth the earth with their foreheads; they even enter into servitude; they consume leftovers; they revile those who have been honored; they deny their own greatness; they betray their friends; they insult their teachers; they sell their lives; and they practice theft.

Ill-minded people, intent on destroying [their own welfare], set in motion illusions, subsist upon their growth, and become obsessed with [the pursuit of] base things—such as the mass of flesh and great heat. Thus, although this [body] is increased through a succession of manifold and extreme efforts, it is suddenly divided like a gathering of low-born men; it does not acknowledge [kindness], it does not count [what has been] cherished, it does not perceive [one's] compliance, it does not see [one's] partiality, and it does not consider [one's] high regard, for its cause of destruction is easily found, and thus it perishes at the very moment of its conception.

He perishes; or he miscarries even while in the womb; or he is born already like a corpse; or he perishes as soon as born; or he dies in infancy. If, by some chance, through the power of karma, the force of time, the will of the Lord, or by mere accident, he passes through that period safely, then the Night of Doom (*kālarātri*), threatening with the pretext of deep coughing and appearing delightful yet not truly so, drags him away by force, seizing him by the hair, as he is utterly exhausted by the constant flow of saliva leaking from his mouth.

Alas! For a creature overcome by old age, the limbs tremble as if from fear at the approaching proximity of Death; a failing of movement arises as if from the distress of anxiety regarding the great final journey. The sight enters within, its function of seeing restricted to life alone, for the purpose of announcing the arrival of the Messenger of Time. The eyebrow, ill-placed due to its loss of position, follows [the eye] as if to inquire after the cause for its concealment.

Due to the further loosening of her limbs, a mass of skin hangs down like a kambala blanket upon her, which is variegated by a network of recently turned white hair and whose sole delight is lying down. Like a cage for a female partridge, O dear one, the heap of her bones becomes visible as she suffers from labored breathing and coughing. The channels of the streams that once flowed with fresh youth become clearly manifest. And, as if it were the ash of youth consumed by the fire of old age, a mass of grey hair is carried upward by her head through constant attachment.

The teeth crumble as if struck by the impact of the Pandava’s old age falling directly upon them. The breaths, foul-smelling and dragging along the remnants of cherished pleasures, creep forward like messengers sent to scout the path of life, preceded by the deep-sounding drums of coughing beaten at the start of the journey toward the realm of the departed. Memory does not approach its distorted form, as if unable to recognize it; and shame retreats, as if feeling abashed by the very designation "this is he."

This thing called old age is most wretched: it is the mother of contempt, the nurse of those who are reviled, the sister of wretchedness, the harbinger of fear, the preliminary state of non-existence, the cessation of fortitude, the end of self-respect, the companion of impermanence, the progeny of delusion, the path for the descent of impurity, the precursor to the torments of hell, the ground where the play of passion becomes unwholesome, and the lamp that kindles desire.

This weapon of Antaka is unfailing: it seeks out those who protect the wicked; it blinds without extracting the eyes; it consists of words that are like thorns; it crushes the power of the ears; it is a battle without fear; it is a tumultuous blow from a mace; it is a face for the weak; it is an ornament of dark spots and moles.

And thus, for one plunging into the ocean of the cycle of existence—which is most terrifying due to these three divisions of time consisting of birth, old age, and death—this body is like a boat that must be feared to break apart at every moment. Furthermore, even though this body is composed of the three humors (*tridoṣa*), the great seers, while enumerating its defects, have not yet seen its further shore. Although it is filled with the essence of the vital fluids (*rasa*), those who understand it perceive it as utterly devoid of flavor; and although it is crowded and teeming with thousands of living beings, it is regarded as nothing but empty.

And yet this [body], though joined with many vital essences, is essence-less; though entangled in a web of manifold uncertainties, it is without true bondage; though a cause of unbearable torment, its form is impure; though it is most clearly filled with the terrifying [senses], it is called "fearless"; though it contains the internal weight of semen, it is without a protector; though it has the throat within, it is impossible [to sustain]; though it possesses the five internal moving winds, it is constantly leaking; though it has internal intoxication, it is extremely clear in the sound of its joints.

It is designated as a conflict, inauspicious, unpeaceful, and the root of misfortune; yet, it is said to be difficult to abandon. Indeed, those who have formed an attachment to this [body] resolve upon some goal to be accomplished through it for the sake of benefiting others, even though it is difficult to assist them.

Although this collection of elements has come together in me in such a way, nevertheless, O Queen Vasumati, you who are the very Fortune of Kingship, the ornament of the Kṣatriya clan—by means of a path that is pleasant, unobstructed, and delightful, illuminated by the light of your lamp-like presence, we have cast off all lethargy and weariness; we have enjoyed our desired riches with unrestrained joy, and the circle of supplicants and friends has been nourished with manifold enjoyments no different from our own.

I see no other duty remaining for me beyond this. However, it may be inferred that some person of great majesty resides within the Queen's womb—a savior-thread for our lineage—based on the continuity of the family line, the signs of her dreams and longings, the favorable words of those who know her well, and the authority of my own inner conviction. This very person is I myself; for there is the saying, "The self, indeed, is the son. Therefore, he alone must be united with the welfare intended for him.

"Then it will be a great service rendered to me, to my ancestors, and to all creatures. Indeed, having cast this body—which is delightful only so long as it is not reflected upon and which is fragile even before its time—at the head of battle by way appropriate to the warrior caste, I desire to attain, without effort, that most excellent body of fame which is as beautiful as the autumn moon, which endures as long as the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which dwells in the world of the immortals, and which is sought after through a succession of many sacrifices.
I do not wish to maintain this wretched carcass for the sake of suffering or infamy."

When the lord of men had finished speaking, Sumitra replied with a mind that, though aware of that resolve to be irreversible, was overcome by affection for his master and had its agitation stilled by fortitude: “O King! It is well known that just as one who is cowardly must live, so another must die when a loved one dies. Furthermore, because of your vow to protect the distressed—which even today remains consistent with justice—the title of ‘Kṣatriya’ is truly borne; this too is not to be denied.”

And this is not because of the constant employment in the duties toward one's own elders, friends, and kinsmen; rather, it is because my mind—having now entered as an auxiliary to the sacrifice of battle—is itself wretched, unworthy, fleeting, and of the nature of suffering, even though its purpose has already been fulfilled. Indeed, it is not Mahāvarāha who uplifts the earth, nor Śambhu who supports the celestial Gaṅgā, nor Hiraṇyagarbha who brings forth the three worlds, nor the Milky Ocean that reveals the nectar.

Moreover, that which has ceased cannot bring about the arising of a continuous succession. Indeed, was the burden not already borne by another than Ananta for the sake of the enemy of Kaiṭabha? It is surely known to you, who have known all that is to be known, how these prosperities are beset by obstacles easily encountered at every step and are accompanied by the means of Duryodhana. Fortune (Lakṣmī), when sought, is difficult to obtain; when propitiated, she is difficult to maintain; and even when guarded, she flees away.

*The Mockery of Fortune*—Her fickleness is indeed evident before our very eyes. For although she was nurtured by Your Majesty’s father and grandfather; though her mind was long cherished, being freed from the oppression of the six internal enemies; though she was protected, disregarding even body and life amidst the clanging twangs of formidable bow-circles formed by the hands of great heroes; though she was increased by obtaining whatever she desired and was greeted with the blessings of satisfied and eminent Brahmins; and though she was presided over by the family deity who was pleased by constant worship—[she remains fickle].

Although her discipline was constantly being inculcated by assemblies of elder Vidyādharas who were ever-vigilant, and although her heart’s desires were honored by the lotus-forests of folded hands offered by the entire host of kings dwelling within the circle of the four oceans; nevertheless, due to the inherent defect of her own nature, that evil-minded woman—unacquainted with the reality—still lives on while he, whose tongue is the flickering sword of his enemies and who is as terrifying as the coils of a great serpent, remains in this world, even though Bṛhaspati has been eclipsed [and the moon] stays here, white as the interior petals of a water-lily bud crushed by moonbeams.

In this [world], this earth—possessing the fame of all kṣatriyas who are agitated by fleeing from fear—is like a female serpent whose body consists of the chariots of the sun; she wanders about without resting even for a moment.

Even when brought before him by fate, she—her sense of right and wrong known yet her eyes agitated by intoxication, speaking indistinctly with limbs that experienced the pain of her own suffering, overcome by rising suspicion and trepidation, unable to find words suited to her condition, like bees of dark hue and base nature whose minds are captivated solely by the audacity of harsh men—this wicked female monkey, having suddenly terrified him, ascended upon that difficult-to-grasp [object].

Having shed its fruit and shaken off its leaves, it abandons one branch and migrates to another; and wherever it clings, it is inevitably extinguished by that very [power], like a flame of fire. I believe that now the Ocean of Milk has become healthy and free from poison, having been rendered so by the emergence of this Blessed Lady and this Kālakūṭa. Or rather, she should not be compared to the Kālakūṭa, for while by that [poison] only the throat of a single Lord was defiled, by her hundreds of thousands of Lords have been defiled in every way.

This very [disease] emits a great heat, its limbs convulsing as if from the impact of the forceful waves of the great ocean tossed by Mount Mandara; it finds no steadiness in standing, sitting, or lying down; it repeatedly writhes, loathes food, and causes the vision to whirl; and as life is being overturned, it brings about a terrifying state, possessing a nature like that of a wind born from the excessive gusts of air fainting within the ocean during the tumultuous agitation of the mountains—a nature whose character is entirely inconsistent.
Unstable, petty, and a speaker of harsh words, she is pale in complexion; having employed alluring stratagems, she torments him intensely with delusions in the form of dreams.

Like the serpent-king Vāsuki, who is overwhelmed by the exhaustion of dragging Mount Mandara, she—due to the circle of smoke from the fire of the poison of her own feverish sighs—sees neither the real nor the unreal; constantly resorting to the untruth that is led by others, she stumbles even on the great path, falls upon human beasts, touches those who should not be touched, dwells in impurity, and is held in contempt by those who possess sight.

Truly, at her birth, even for this mountain—though steadfast in conduct and lofty—there occurred the coiling of double-tongued serpents and a most terrible delusion. For she, having surpassed all the gods headed by Brahmā, approached Nārāyaṇa himself—the founder of the entire system of Māyā-siddhānta-tantra—and worshipped him; thus she proclaimed an extraordinary audacity.

By this Adhokṣaja, who protects [the world] through supreme illusion, this [earth] has been stripped of its former state of honor and subjected to various humiliations. Intent on mockery, she has departed from the mass of milk [the ocean]. With men maddened by the casting of her flickering side-glances, she wanders through royal courts like one possessed, observing the conflicts and alliances brought about for her own sake; she roams with boldness, intoxicated by the savor of playful arrogance. She causes her very lineage to wither as if by heat; she consumes the continuity of her dynasty as if it were of the nature of fire.

As if out of her very nature of darkness, she defiles the abodes of the virtuous; as if through her own inconstancy, she makes noble lineages dusty with scandal. It is a marvel that she increases the power of one who is not Yaśodā, attracts one who is not Subhadrā by virtue of her triumphs, and, though not Damayantī, treats the world-protectors with contempt and regards Nala as her only prize. Because he is the sole being among the immortals, she does not dwell even in the Pārijāta tree, nor does she inhabit the ocean, the mine of jewels; and because he is the God of Love whose battles have ceased, she does not welcome him, perceiving him merely as a mortal man.

I suspect that, as if unable to endure the embrace of a family, she does not dwell even upon the moon; I think that, unable to tolerate another endowed with fragrant scent, she does not set foot even upon the great blue lotus; and surely, resenting the acceptance of the service of an Asura’s affection, she does not even walk upon the edge of a sword.

I conjecture that by her very presence, a stain has become manifest even upon the pure orb of the moon; a transformation of dust is caused to burst forth even within the sanctifying groves of lotuses; and a power to cleave is produced even in the clear water of a sword’s edge. Displaying, as it were, a preeminent power of renunciation, she abandons those very people who are themselves of a generous nature. Manifesting valor as if in the company of heroes, she remains in a state of constant conflict.

Even toward the disciplined, she acts as if more disciplined, yet she does not rest in ease because of her [hidden] passion; toward the modest, she acts as if excessively modest, yet she does not manifest her own beauty; toward the learned, she does not enter them as if unable to endure the constraint of intense passion for the Dharma and aversion to it; she offers affection to the ignorant as if they were dull-witted; toward those who are not base, she acts as if of base nature, as if unable to maintain friendship for fear of violating her character; and toward those who are exalted, she does not dare to ascend, as if being a lowly fish attempting to leap onto a high mountain.

She proceeds, scattering at every moment a modesty that has withered under the heat of Śākaṭa’s prowess; she, like a cloud pregnant with water, at every instant wipes away her noble birth—which had been defiled by the burning of passion—and casts it far below, as if it were a foot that was once devoted. She makes it exceedingly thin, as if it were a pillar of the thigh, yet she afflicts it by placing a web of thighs upon it. She covers her hips, which are like a vast expanse of enjoyment, and she emits a broken luster from her waist, as if it were situated in her breast.

It produces a depth like that of the navel-cavity, abounding in eddies; it binds [the body] as if with the slopes of swelling breasts; it bends downward the soft [limbs] like the noose of an arm; it brings about a state of wounded stability in that which is throbbing like the lower lip; it fashions a placement of teeth, pure and surpassing the lower lip; it endows the pair of eyes with affection through its playfulness; and it restrains the long-reaching mass of hair.

Cast among the most cruel and wicked like a bundle of grain, she is rendered fruitless, stripped of her fearlessness by the mere obstruction of the base. Yet, fearless and undeluded, she approaches even intoxicated elephants like a female bee. Fickle with the playfulness of lightning, she terrifies even the royal swans like a bank of clouds.

She captivates even the dull-witted, the blind, the mute, those suffering from consumption, the lepers, the deformed, the crippled, the ugly, the aged, the impotent, the wretched, the greedy, the simple-minded, the cruel, and even the wanton. Though mercilessly tormented by the enjoyment of many dissimilar and wicked men, she feels no shame.

What need is there for more? She does not increase by regard for virtue, nor does she turn away because of a fault. For instance—while taking into account the righteousness of Ajātaśatru, the power of resolve of the Wind-born (Bhīma), and the prowess of Arjuna, as well as the superhuman form of the twins (Nakula and Sahadeva), Lakṣmī disregarded the deceitful game of dice devised by Śakuni and embraced Duryodhana with intense fervor, casting aside the pride and conceit of the base-minded world.

What has she not practiced in sorceries? What has she not mastered in deceits? What remains for her among great sins? What has she not reckoned as an improper act? What has she not engaged in regarding the mixing of castes? What has she not violated in the bounds of propriety? What has she not manifested in the play of delusion? And what is there that is unimpeded in the paths of deception?

This rope is for the hanging of truthfulness; this poison is for the taking of life of magnanimity; this weapon is for the slaughter of the conduct of virtuous men; this fire is for the burning away of righteousness; this water is for the drowning of goodness; this dust is for the soiling of character. And yet, one is struck with wonder by this conduct of hers, which is inconsistent with her being a woman of noble birth.

This woman clings of her own accord to a man who is like water itself, and she herself joins that man of unrestrained passion with thousands of other men’s wives. Even when he is drinking wine, she encourages him to consume it right before her eyes. She turns virtues into faults and faults into virtues. When her excessive fickleness has begun to manifest, even the rays of light find no opportunity; there is not even a whisper of news regarding the tender sprouts of an elephant’s ears.

Not even a word can be spoken of those who wander at the edge of a plantain grove; only one of ignoble intellect has the capacity to follow her due to her instability. And yet, even though she is of such ill-conduct and repeatedly unfaithful, it is possible—by virtue of her own natural fickleness—to win her back only by men like you, adorned with extraordinary manly effort.

Although she was lost through that deceitful game of dice which the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra had raised aloft, this Fortune of the Earth—consisting of a multitude of vast armies augmented by excellent troops and teeming with many hundreds of thousands of elephants—was indeed recovered by the sons of Pāṇḍu upon their return from their forest exile. Having entered the ocean-like army of the Kuru clan, they retrieved her like the beauty of pearls produced from a pearl-oyster. And rare is he who possesses her so steadfastly.

Indeed, having repeatedly seized and bound this very woman—who was like a wicked servant—as soon as she moved, they brought her [to this place]. The kings, whose broad shoulders and flesh were as formidable as the peaks of Mount Acala, whose feet served as thrones for all the kings of the seven continents which they had made into their own seats, are well known. And it is heard that even the thousand-eyed Indra, while hidden within the fibers of a fresh lotus stalk, endured the entire period of Nahuṣa’s power.

Furthermore, when that [city] was ascended by the beautiful daughter of Puloman, the wife of faultless conduct became a python due to the curse of the great seer Agastya, who was provoked to anger by her [attempted] restraint; and the celestial splendor became leaderless. Indeed, the god Divākara himself was visibly drawing back the beauty of the lotus from her face. Thus ends the imitation of Lakṣmī.

Be gracious, O King! Turn back from this rashness. You have taken up your position in a fortress that is difficult to traverse due to its surrounding encampments and immovable mountains; wait for the right time. Satisfied by the employment of excellent troops that have been procured, having achieved the fruit of your expedition through the acquisition of the kingdom, and with your mind drawn by the beauty of this fruitful land, you should remain right here and take up residence in this very region. Furthermore, even if your purpose were accomplished, there is no benefit for us in attacking an enemy who dwells in a rugged mountain fortress and has abandoned his own life.
For even that powerful weapon obtained through the grace of the Immortals is said to be effective only against those who remain within the range of one's vision.

And when the boy—whose childhood has passed, who is endowed with learning, capable of governing, and the sole remover of the armor of Māyā—is present before you, you will either wage a slaughter against your adversary regardless of yourself, or you will spend your time in the thickets of your enemies through inexhaustible asceticism. This is not the right moment for you to offer your own body as a sacrifice to the enemy today, merely to produce pleasure by saying, "The maidens are thus."

Then, if you consider that everything is accomplished by mere chance and is not brought about by the sphere of human effort at all—then, alas, let the noble lineage of the Lord [Mahendra] be transformed by his own will during this time of distress! As for us, we too shall employ ourselves here, who are otherwise useless, through our own death. Having thus offered salutations with palms joined, he touched the earth with his head, its crest-jewel trembling.

But the lord of the earth, with a sweetness and gentleness that had been extinguished, raised him up and spoke these words of powerful import: "As for what you say—that one dwelling in the forest should maintain even his life-breaths, though they be stained by the loss of honor, for the sake of assisting his own kin—this must be considered: Is this enemy, who is arrogant in the strength of his cuckoos, [capable of] releasing the city and the countryside, being deprived of his principal resources, defiled by the reproach of the subjects for his improper conduct, and having his majesty extinguished?"

Would he not pursue this man, who has sought out the shade of some forest tree to ward off the heat of the sun’s rays, his own shadow having departed? Is Duryodhana—now with only his own body remaining—though hidden at the bottom of the water like a fish, not assailed by Vṛkodara, whose belly is filled with blood and who is cruel in his recollection of former insults?

Proud, arrogant, and having spread his majesty, he was once a benefactor to me; yet, now considering us our enemies, he has withdrawn from our kingdom and elsewhere. For one who is sustained by the waters of patience, whose own splendor—long accumulated and present—is manifest, it is impossible for him to remain hidden within the dense thickets of profound darkness like a serpent, as if with an invisible self. Indeed, one whose body is the fame arising from the destruction of his own calamities cannot possibly exist anywhere in the belly of a thicket, like a hare.

And this being so, even if I were to flee far away from my pursuer, my own body would surely perish; moreover, since my wife is left behind with me, she too would fall into danger should I meet with disaster.

For the sake of which you would exert yourself even for a life that is as light as a withered blade of grass and defiled by its lack of color—[that purpose] you must now await until it is achieved. By employing whatever means are at hand, you must win over the forest-dwellers suitable for our cause, who have seized the treasury from the powerful ones—those who, under the pretext of performing service, do not disregard the time while following the chief ministers and principal servants, and who are unaware of the circumstances of our misfortune—and having brought the Queen here, though she is exhausted by the pains of pregnancy, you must remain there in joy until the opportunity arises.

The matter at hand is established. Indeed, this prosperity is beset by many obstacles and is constantly threatened; it is ruined, difficult to obtain, difficult to protect, and characterized by a corrupted nature. It is beloved only by the wicked, merciless, alluring for no reason, and devoid of auspicious marks. This path is trodden by the enlightened; there is no doubt about this. Nevertheless, what recourse is there?

Once born into this world, for the sake of livelihood, one must necessarily exert effort through the methods prescribed by the scriptures—such as conciliation and so forth—or by following the path of agriculture and other such vocations. Even when wealth is acquired through such application, it is fate alone that bestows it, not human effort. In this regard, one must strive for the birth of a wife, and for her nourishment, protection, and the instilling of discipline; a man’s authority extends only this far, for beyond this, fate prevails and human effort does not reach. [Thus he attains] prosperity.

For it is heard that those such as Kuśa and Lava, having grown old in forest hermitages together with wild deer, returned once more and took up sovereignty; they bring back to fruition a destined purpose, whether it be pleasant or unpleasant. Yet a wise man, striving to the best of his ability, renders himself beyond reproach.

Then, by you all, in a single instant, [all this was cast aside]: the state of being a kinsman inherited through family lineage; the accumulation of affection nourished by playing together in the dust, whose sweetness reached its highest degree as it developed further and further; the intimacy built upon conversations free from fear regarding all secrets; and the conduct, naturally beautiful and requiring no artifice, which was practiced as if toward one's own body, yet now rendered harsh by a lack of engagement in this difficult task for those of unrefined wisdom.

Fading away should not be brought about by those who are like common folk, lacking self-mastery, incapable of discernment, and unpracticed in the application of policy. For how could the scattering of these trivial blades of grass—my very life-breaths—serve as a recompense for the high regard you have conceived toward me, a regard that has risen to such heights?

For the sacrifice of one's life must be accomplished through a momentary concentration, whereas the protection of a deposit lasts as long as one's life. Therefore, let this deposit be protected; let the self be made firm; let cowardice be abandoned; let the banners of fame be raised; let the power of sacred learning be displayed; let the conduct of the virtuous be established; let the vision of reality be proclaimed; let the lineage of one's own master be honored; and let it be well observed.

Let this person, whose departure for the next world has been brought about by the impossibility of ever seeing you again, be permitted to depart. Let him be the son of my father, whose fame was vast and who surpassed even Māruti and Kārtavīrya through his unfeigned valor; let him be the grandson of my grandfather, who drank up all his enemies with the heat of his manly prowess and for whom the great festival of incessant warfare was a constant sacrifice. For a thread of deer-skin is not fitting for the noble lineage of lions among kings.

Therefore, in this autumn—when the sky is whitened by a canopy of dense, thick, and widespread reeds; when it is terrifying with its unaging [beauty] adorned by bandhujīva flowers throbbing pink like masses of blood; and having overturned even the power of Fate by my own strength—I shall put thousands of men to sleep so that they may not awaken again.

And here, if my lords, out of distress at this improper separation, should utter a word that is harsh with syllables of refusal or connected to offering me assistance, then—once these words have been concluded—I shall cease [my life] in a fire of uneven flames, wherein the embers are whirled by the grasping of mouthfuls of dry heartwood, wherein the abundant clarified butter has been consumed, and wherein sparks fly about; for the battles of great men, due to the majesty of Indra, never result in the departure of their honor, and they are incapable of being turned back.

Because sovereignty is accumulated through unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), because the state of servitude is incapable of obstruction, because the activities of fate are beyond remedy, and because the accumulation of misfortune is accompanied by resolve on the part of those of great being; and because the power of knowledge blossoms at the time of calamity—he, having suppressed even the most powerful onset of grief, having supported his uplifted heart, having cast aside rising longing, and having restrained the torrent of hot tears that had welled up—[remained steadfast].

Having turned back [the enemy] and even having brought about the cessation of the enemy’s life—which was like a death-in-life, though its form was still beautiful due to the lack of finality—the ministers, finding no other course, accepted their lord’s command with the words "So be it," spoken in a voice determined by distress.

And he had the queen—already acquainted with the details of the worship of the goddess and, knowing her husband’s resolve, personally preparing the equipment for the expedition—prepare the necessary provisions for the journey. The king, too, desiring an attack upon his enemy like the rising of the sun, and because of his great fortitude having set aside the sorrow of separation from his own kin through his passion for valor, passed that latter part of the day and the entire night with a tranquil mind.

Then, on the following day, as the sun—reddened like the hue of blood, having ascended its peak; as the lord of the river (the ocean) roared, agitated by the impact of his [the sun's] descent upon the foot of the mountain; as he who bears the red discus (the sun) caused the brilliance of the moon to fade with the striking of his exceedingly sharp rays; as the mass of rays from the tip of his clearly defined halo shone upon the crown of the earth; as he whose unbearable heat expanded at every moment; as he who, out of enmity toward the moon, offered praise to the enemy of the moon (fire)—as he thus turned about, mounted upon his supreme chariot like a great warrior.

When the time had arrived according to her own destiny, and when the auspicious morning rites had been performed by the gods, while the [elephants] were sluggish with the heavy burden of their full term of gestation... [the queen], adorned with ornaments like the autumn twilight when the orb of the moon is hidden by the eastern mountain and only a few stars twinkle, attended by her chief elders and eunuchs, followed by a group of elderly women like the Mandākinī river followed by a flock of aged swans—the queen, eager for her beloved son...

Placing at their head the female attendants who followed in agitation after having been delayed for a moment by the people, the ministers turned toward the Vindhya mountain; driven by the syllables of their master’s command—which, like messengers of Death, impelled them toward an undesirable fate; with the luster of their faces struck by grief and the limbs of their bodies dragged along; though accompanied by their wives, they found no other refuge.

Immediately thereafter, throughout the entire earth, portents of terrible form began to manifest like the very embodiment of Death, foreboding the destruction of all the kṣatriyas. For instance—the earth trembled at the very outset, as if out of fear at the imminent end of its own master; and the lords of the rivers surged and roared with redoubled force, as if at the approach of the rising sun.

As if to produce the conviction that it would be easy to break the heads of the moving mountains, someone broke apart the stationary mountain peaks, which were composed of stones glittering with gems from the earth. All the seasons, their identities marked by their own characteristic signs, arrived simultaneously from every direction, as if to provide assistance to the assembly of kings eager for battle.

Making the entire surface of the earth as if a mere wrestling ring, violently uprooting and casting away trees and creepers, crushing stones and pebbles, and wandering for even a moment with a fierce roar, the winds entered the bedchambers of all the kings like black cobras gliding along. Like tigers and other beasts in a forest, they besieged the cities with the flailing of their staff-like tails.

In the royal assemblies, women of the Rohita species appeared in great numbers, as if they were the very personification of the attendants of Alakṣmī. With their hands, feet, and heads either deficient or redundant, and possessing deformed and terrifying forms, these numerous beings—resembling floating bubbles of foul and heavy sin—were a source of great dread to the world, portending misfortune for both humans and animals.

Tears fell from the faces of the elephants and horses, who, like those terrified by thoughts of non-existence, had no relish for the grass and sprouts; though restrained with all their might by the sounds of conchs and drums, they did not let out even a single cry. The statues of the deities wept as if in grief over the destruction of the vast multitude of living beings. A swarm of bees hovered over the parasols like the head of Rāhu moving across the full moon.

The faces of the kings, as if out of pride, did not wish to fall even into their own mirrors, though they were reflected in their weapons. The shadows of those proud men approached even the radiant sun. As if in the heat of battle, the weapons blazed forth and emerged spontaneously from their scabbards. The ichor of the female elephants clung to their temples, as if to mock the scent-elephants who, when challenged, could not endure the humiliation of being mounted.

As if driven by a refusal to bow down, the mounts repeatedly turned back from their stations; even though they had traveled a great distance, the royal insignia—the parasols, banners, and flags—fell away at the very outset, as if out of the impetuous haste of the approaching calamity. Chariots, carts, and other vehicles were shattered. And tears, appearing like coral beads upon the girdles fashioned from the luster of the Black Night (Kālarātri) enraged by the offense of a few people, were seen falling upon the temples of the elephants.

The horses of the Kṣatriyas, as well as those of various other breeds, seemed to leap about their limbs with reckless abandon as if to obstruct [the enemy]. A reversal of qualities occurred among the steeds—both slow and swift—at the time of action, as if they were witnesses to the path of truth and falsehood. Bellowing like bulls, the humped oxen charged head-on against the forces.
Birds flew from left to right, while forest deer ran clockwise; plunging fearlessly into the fray, they seemed to divide the armies from one another by treating them as mere prey.

Even by the crows, as if through the power of Time itself... for those horses, withered by meditation and whose limbs were being scarred upon the ground by the hooves of other horses and elephants, their bodies sank down as if pierced by the thunderbolt or as if kissing flowers... and by those displaying most terrible sights such as headless trunks (*kabandha*) with severed hands.

The hearts of the soldiers shattered into a thousand pieces as they were tormented by fierce winds accompanied by thunderbolts—terrible and harsh roars contrary to the whirlwind—and by rains of blood, honey, fat, oil, stones, serpents, crocodiles, and lightning-streaked golden staffs. The quarters of the sky were scorched by the golden thrones set up by the world-protectors for the spectacle of the great assembly; and the cities of the Gandharvas trembled, fleeing out of fear of the upheaval caused by the Kshatriyas.

In the nights, rainbows appeared as if sent by Indra to the awakened planets. At the hour of twilight, jackals howling with voices harsh like the cries of Bharadvāja’s peacocks fell upon the city; they seemed to rise up in greeting with the firebrands from their upward-turned mouths, blazing as if smeared with streams of blood from the hare-mark on the moon torn apart by many fangs. Meteors, like the arms of Death dancing, covered the heavens in manifold ways.

The sky itself became dark with stars that had fallen of their own accord, as if unable to endure the sight of the destruction of all beings. Lamenting such a heaven, the sun, its radiance extinguished like dying embers, was eclipsed by its enemy, Rāhu. The moon and the sun, soiled and tormented, were swallowed by the fierce Kabandha, appearing like Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.

Thus, although restrained by these great portents from the earth, the atmosphere, and the heavens, the circle of kings nevertheless assembled for battle, drawn forth by the command of the lords of Magadha and Mālava as if by the messenger of Death.

And then King Rājahaṃsa, his circle of troops mostly ready for action, received from the gatekeeper the messenger of the Lord of Mālava who had arrived at the gate; having already largely discerned the purpose, the lord of men, with a mind slightly stirred by indignation, granted him entrance.

Having entered, that Brāhmaṇāyana, restraining his heart which was filled with trepidation born of the king’s majesty, raised his right hand and uttered the word "Svasti" in a loud voice. And the King of Magadha, perceiving from the man's appearance that he was no commoner—judging him by his refined speech, his noble and gentle form, and the movement of his eyes, which were neither harsh nor arrogant—graciously welcomed this virtuous man to a seat of darbha grass.

When he was seated and rested for a moment, the messenger approached him with a naturally affectionate gaze and inquired after the welfare and health of the Lord of Mālava. Having shown his respect and replied "So be it," the messenger, after the report of welfare and health, spoke in due order regarding the purpose of his arrival: "O King! I have been sent to your presence by the Lord of Mālava to ascertain news of your well-being. That king is naturally affectionate toward you, having long cherished a bond of friendship."

Whether it be without cause, or by the force of karmic impressions set in motion from previous lives that persist without fail, or by the power of the abundance of elements constituting the body, someone somewhere, merely upon seeing another, projects a tender affection; and elsewhere, one projects a malice that is cruel and irrevocable. Such is the nature of the world.

And he remembers that experience of combat, which was more delightful than anything seen by other noble men; an experience in which joy and wonder were seized by his prowess expanding without artifice, which was terrifying due to the falling of weapons raining down fire, and which struck terror into the hearts of the faint-hearted.

With his cheeks bristling with thrill from an excess of aesthetic rapture (*rasa*), he never reaches satiety as he narrates various other stories—each connected to him and imbued with heroism, generosity, truth, and fortitude—within the assemblies. And he says this very thing through my mouth, looking at the Blessed One here with eyes full of affection as if unable to look enough: "Blessed indeed is human existence, wherein you [dwell]...; blessed indeed is the divine Earth, the sustainer of beings, who has been made her true protector by you."

And that very same highly fortunate goddess was like a purification through bathing at a sacred ford for the creation of women, which had been defiled by the fault of a thousand [sins] at their first menses; she, possessing no small splendor, dwelt in the eastern quarters. His roar—[was it not] swift with speed? Even today, in the stream of the evening twilight, something of such a former nature... the radiant universal monarch, like the god of fierce rays (the Sun), possesses a power capable of subduing the circle of many kings.

The cry of the swans, raised in the joy of many colors, does not disturb those whose passion for the color of the unshaken *dhātu* is undiminished; nor are the *kṣatriya* lineages eclipsed by this splendor.

Granted that he is of great strength, the very soul of the wind, and the beloved of Añjanā’s heart... yet, having caused the forests on the shores of all the oceans to tremble with the force of his power, he has repeatedly bent the heads of the many uplifted *cakravāḷas* of the earth. Nevertheless, like you, he is ever free from dust [of passion], having made a vow to proceed according to what is right.

I consider those births to have fulfilled their purpose, for those who, having arrayed themselves against your honor in great battles and then ceased from combat, possess here an enduring body of fame that exists beyond the occurrence of material beings.

And in the hereafter, for those who sport with Apsarases of faultless youth—women who praise them as heroic husbands—in the grounds of the Nandana grove where the Pārijāta, Santānaka, and Mandāra kalpa-trees are in full bloom, while the breezes from the waves of the Mandākinī gently fan their limbs after the exhaustion of lovemaking in hundreds of lakes of young golden lotuses, and while the fire of Kāma is fanned by the favorable union [of passion], a mass of unbroken, perfect, and auspicious blessings shall attend them.

But for me, unfortunate as I am, whose mind was stolen by the darkness of a swoon born from many pure blows, as I lay upon a blanket spread on the floor of the battlefield, you—your indignation aroused by my powerful roar in return—impetuously struck and shattered my helmet-case, scattering its contents so that they filled the air with a mass of feathers; and thus, in the presence of all the Kṣatriyas, you made yourself light by having crossed the heavy burden of the great battle.

And I have been made an object of ridicule by those high-minded men who adorn themselves with the pearl necklaces of their own flawless deeds and reputations; for the burden of the earth, when resting upon the heads of the lofty, is easily borne, yet not so the minute dust at the feet of another. And for a man whose head is trodden upon by the feet of another, his heroic vow—though naturally white—is cast far away like a turban from the crown of the head. His innate, dark stains suddenly fly up like swarms of bees from an ornament.

Like a garland of flowers, his fame—once tender and bright—now withers away. Like a heap of fragrant powder carefully applied, his family pride leaks away. Like a crest-jewel whose brilliance has faded, his self-respect crumbles to dust. Like a mass of hair grown long and tangled over time, his power becomes disordered. Furthermore, his very states of being have turned into non-existence.

I think that upon this very root of the lineage of my enemies, once it has been severed by another who touches the earth with his head and cast down, the world’s contemptuous gaze—extremely cruel and tearing at the heart like a sharp-edged axe falling upon a tree whose branches are all lopped off—will descend. Therefore, I entreat you, O sole hero, to engage in battle once more, so that this great heap of dishonor may be scattered upon me by the wind blowing from the forest of the arms of trembling heroes, or else so that my head, bowed down by its excessive weight, may become difficult to bear.

Superior indeed is that solitary hero who, amidst the dense thickets of Aśoka, Punnāga, and Nāga trees obscured by the falling of his arrows; in the forest-like rows of female cuckoos—the friends of the root of desire—resplendent with the laughter of groves of shimmering creeper-like flashes of light; during the endless days of the forest of battle; who is habituated to sporting with the bodies of his enemies; who strikes with teeth and the harsher blows of his claws upon their bodies; who is intent on releasing [his victims] reddened by passion; who bites their lips impetuously; whose slender frame is thrilled with horripilation; and who, acting with grace, attains the Goddess of Victory.

He draws [his sword] to sport with it by the hilt. Therefore, gird your loins! For when the great dust-clouds of the battle, thickened by the myriads of soldiers filled with unrestrained pride, flow like a river of blood from the army faltering at the moment of engagement—then, O Kārtavīrya, you shall once again perform those fierce and beloved deeds, deep as the roar of massive rainclouds swollen by the thundering of abundant waters, which cause circles of proud warrior-peacocks to dance while their necks resound with roars.

...beautiful with a vermilion porch for her six faces, possessing the dark blue hue of an *indīvara* petal like the Night of Doom (*Kālarātri*), terrifying the world with her yawning displays, her pair of fierce and crooked frowns, her two eyes from which streams of nectar-like tears flowed like a garland, and who—just as in the Bharata war—by destroying the entire faction of arrogant Kṣatriyas even now, has caused rivers of blood to flow upon the earth, [anointing] the [mountains] with sandalwood-paste of blood.

May the warriors, their bodies smeared with blood and marked by the longing side-glances of the celestial courtesans, sport with the play of valor! May the host of Piśācas, exhausted from dancing, abandon the mangled flesh of the great heroes fallen into every pore of their skin and instead indulge in drinking the blood! And may the blessed Lord Vaivasvata, his pride and fever abated, be satisfied by this offering of the life-force of the noble soldiers as his sustenance.

"And independent as he is, this destroyer of the vital points, having abandoned the hero out of a desire for pleasure, will cause his own kinsmen to flee with their faces turned away—this is the message from my mouth, sent by the Lord of Mālava, who desires the welfare of your body of glory, O you who are connected to him in battle."

When the messenger had finished speaking, the lord of the earth, with a smiling face, replied: "This entire proposal is appropriate. For the stream of fame of great souls is a continuous succession of achievements. And that fame, O scion of the warrior caste, cannot be attained by any other means than human effort (*puruṣakāra*). Even prosperity must be drawn forth by the relentless whirling of the circle of kings with the staff of one’s own arms; this matter has been settled according to the very path of the churning of the nectar by the gods and demons."

And for a king, battle—known as a sacrifice—is the gateway to victory in the next world; it is a sacrifice that is not performed with large sacrificial animals, but is augmented by the beautiful whirlpools of clarified butter produced by his majesty-fire; it is terrifying due to the expansion of great heroes; it involves the employment of weapons; it is a long-lasting rite where the wine, though not truly ambrosial, serves as the cause of exhilaration; and it is death itself, undertaken because it is impelled by destiny.

There is no other means for achieving the three goals of life (*trivarga*) so free from meanness as this: a life sustained by the sovereignty over the four quarters, won through the sacrifice of expansion and the conquest of battle, which serves as the powerful gateway to that prosperity that is obtained through death. What more need be said? Battle is indeed the foremost among the gates to success.

And thus, I perceive that which this Lord of Viśālā, desiring to engage in such an exceedingly delightful undertaking, has spoken so much about as his dearest [desire] to be—this is, as it were, a mere lure with the bait of nectar.

Or rather, he does not know how to express anything other than what is dear to him in a refined manner. And though I desire it, I shall wait for Mānasāra—who seeks our welfare and happiness—to assemble with me at the head of the battle in the Mālava country, and then respond to the substance of his message in a fitting way. Or else, let this most meritorious place of performance be our destination; let us go there. Granted, this day is unfavorable, yet even so, it is not incapable of accomplishing our purpose.

"Delaying for auspicious lunar days and constellations is indeed an obstacle to gain, a source of contempt for the Lord of the Center (the King) by those of mediocre intellect. Therefore, let the army be prepared for assault this very day; let the drum be sounded for the march. Thus he commanded Harṣa, the commander-in-chief, who stood before him with palms joined in reverence. Having honored the messenger with a great gift of wealth, he dismissed him with cheerful countenance to report the orders as given.
He himself, having dismissed the circle of courtiers to don their armor, rose from his throne.

And when the king arose, the assembly of vassals trembled like the ocean, with their upper garments—the masses of foam from tossing, surging waves—being cast aside; and as they rose in agitation, the tips of their gems on arms that were bent and flailing against one another seemed to roar, as if with the intense pride of those accustomed to the battlefield nearby.

The jeweled pavements wailed as if mourning their own misfortune—pavements whose cheeks were rubbed by the ichor flowing from the temples of kings when they were restrained by the bars of their arms; pavements overwhelmed by the news of the terrible battle; pavements whose luster was eclipsed by the nearby lunar discs of the beautiful courtesans who held lovely chowries over their left shoulders; pavements whose surfaces were grey with the devotion of various offerings of flowers; and pavements where swarms of bees, their wings broken by the impact of hundreds of moving feet, seemed to lament as they were struck by the tinkling sounds of the jeweled girdles of those women.
The king also, surrounded by a retinue consisting mostly of hunchbacks, dwarfs, and Kirātas, entered the interior like Nīlalohita entering the cave of Kailāsa with Gaurī.

Then the astrologer, approaching him together with the family priest, made this representation: "O King, since Your Majesty’s intellect does not fathom the results of the conjunctions known through the true paths of observation of many teachers such as Guru, Bhārgava, and Garga, this matter is therefore explained to you."

"How indeed can one determine the merit in such a transformation of nature, amidst these most fierce portents, under this constellation presided over by the god Agni, on the ninth lunar day when the western quarter has been commenced? By what authority of the scriptures of illusion is the Lord [to be known]? To him, whose mind was shrouded in darkness, he replied: "This is appropriate; I have been enlightened by you, noble sir. However, for those desiring the conquest of the earth, this is the path: that we must await the excellence of the day and other favorable conditions."

The arrow of one who desires victory in heaven shines only when turned back; therefore, he looked toward the followers of the Atharvaveda, saying, "Let propitiatory rites be performed—rites whose power is seen to pacify ill omens—for the sake of calming the oppression of the subjects."

From the very commencement of the portents, he likewise performed—according to the rules of initiation—the reception of guests at home, the taking of water, the pacification of the site, the *nirṛti-homa*, the separate ritual manual, the *apratiratha* hymn, and the sacrificial fee; and for the eight or eighteen [deities], the arrangement of the *amṛta-vākya*; and for the Rudra-group, Gandharvas, Airāvata, Earth, and Lakṣaṇā; and for the sake of protection from fear and for the purpose of granting fearlessness, the *mahāśānti* (great pacification) beginning with the *ghṛtakambala* (ghee-blanket) and other rites for Rudra, Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, Viṣṇu, Santati, Tvaṣṭṛ, Prajāpati, Agni, Kumāra, Nirṛti, and the Rudra-hosts.

The performance of the most meritorious rites and others prescribed in the Atharvaveda is indeed carried out. When this very creation [is thus established], may there be well-being for the Lord; "May there be a bath for the sake of victory"—repeating these words of the domestic priest, he has performed his ablutions according to the prescribed path. As if longing for splendor, he approaches the venerable Sun and, with the assistance of the priest, having his head sprinkled with the waters of the holy Atharvanic *śānti* mantras, he worships him according to the ritual.
For the sake of pacifying all that is born of evil birth in this world, he gave away his entire hoard of white garlands and garments to the twice-born.

Then, in an instant, there arose the mass of rays [of the sun], resembling the dawn stained with the hue of Aruṇa; it was like a mass of liquid lac that turned the crystal orb of the sun pale-red; it was a forest fire for the woods of the world’s calamity-trees gathered together; it appeared tawny like the descendant of Kakutstha plundering the camp of the Kṣaṇadācaras (demons); it was like a refuge for the collyrium of the faces of the quarters, which were like a cluster of lotuses in the lake of the sky; and it seemed to be fashioning the primordial root of the Kalpa, as if creating the birth of the golden egg.

A vast stream of light, as red as the glow on the cheeks of beautiful women from the land of Śaka, surged upward toward heaven from the opening of the peak of Mount Meru, which had been opened wide by the intense joy of the host of brahmins; and as it expanded, the entire collection of ill omens vanished as if to make way for it.
