As he accepted gold and jewels at will from the assemblies of Brahmins who were free from pride, various exclamations arose, their eyes wide with abundant wonder and heavy curiosity: "This vast collection of wealth has been obtained; with this, it is possible to perform the Soma sacrifices. This gold is full and is being acquired without hindrance; surely every desire can be fulfilled."

"This is a great heap of gold; it shall serve a useful purpose for my eldest son, who resides as a neighbor. This radiant pearl necklace, with its face like the full moon of the abundant month, my wife generally shudders to bestow upon a Brahmin. This entire set is the bridal ornament for my daughter; I shall give her away adorned with this. This emerald is a poison-destroyer and most sacred; I shall fasten it upon this ring."

"This birth-gem of ruby is of great value; even as I reflect upon it, I see no purpose for it. This girdle-ornament, variegated with gold and jewels, he will now purchase at its proper price. How could he not treat this [ruby]—which has eight thousand spokes...—with such contempt? This lovely coral sprout, with its curved joints, I shall make into a single necklace for a child."

These are of great value... [someone] will offer something to my father’s ear-ring. This is the one called *kalitapanīya*, made of five-colored gold of unsurpassed hue. These are those pearls—born from the Himalayas, from oyster shells, from conch shells, or from miscellaneous sources. These are the gems: lapis lazuli, *śirīṣa* flowers, *kādamba* reeds, *vaṃśarāja*, sapphire, moonstone, and so forth. These are the various types of sandalwood, possessing diverse fragrances and colors, and endowed with lightness and other qualities.

These are various sources of qualities of color and fragrance, such as black aloe-wood oil, *parṇika*, and other collections of articles for enjoyment. This gem, named *nīlakaṇṭhakaṇṭhakānta*, belongs to the *praiyyaka* variety; it is variegated with blue, yellow, and white streaks, and marked with spots resembling a rainbow. This is a *visī* from the twelve-village region, measuring twelve finger-breadths in length, and it is a *mahāvisīcī*. This *śyāmikā* is tawny and marked with spots. This *kālikā* is tawny and the color of a dove.

This plantain tree is as long as a man’s arm; this is a *candrottarā* [variety], variegated like the moon. This is a *nyākula* [variety], a third part of a plantain tree, variegated with circles of *kola*. These are many precious skins (*ajinaratna*), smooth, thick-haired, and delicate. This is woolen cloth (*āvika*) of various Yavana types, such as *kaṭambala* and so forth. This is a class of fine silk (*dukūla*) produced in Vaṅga, Puṇḍra, and other regions. These are varieties of woven leaf-fiber (*patrorṇā*) originating from Magadha, Puṇḍra, Suvarṇa, Akuḍya, Deśya, Nāgalika, Kucavakuḷa, and Vaṭa.

"This is silk; these are Chinese silks; this is cotton, from Aparāntaka; this is from Mathurā; this is from Mahiṣaka; this is a heap of base metals—who will carry it for you? Tie it firmly so that the chest of jewels does not fall on the road. The load is too heavy; he is unable to carry it! Fie on you—you were born only to eat! Lift it with effort, place it [on the shoulder], and carry it carefully; otherwise, your Vedic recitation will be broken today."
"O plowman, why do you even lay your hand upon my body? O angry one, carry yourself far away from me! Alas, you turn me, whose essence has been seen by Phalguna, upside down!"

"O Durmukha! These men have seen the most excellent thing I have obtained: a horse-hoof, hard as a stone, devoid of skin, and free from the work of worms; and this pearl-oyster, unblemished by the work of crabs. How, indeed, has this come to pass that I am so satisfied? Yet, how is it that I am not satisfied by this one wretched, wicked man? Here are many pearls, pierced at their broad, thick, round, smooth, lustrous, heavy, and white centers; and here are abundant vessels made of gold, silver, and copper."

"You too must carry out their purpose; this great gift has been set in motion. Oh, neither the Great-Souled Mahārāja, nor Karṇa, nor King Yudhiṣṭhira has ever seen such riches in the morning or the afternoon! I believe the reason for this is the absence of the ministers. "Do not say so. Even they do not have their vision of the next world blocked by a faith in the dry application of the *Ṣāṅguṇya* (the six measures of statecraft). Moreover, here is a *haṃsa* (swan/virtuous man) with a retinue of *haṃsas*. In every way, may the World-Guardians, headed by Śakra, protect him in battle!"

"May he obtain as his inheritance this sovereignty over the eighteen islands, and may he have a son who is the foremost of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and possesses a splendor exceeding that of the sun"—thus, while the paths were being blocked by twice-born men who, according to their faith, were uttering, carrying, or causing others to carry such blessings and other riches; and while the throngs of young citizens, their passion kindled by the sight of the army's departure, were climbing onto [the vehicles] amidst a crush of mutual jostling.

As the sound of the marching kettledrums fell upon the palaces, mansions, roof-terraces, assembly halls, temples, sacred trees, circular walls, and gateways—its exit obstructed by the streams of tears from the eyes of women overwhelmed and agitated by love for their husbands—it spread a roar as terrifying as the thundering of the massive wings of the principal mountains when rattled by the vajra-strike of Indra’s horse, as if it were leaping over them with great force while remembering its duty of service.

As the drum was struck by the golden mallet—which, with its fierce descent like a staff of lightning at the time of universal dissolution, resembled the arm of Vālin—the sound caused the three worlds to tremble and shook the ten directions to their very limits. Struck violently by this sound, the Lokāloka mountain seemed to cry out even more intensely through its cave-mouths, which were distorted like the coils of a serpent writhing in fear within its own uneven interior.

And at that moment, the war-trumpets of the entire host resounded with a hair-raising roar, following the deep thundering of the clouds like flocks of peacocks. And in that very instant, as the circle of conchs—filled with the breath from their mouths, sounding shrilly as if alive and as if out of fear—was being blown with great care, the rows of waves consisting of the flickering horses surged upward like the cosmic dissolution (*saṃvarta*).

And the oceans of the army, filled with hundreds of thousands of chariot-divisions laden with the choicest weapons for sale, and whose ten directions were blocked by dense throngs of swelling men, surged forth like the oceans of the world.

The king, however, having performed the entire array of departure rites according to the path instructed by his domestic priest, wearing a pair of white garments as pleasing to the eyes as the light of the moon, anointed with sandalwood paste that followed him like a mass of autumn clouds, adorned with almost all his ornaments consisting primarily of pearls, and—as if out of excessive pride—sportively assuming for himself alone the very appearance of the terrible Kali age, which portends fear; ...[the rest of the sentence continues]... he set forth.

He was entirely white, possessing a fame that—like a garland of flowers made from jasmine buds with faces smiling like white mālatī blossoms—was soft and delicate, and which, by its lofty peaks reaching upward as it traveled through the quarters of the sky, led the way for the highest of mountains; and he stood firm in a resolve more steadfast than Mount Kailāsa, which caused the arms of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa to tremble and shook all the world-protectors.

He went out on foot alone, his feet supported at every step by the reflections of his own image in the jeweled pavements—which were like lotuses—serving as if they were *ūrmi-kara-kamalās* (lotuses with moving hands) to avoid contact with the pollen of the lotuses; these pavements were accessible for easy passage due to heaps of golden jewels and gems suspended from pegs fixed along their lower sides, rising above a floor of precious stones green as a fresh bed of lotuses, and crowded with thousands of railings (*pālikā*) entangled in networks of young arches set in place.

And having emerged, he beheld the surface of the sky, which was wondrous to behold as it spread out even over the kings who were eager to prostrate themselves; for when the radiance of the clusters of rays from their crest-jewels began to shine forth, the sky became variegated with the darkness of swarms of bees hovering about the flower-ornaments fallen from their turbans as they hurriedly bowed down, while thousands of lotuses in the form of tender palms joined in salutation blossomed like buds.

Beholding her—whose voice was mingled with the sound of long-blown conchs followed by the deep resonance of drums as throngs of bards sang out "Victory! Victory! ever more loudly; who was surrounded by a tumultuous noise of *kāhala* horns blended with extremely sweet, low-pitched melodies (*kākalī*), accompanied by the forceful striking of *mṛdaṅga* drums, the smooth *nihrāda* of cymbals, and the clashing of bronze cymbals (*kāṃsyatāla*); and who was like the Goddess of Victory herself, beautiful with ornaments of pure gold, possessing a mass of dark blue yak-tail fans hanging down from her ears to the ground like sprouting leaves, and holding a lovely, soft lotus in her hand—he gazed upon her.
Jayalakṣmī mounted the young female elephant, which was signaled by the driver in a state of great haste.

Having ascended a great golden saddle-platform, well-fitted with weapons and bows, he sat comfortably upon it—a platform provided with a soft Chinese silk cushion stuffed with swan-down, covered with a rug, and adorned with borders variegated with many jewels, appearing like the very wheels of Indra captured at the start of his conquests. He was accompanied by the son of a feudatory lord named Bāṇadeva, who sat on the seat behind him, wearing a variegated breastplate that shimmered with clusters of light from golden armlets, bracelets, and jeweled necklaces, resembling a wish-fulfilling tree.

He was shielded from the oppressive heat of the sun’s rays by the naturally cool shade of a great white parasol—which resembled a blooming silver lotus, was adorned with a playful canopy of pale-pink silk shimmering with the mass of rays from a great central gem, imitated an autumnal cloud reddened by the morning sun, possessed a massive golden handle, and had its edges smiling with long, dangling clusters of thick pearls—while young women, as beautiful as female elephants, fanned him with chowries held in their hands.

Shining like a rain-cloud with flashes of lightning clinging to its edges—lightning that resembled rows of restless cranes—he passed through the city; and, drawing deep breaths as he advanced, he entered the royal highway, which, due to the great multitude of people, seemed to be vomiting forth the world itself, and which was covered by thousands of eyes cast from the lattice-windows of the beautiful women of the citizens who gazed on him with curiosity, making it appear dark like a cluster of upturned blue lotuses, like a royal swan entering a palace pond.

And suddenly, the city appeared in a state of extreme agitation and tumultuous clamor from its people, who—like women separated from their husbands—were wringing their arms as if to twist themselves away from the sorrow of parting; its mansions were swaying with their foundations loosened by the earth being pressed down by the army, and its banners and flags were struck by the wind from the flapping ears of intoxicated elephants. Handfuls of parched grain fell upon the king like teardrops from the city goddesses, moistening the bamboo enclosures.

The sky over the earth seemed as if swallowed and obscured by a circle of black agalloch incense smoke, like a mass of clouds covering the victorious shoulders of the king. The ocean of the firmament was filled with the fierce rays of the sun, which turned crimson upon mingling with the dust of vermilion from the frontal globes of elephants tossed by the wind from the forest of banners—rays that were like the king’s own golden arrows as he prepared for battle. And the monarch emerged from the city, drawing forth the world like the Golden-Wombed Creator (Hiraṇyagarbha) emerging from the cosmic egg.

And in that city, due to the mutual friction [of the crowds], sounds arose throughout the circle of the quarters, resembling the rush of the waters of the Revā river when its flow is obstructed by a dam, accompanied by a continuous clamor.

There, some proceeded along the paths lined with creepers, accompanied by excellent horses eight years of age, which were filled with the rapid sound of their hooves, repeatedly shedding excessive froth from their mouths as they galloped, appearing like students who had completed their world-renouncing celibacy and were now swiftly taking wives; like reciters of the *Kāśyapīya* school who maintain their positions through the sequential order of the text; like seekers of victory whose bodies are engaged in the exertion of following the cool breezes of the battlefield; and who shook the very head of battle itself.

Others proceeded on horseback, their steeds—whose nostrils were flared wide with great gasps as if agitating their very roots; who, as if constrained by long-standing training, seemed to coil themselves about as their gait was checked; who, as if through skill in prowess, bore the yoke with relaxed jaws; and who, through their agility, leaped over the rows of *tūpacālī* creepers lining the path, moving with the left horses on the left, the right on the right, and those in between crossing over.

Others set forth on a path praised for its excellence, with horses whose forebodies were held high as if out of pride, who seemed to linger over their haunches as if to steady themselves, and who—with heads and feet corresponding to those limbs—seemed to stretch out and pull back as if to conquer the speed of the wind; they galloped along in such a manner.

Likewise, others nurtured their young ones, whose entire bodies were so compressed that they were unable to move, whose limbs were raised up, whose posture was well-settled, whose four hooves had left the surface of the earth, and who were as if unable to breathe because they were not too high.
Some, as if their feet were burning, quickly left the ground and, with their necks bent upward, began to leap like serpents hissing through both hands.

Then certain Vāhīkas, having contracted their fore-limbs and drawn back their hind-quarters, displayed the low-flying path called *sahita*, which is a confused aerial movement resembling the flight of sparrows.

Others performed the *āyata* [gait], with their chests held high in the air, moving with great impetuosity and slow grace, their feet clearly separated by a wide interval, and releasing long, continuous reins.
Others, having taken hold of the hands of those being led over uneven fields, mud, stones, and ditches, maintained the *sanna* [gait] even when exhausted by the effort of stumbling.
Likewise, others proceeded with the *bāhyānuvṛtta* [gait], as if dancing with the playful movements of the intoxicated, moving in a highly curved manner while following the lead of the outer rein.

However, some employed what is called the *prakīrṇaka* (scattered) style, which is more beautiful when performed at a low pitch; it consists of various partial sittings in the first half [of the measure], with the head slightly shaken during the minor transitions (*alpa-saṃkrānti*), and the limbs scattered about.

Some, with their bodies slightly bent as they display a playful form for the sake of others, have their limbs scattered about; this is called *prakīrṇatara*. Some, having first raised their forelimbs, with knees and manes quivering and their bodies well-positioned, move with a slight, upward-turned gait like a cow; with their heads held level and covered, this is called *vellita*. Some, quickly seizing one another’s hands, shifting to the sides, and moving with a playful gait while seated on the other side, perform what is called *siṃhāgata*. Some, with a sudden flash of light... [text ends].

Some, with their front limbs positioned as if suspended in space and their feet bent and tossed upward, stood with their sides evenly distributed and curved, performing the posture named *svastiṣṭhāhita*. Others, with their left feet bent and their right feet striking the ground, moving slightly from their tufts of hair, carrying themselves while seated and motionless, performed the posture named *śārabha*. Still others, with their hindquarters touching the earth and their upper bodies raised toward the sky, leaping in many ways and displaying playful movements that clearly crushed their limbs, performed the posture named *śarabhakrīḍa*.

Some call it *nāma ūrmigata* (the Wave-like), characterized by a body that is both contracted and expanded, with the navel visible while seated, and with balanced physical movements; others call it *trītāla*, characterized by a slightly bent and shaken head, a visible navel, well-composed and extended limbs, a very heavy and harsh sound, a vehicle-like motion through the air, a floor that is mostly untouched, wings displayed unevenly, and a rapid, scattered, full, and restrained movement; and others [call it] *gātraviṣama-samāsana*, where the right foot is gained, the left side is bent, and the body is positioned unevenly.

Some, delighting in the five gestures of the hand, displayed the *pañcapāṇi* style, characterized by grace as the hands moved apart; others, with their bodies first lowered and then raised again and again as they grasped the reins, moving swiftly while showing their wings, displayed the *drāghita* style; and some, with their feet placed upon the ground and not sitting down, slightly bent yet perfectly upright, with their shoulders fixed in the air and their foreheads barely touching the earth—capable of rolling like a pestle even on the ground—they demonstrated the *antari* style, covering a great distance even in a short space, O horses!

Then some [performed] the *māyūra* [gait], which is initiated by the wings of the *dhurita* path, with the neck raised and bent; some [performed] the *suba...* [gait], in which the limbs are contracted, sweet, and swift; some [performed] the *sthitavāma*, in which the body is extended and rigid, the limbs are exceedingly harsh and soft and swift, and the gaze of the *dhurita* and *tvarita* is forgotten; some [performed] the *naṭanākula*, in which the left side is lowered first as the right is released swiftly; and some [performed] the *tvaritavīkṣita*, characterized by frequent glances.

Some [horses] were named Velagātra, their bodies touched by the auspicious western seat that vibrated profusely from front to back; some were named Muktavalāhaka, touching the sky as if they were reaching the heavens, their thunderous hoof-beats rivaling the roar of clouds, their limbs restrained yet free from mist; some had foreheads, hips, flanks, ears, bracelets, bellies, side-glances, and manes... [moving] with a single channel, capable of traveling half a *yojana* on a single stride.

Having approached it, they proceeded on horseback following the mind of their riders, toward that [lake] named Utkṣubhitaplavamārga, which resembled a ship sailing upon the ocean and whose path was agitated by waves.

Displaying their heroic youth through various playful maneuvers on noble steeds, with their bodies bent, straightened, tossed up, cast down, and rapidly agitated by their riders, they followed the gait of cows near the necks of their mounts; and while showing left, right, and middle turns, as well as neighing and side-leaps that were not overly charming, they moved slowly, occasionally stepping a little further due to the intoxication of youth before resuming their pace, yet unable to avoid perspiration and being held back by the crush of the crowd.

And the elephant-drivers, with their bodies composed and held high, displaying a graceful and beautiful gait characterized by the rhythmic movement of the *paṇava* drum, led the elephants—whether moving slowly, in thick clusters, or at a moderate pace—with playful ease through steps that were half-knee-deep, full-footed, half-knee-deep, or one and a half steps long, according to the occasion; they proceeded at a comfortable pace after having paused for a moment, while those who watched them felt filled with wonder.

Gradually, he acquired the prosperity born of his rule over the countryside; his resources were augmented by hundreds of thousands of troops consisting of elephants, horses, and chariots moving in dense columns. Through the acquisition of vast territories, he assumed various distinct colors; and as he seized the entire circle of the ten directions, falling amidst the cage of swords playfully brandished by thousands of soldiers of unrestrained pride, he carried with him umbrellas, chowries, banners, and flags. He passed over the entire assembly of kings with impatient disregard, their facial complexions soiled by their hurried retreat.

A mass of dust belonging to the king—acting as a crest-jewel upon the head of the wretched [people], encompassing all the mountains, forests, oceans, islands, and coastal regions, and having forcibly obstructed and condensed the flow of all the rivers by its own will—set forth, turbid with excessive growth, like King Nahuṣa ascending even to heaven.

And he, like a mass of frost, turned the lotus-faces of the women in the camp grey; as if out of indignation at being seized by those lotuses, he swallowed the scorching rays of the sun; as if his intense thirst were fueled by the internal burning of that heat, he drank the ichor of the elephants to his heart's content; intoxicated as if by drinking the wine of their rut, he stumbled upon the edges of sword-blades; and as if overwhelmed by wounds from swords, he fell unconscious upon the frontal globes of the elephants.

Then, smeared with the vermilion from the jars being shaken up, as if drenched in liquid and fanned by palm-leaf fans, he rose up slowly and slowly. Having risen, he approached the silken cloths of the banners as if to seize the edges of his bandages. And struck by the wind of the banner-cloths, the mass of dust once again ascended into the sky like a man of merit returning to heaven.

And with that amassed host, he overspread the surface of the sky—which was green with the gold and jewels of many bubbles—like a bed of lotus leaves, where the orb of the sun was rosy-red from being drenched by the lustre of the crest-jewels of the entire circle of kings; where the swans of the gods were struck by the wind from the fluttering banners, as if they were circles of lotus stalks upon the shoulders [of the earth]; and where the walls of the serpent’s hoods were white and formidable due to the clatter of thousands of hooves filled with the force of a swift gallop, appearing dark blue like a swarm of bees amidst thick pollen.

And then, like a submarine fire, the flood of light from the ornaments of the lords of the earth leaped up here and there from the ocean of dust. In some places, they discharged what seemed like a shower of portentous meteors, foreboding the defeat of the turbid dust. And in other places, the moon-like chowries, moving their handles as they were fashioned by the trunks of herds of elephants and scattering a spray of water-drops from those trunks, seemed to sweep away the darkness, yet in another sense, they seemed to sweep away the very dust itself as they whirled about.

The dust of the army, resembling the mass of smoke from the fire at the end of an aeon, with its banners—whose tongues of fluttering, curved silken cloths seemed like serpents—acting as pillars for the heavens, appeared as if it desired once more to conquer the netherworld (Pātāla) out of pride; indeed, because of such a vast accumulation of battle-dust, which resembled the submarine fire consuming the depths of the ocean, the oceans did not turn into dry land, even though they were no longer overwhelmed by water.

Then, having dispersed the king of sages as much as possible by wandering here and there as if to remove the congestion of the camp—with a wind from the army that carried a stream of water like the spray from the trunks of elephants, which rained away the sweat from the cheeks of powerful courtesans; which was variegated by clusters of frothy saliva forgotten from the tossing mouths of horses clinking with harsh bits; and which was grey with the pollen of lotuses crushed by the petals of its force—[the king was] impelled by the words of the polished sword-blade, which had been brandished with the arrogance of swift and skillful maneuvers.

And when the dust had subsided, the mirror of the sky-jewel attained clarity as if polished by the silken garments of swaying plantain trees. The quarters of the horizon receded as if scattered by the force of a troop of most fleet-footed horses. The day shone with its surface reddened by the light of gems, as if emerging from the sea-monster’s mouth within the crowns of a hundred kings. The mountain-like herds of elephants appeared like the waters of the ocean rising up, their fluttering wings—the waving chowries—interlaced with the rays of jewels.

The earth, though solidified by the trampling of thousands of elephants' feet as if made of adamant, did not again succumb to agitation even during that powerful upheaval of the army. The three worlds became stainless, freed from the thick dust as if from a freshly washed womb of blossoms. Like does whose range is unimpeded, the glances began to roam at will across the quarters dark with fresh durvā grass.

Having traversed a road of about a *gavyūti*—which was difficult to pass due to the mire formed by the streams of ichor flowing from the temples of rutting elephants, and where it was hard to find a place to set foot because of the pressure of the army’s weight—he reached a place where a continuous hedge of thorns had been constructed as a perimeter, where the stables for the favorite horses were divided into very spacious inner sections, and where a vast collection of cloth tents and awnings had been pitched in the riding grounds; here let there be thatched walls for those who are weary.

Thus shall the protection be ensured. Let the ropes be arranged here in rows; let the winnowing-basket be placed here. Here, a long piece of coarse cloth serves as a kitchen curtain that encloses this entire area. Fetch straw from nearby, O princes, before others carry it away. Quickly gather the water in the pitchers; the sight of them will soon become turbid at the edge of the milking-pail. What is this arrogance, that one wanders unawares into the midst of another’s dwelling?

"Indeed, why is this enclosure fashioned of jewels being broken? This region is level; yet why is this anthill so terrifying? This marshy bank is shady, but the river is fickle. This circle of shrubs is like a kingdom of gods, yet this seat—a banyan tree as smooth as a rutting elephant—is surrounded by borders that are not very pure, though this perimeter of *naktamāla* trees is pristine."

"Not far from the market of the gods, you have become thin with hunger; yet, though sent ahead to heaven, whom did you not seize? Many powerful favorites of the king have seized the places I had taken. For what purpose were you sent first? Surely the surrounding lands are bright, but this black soil is fit for the lowest caste; it is not auspicious for me, a Brahmin. Only the white soil produced in Malaya was sought by me for a long time. How is it that this yellow soil, fit for a Vaiśya, has been prepared as a site for me, a mere kṣatriya?"

It is as if it were red, like a milk-bird; yet this earth here is not that [red] earth, for when dug up, there is only red sand. It does not suck up water like a sponge, being covered by its own dust. O you who travel on the road, go away quickly! These storytellers are hanging about. Once we have entered, all the camp-folk will surely follow us, leaving behind only our men. This place is exceedingly brave, yet let none of us wander here; not even a single person is seen who might approach us. ... [This is] in the service of a wicked master.

Surely one’s path here is obstructed by the chatter of rogues; for whom is progress possible when the way is crowded with complications? The roads are knee-deep in the mire of rutting elephants, difficult to traverse due to the darkness of dust, and the tracks of horses are blocked by a powerful throng of oxen. Amidst this, the sound of signal-drums—announcing the shifting of the feudal lords' encampments—is raised like the rumbling of fresh clouds, mingled with the shrill blast of conchs, and accompanied by the cries of those accustomed to the talk of the *la*...ṭāls.

A great clamor of troops, as thick as the roar of the Bhāgīrathī falling into the vast caverns of the Himālaya when she has slipped from the mass of matted locks of Śiva, filled the air; and he, with all his activities and efforts concentrated on valor for the march, passed the day unhindered, as if his exertions to receive respectful offerings had been suspended.

Then, its splendor eclipsed by the thick dust raised by the vast armies, the day departed for the forests of the western mountain like the submarine fire of Agni, having seemingly renounced its beauty after being swallowed and released by the circle of parasols belonging to hundreds of kings—its crimson robes stained with the liquid red chalk of the mountain. The twilight, turning blood-red, appeared as if it were a flow of blood dripping from the sprouts of the sun’s chariot, which had been split at its hard, sharp tip by the crowns of a hundred monarchs.

The path through the quarters, darkened by the speed of the army’s march and the lashes of the whips upon the plantain-like banners, caused the emergence of shimmering stars in the sky to quiver as if with a thrill of fatigue, like the rising of goosebumps on one who had fled in terror from the blows of the flapping ears of elephants that resembled streaks of darkness. Even the dense mass of gloom did not cause the pairs of cakravāka birds to part for a moment, as they mistook it for a herd of elephants.

The lotuses closed their petals as if to conceal the sun, who was shrinking in fear of the re-emergence of Balarāma’s dust; the lilies, with their dark locks of bees clinging to them, began to blossom like ears with sprouting leaf-ornaments, startled by the harsh and manifest clamor [of the army]; and the night, its feet reddened, rolled out from the womb of the eastern horizon like a fetus agitated by the trembling of the forest-arms of the earth, oppressed by the rising of the powerful force.

Like a fraudulent army relying on a nocturnal ambush, the flower-bowed god roamed about, throwing the camp—where everyone was stationed with trepidation—into utter confusion with a rain of arrows. He pierced the host of lovers, who were already overwhelmed by separation from their young jasmine brides, as if he himself were afflicted by both sides; for the moon, the kinsman of the night-lotuses, having pursued them, struck them violently, as if displaying the plight of a military force beset by its own ally, the fish-bannered god of love.

The *kalakala* sound of lutes being tuned was heard—the very cause of passion—displaying the skill of striking as if they were the armies of the God of Love. The army of amorous women drank deeply of sweet wine, as if for a heroic draught before the battle of love. With the setting of the sun, the moon-like faces of beautiful women, rendered helpless, seemed to borrow the shimmering glow of twilight from the Mandara-colored rays; the masses of light, like great warriors, drank from the fire-like flame of desire, which had its sprout-like lower lip as its source.

Girdles, adorned with tinkling bells, jingled upon their hips like the war-drums heralding the expedition for the conquest of the quarters by the god whose banner is the sea-monster (Kāmadeva). Their cheeks were mottled with clear drops of perspiration as their lips were bitten in the throes of pain caused by the strikes of cold nails concealed by intense passion; they were filled with fury provoked by unrestrained insults born of arrogance, while their chests were struck by the palms of hands that had momentarily paused to praise one another’s deeds.

A duel for sport commenced among the youths, who were unbroken in their self-respect; it was crowded with the seizing and retreating of blows exchanged, marked by the mutual glances of blood-red and crooked eyes, full of resolve, and consisting of many difficult feats of skill.

In this very manner, the night reached its conclusion. Then followed the pairs of swans, moving with slow and gentle steps as if weary from amorous play; they were accompanied by throngs of bards chanting auspicious songs. Their swift flight was stirred by the shaking of the lion-manes, which had been turned grey by a shower of frost-drops. They drank in the beauty of the lotuses, whose honey was sweetened by intoxication, while they ruthlessly dispelled the sleep that had firmly settled upon them. They drew along the tinkling sound of chains rattling on the feet of intoxicated elephants rising from their beds.
The morning breezes began to stir the camp as if they were themselves being drawn along.

But the lord of men, having passed the night in the company of his heart-stealing beloved and in the very thought of battle, arose at daybreak with his army already arrayed for combat; like the sun emitting its thousand rays of light, he set forth facing westward. When the king had halted after a few stages of the journey, a certain man arrived from the enemy's camp and addressed him in private.

The King of the Mālavas, arrogant due to the power of his divine tutelary deity, has indeed come for the victory of Your Majesty; he is currently at a distance of three *yojanas* from here. It is said that his forces were formerly subdued by Your Majesty in battles where favorable omens appeared; having been conquered, they now remain exceedingly joyful, their heads adorned with turbans fashioned from the moonlight of Your Majesty’s toenails, while the sounds of "Victory!"—uttered with difficulty as their lips were parched by Your Majesty’s hot breath—reach them.

The eastern kings, fragrant as the *pārñjana* flower, follow you like winds following the rainy season. [Your] essence is like the thunderbolt. Indeed, you are the master capable of bringing even Death itself to its end. (Why so? Perform an unsurpassed slaughter of all the Kṣatriyas intent on seizing the cattle!

This being so, Vijaya was also defeated... having been dismissed from his position in the assembly, he spoke these words with wisdom in the presence of all the vassal lords: "In former times, it is said, the subjects, distressed by the lack of a protector, took refuge under Manu, the first king; protected by him, they lived in peace and entered into the three goals of human life according to the law of the fish (*mātsyanyāya*)."

From that time forward, there arose the caste known as Kṣatriya—a name of exalted merit—whose support was its own arms, whose kinsmen were weapons, whose wife was the earth, whose essence was fame, and which awaited death in battle. And just as gold shines with increasing brilliance the more it is heated, so too did that caste blaze with excellence. Yet, for him [the king], that caste remained in a state of unfulfilled potential, for he had not yet attained the mastery of the battlefield.

In this world, indeed, a poet who lacks inspiration; one who desires to debate but is lacking in confidence; a commentator who is unable to discern the meaning; a physician who does not wish to treat; a judge who is intolerant and lacks discrimination; a merchant who is indolent; a minister who speaks untruths; a priest who is ignorant of the Atharva Veda; a king who acts improperly; a servant who knows only grand gestures but lacks practical skill; a woman of ill character who is difficult to approach; a relative who makes no effort; a singer who has no throat [for singing]; a dancer whose limbs are untrained; an ascetic who cannot endure hardship; and a person devoid of compassion—[all these are failures in their respective fields].

Śākyamuni is a son of noble family who lacks shame; he is a friend who provides no benefit and a king who is lacking in prowess—thus, this class [of allies] is of no avail. Now, however, the time for valor has arrived, for the enemy is close at hand and has assembled his forces. Therefore, in this great sacrifice of battle, where the fire of friction is kindled by successive steps, let those who desire to ascend to the realm of Indra offer their bodies as oblations and enter by this straight path according to their pleasure.

"Let him who has no concern for his purpose, nor for his beloved life, nor for the discharge of his debt; let him whose lineage is yet unestablished or whose desires remain unfulfilled; let him whose mind is unsated by a wife recently acquired; let him who is the only son of his parents, or upon whose death the heavy burden of the family falls; let him who has faith in asceticism, or who seeks to conquer those worlds by other means—let such a person turn back from here. Thus he issued this proclamation.

And so, when her husband had spoken these words, there emerged from the ranks one named Siṃhavarman, the King of Aṅga—a man radiant as molten gold, with rounded, long arms, a broad chest, and tall as a tree—who, inflaming the hearts of the kings, spoke with knitted brows, his voice deep like the roar of a thundercloud: "What Your Majesty has said is true; indeed, the name 'Kṣatriya' is utterly useless for one devoid of valor, like a sesame seed without its oil."

A man devoid of human pride does not disregard the arrogance of others; yet that wretch causes prosperity that has come face-to-face to fall away, screens out the autumnal moonlight, leaps over the stream of nectar, obstructs the Malaya breeze, closes his nostrils at the scent of the *pārijāta* flower, shuts his eyes upon entering a spring garden, and puts on a cloak when sandalwood paste is being applied—such is he who...

Having failed to experience the great festival of battle—which has arrived as sought after by hundreds of mental longings—he turns back. What kind of contemptible man indeed is such a person? These kings are not like that; for their valor is bound to their horses, like that of wild elephants with rutting ichor flowing; their natural roar obstructs all directions, like the thundering of clouds; and their innate, great majesty is unbearable to others, like that of venomous serpents.

They possess an innate strength capable of crushing the lineages of rival kings, like the power of the winds at the end of an aeon; they possess a majesty that devours vast quantities of water, like the oceans under their own control. Furthermore, the knitting of their brows never fails to result in the defeat of their enemies.

There is no throbbing of his firm lower lip, no twitching of the right eye of his enemies' wives, no emergence of sweat upon his forehead, no dullness in the rising of his life-force, and no trembling of his head despite the brilliance of his wrathful gaze at the enemy... here the frown ascends like a mass of sprouts from the forest fire of the playful night of Kālī; here the horripilation plays upon the surfaces of his cheeks as if arising from the essence of his valor; and here, having found their prey, his harsh and blood-red glances of pride fashion their sport.

They were like the Śabarī of Fortune, whose passion was fixed upon his feet. They did not possess such intense longing for the fruits of sovereignty as those who long for the fruits of arrows upon their bows; they were not so thirsty for the streams from water-pitchers as they were for the blood flowing from the edges of swords; they were not so eager for the application of saffron paste as they were for the application of vermilion; they did not have their affection bound by the sight of death as others are by the sight of death itself; and they took no pride in the binding of vassal-bands as if they were the binding of bandages upon wounds.

In pleasure groves like forests of plantain trees, these lords of the earth—following in the wake of Jarāsaṃdha, Vṛkodara, and the noble lion-like Māna—do not lie upon their couches with bodies weary from toil, nor do they sleep soundly upon beds as soft as the fur of a tiger. Yet, under your command, there is nothing whatsoever difficult for them to accomplish; they would even thirstily drink up the oceans, whose waters are like blue lotuses reddened by the submarine fire.

Like flowering creepers, they might gracefully bend even the quarters of the sky, which are themselves shimmering with planets and stars; like a wheel, they might whirl with their fingers the heart of the rising sun, flushed with crimson; like a white lotus with its stalk, they might fashion the moon—with its white rays—into an ear-ornament; they do not care for the lifting of the earth, considering it merely the discarded remains of the Great Boar’s meal; nor do they hold in high regard the displacement of the mountain ranges, regarding it as the mere leavings of another’s prowess with the bow.

They maintain that even the reduction of the entire world to ashes is merely struck by the fire at the end of an aeon (*kalpānala*); what account, then, can there be for these lions among men in their seizing of the multitude of enemy hosts? As for that which was proposed by Your Majesty as a cause for desisting from battle—that heaven is uncertain in death on the battlefield—this doubt regarding the scripture applies equally to sacrifices and other such rites. As for the fact that life is dear, that has already been secured by your own previous meritorious deeds.

"Debt must be discharged"—the debt for the sustenance provided by a powerful master is indeed heavy. "Offspring has not been produced"—in this matter, offspring that remains barren is easily found. "Desires are unfulfilled"—this is not the case for you, who are like a wish-granting tree (*kalpataru*) upon the earth. "Not satisfied with wives"—for one whose virility has ceased through the abandonment of battle, what is the use of wives? "The only son of his parents"—he alone is the one who possesses vital warmth, by whom his parents truly possess living sons.

What person of sound mind would destroy his own self for the sake of an external object? As for the thought, "I shall practice asceticism," that involves long-term suffering and yields but meager fruit. It is possible to conquer the next world by other means as well; what kind of victory is it that one dies without hearing the whirring of a sharp sword, without the discharge of a drawn and formidable bow, and without the hurling of spears, javelins, and iron clubs?

"Then, like at the time of universal dissolution, flood the entire circle of the quarters with great clouds that possess the thundering of mad elephants and the roar of lightning, with millions of high and low waves. Let it be today or tomorrow; let the earth be filled by the weight of the crowns upon the heads of the enemy kings who are as terrifying as mountain peaks, and let the expanse of the city be covered by a canopy of spreading, vast coral creepers, so that the four oceans joined together appear as one. Thus he ceased speaking.

The other swift warriors also roared according to their respective natures—a sound as deep as the resonance of a mṛdaṅga drum accompanying the playful song of royal fortune, and generating a fever throughout the world with the speed of their impetuous onset.

When those thunderous roars had ceased and the preceding winds had subsided, and when their cheeks—once flushed with the flickering redness of indragopa insects—had become clear, the Royal Swan (Rājahaṃsa), casting his eye upon the commander-in-chief, spoke in a voice that mimicked the tinkling of anklets upon the beauty of a blooming lotus-face: "Has the battlefield been thoroughly searched?"

Having prostrated himself, he addressed him: "O Lord! This ground, extending for about a *goruta* from here, has indeed been thoroughly searched. Beyond this lies a region that possesses an abundance of water and is endowed with desirable taste, color, fragrance, and configuration; it is free from pits, devoid of instability, and contains no terrifying places, chariot-paths, or rat-traps. It is free of stumps, chasms, and mud, and is capable of accommodating the free movement of even the entire multitude of living beings in the world. It is as if this earth were intentionally fashioned for the very purpose of battle."

Then the lord of the earth, having dispatched a message through the mouth of a certain messenger to the King of Mālava—stating that "we have not yet been granted [the lands] requested by you in this vast forest"—and having commanded the military commander, "Show the excellent elephants and horses tomorrow," dismissed his court and entered the inner apartments.

Having performed his daily duties, and having worshipped the divine Twilight—who was like the vermilion-streaked lip of the maiden of the western quarter upon the lotus of the day—at a time when the darkness was intense, the stars were obscured, the sky was agitated, the birds were nestled in their nests, the owls rejoiced, the moon shone upon the night-lotuses, and a gentle breeze blew; at this hour of evening, when the light of dawn was beginning to arise to subdue the gloom, he lay down to rest.

When the morning breeze blew gently—caressing the trees and creepers, shimmering with fragments of blossoms, and scattering drops of frost; when the flocks of birds raised their wings again and again to prepare for flight toward the ten directions, their mouths resonant with song; when the lotus-beds were smiling and the groves of night-lilies were fading; [the king], awakened by the auspicious songs of bards, performed his morning rites appropriate for the break of day, and having completed his ritual observances and personal adornments, he went forth.

Having ascended a couch constructed from various choice timbers, with a smooth earthen floor fashioned upon it and draped with a cluster of offering flowers, the lord of men sat comfortably, leaning against a cushioned coverlet. Shielded from the sun by the circle of a peacock-feather parasol as grand as a polished golden staff, surrounded by a few trusted vassals, and with the tips of his curly locks dancing in the breeze of the fly-whisks waved by the vine-like arms of courtesans, he remained there like the Lord of the Gods in heaven.
Of him, who blazes with his own splendor, the orb of the young sun is perceived as if it were a reflection transferred into the ocean of the sky.

Then, in an instant, his approach was heralded by the fierce and violent clamor of the preceding infantry, sounding like the warbling of flocks of *pattikala* birds; he was like Vainateya, before whom the entire world of serpents had fled in terror at the news of heaven; his vast army was inferred by the nearby trees, which—trembling as if agitated by the fear of being broken by the shaking of his lord’s arms—seemed to support his massive force; with the peak of his head stained by the crimson glow of abundant vermilion, he appeared like the mountain of setting suns, fixed firmly for the purpose of causing the sunset of the entire circle of radiant kings.

Supported by his feet, with beautiful *puṣkara* drums held by long, thick fingers capable of delivering clear blows, possessing well-proportioned and sweet *vaṃśa* flutes and *paṇavaka* drums, and resounding with the rhythmic sound of *tāla* that was lovely to hear; beautified by the singing of intoxicated female bees and displaying the splendor of love through the exquisite beauty of its wonderful canopy; it was like a moving pavilion for music belonging to the Royal Fortune (*rājalakṣmī*), who moves with the grace of variegated steps—[a pavilion] where the white silk of the Lord of Beasts, crushed by innate enmity, [was spread].

With his two forelegs entwined as if by a continuous web of matted hair, and his forearms thick with a network of veins, he sat upon the lap of Lakṣmī resting on the lotus-throne of the chariot-pole; his two exceedingly glossy eyes, like two cups of honey for the increase of intoxication, were fixed forward by some unseen force, as if longing to drink from the waves stirred by the wind of his flapping ears that struck against his bracelets in the lake of light, repeatedly manifesting a gait bent low as if out of thirst.

Drinking in the fire of the rival elephants' prowess, with his lips, palate, and tongue red as if from the heat, repeatedly brandishing his body as if it were scarred by the whirling of the discus in his desire for victory; touching the earth with the tips of his young sprout-like trunk-tendrils out of devotion to his master; wandering about with a companion elephant, occasionally sniffing out another elephant's track and, out of indignation toward the unheeding driver, sidling his foot and casting a sidelong glance.

Having, as it were, smiled slightly with his face, he set out once more according to his own will; like Śrīparvata, he was honored by the Lord; like Kailāsa, his nature was resplendent; like Mandara, he possessed golden peaks; like Maināka, he was capable of protecting his own side; like Malaya, he was intent upon the south; like Sahya, he was joined with the western region; like Vindhya, the weight of his birth from the jar [Agastya] was to be inferred from the slopes of his head; like the Wind-born [Hanumān], he was capable of seizing [his prey]; like the Snowy Mountain [Himālaya]—

With a singular nature of lofty beauty, rising high like the mountain of sunrise (Udaya-parvata), and possessing a strength equal to all other mountains, Hemakūṭa—another lord of mountains as if fashioned by Prajāpati—approached that region, as if anointing it with his splendor. Though difficult to restrain today, he was not subject to his own passion; though possessed of desire, he was not devoid of limbs; though possessing a peak, he performed virtuous conduct; and though bees clung to his temples, he was beyond the reach of worldly objects. Thus the golden-peaked Hemakūṭa arrived at that place.

Beholding that royal forest—which was like the Nandana grove, with its fluttering wings and its king of birds (the peacock), and which was to be gazed upon by the gods without blinking—the lord of the earth considered his enemy’s army truly invincible. Cherished by the conciliatory words of his chief counselor, and regarding everything as if it were composed of nectar, the officer in charge of the forces, following the king who was thus being protected and gathered [around him], spoke these well-formed words with palms joined in reverence: "Behold, O King! As if desiring to seize the sun in the sky, the king of serpents opens his mouth wide, as if to swallow the thunderbolt."

And his trunk, acting as a victory banner that terrifies all the Dānavas, is long like the stride of Nārāyaṇa expanding at the time of the cosmic dissolution; it is sprinkled with white spray from the celestial river and resembles a face-covering garland cast upon the water. Furthermore, the great cave of his mouth appears like a cavern of the Golden Mountain (Hemakūṭa), resembling a house of ruby-encrusted gems that showers a soft, dark-red luster.

This Nardana, possessing large manes, endowed with a heavy strength difficult to bear due to the quality of his rut, guarding his circle [of followers], and crushing donkeys, horses, carts, and elephants, stands here making a great roar.

Like a lover, he does not fail to delight with his virtues those standing at his sides, as if they were the breasts of a beloved pressed against him; he has attained equality even with Maināka and Vainateya, who dwell on both flanks like his own shoulders; he is firm in prowess as if his own shoulder were built up, and broad in fame as if it were his broad chest; and his body—capable of enduring the action of thunderclouds whose roar is as terrible as the fall of Indra’s thunderbolt—is long, expansive, and of great luster, while being unemaciated, straight, and well-rounded.

His body, like an excellent wife, carries even a most heavy burden as if it were light; his feet are observed to be free from hair, as clear as autumnal water, as devoid of down as the youth of Devayānī, and as smooth and unblemished as a surface of jewels.

Though endowed with oiliness and softness, it is harsh from the impact of arrows; though limited by the number two, it possesses infinite divisions; though its pair of ear-leaf-like ears kisses the maidens of the quarters, it is filled with internal fear due to the pretext of the glossy hooves cast wide by the tips of its hoofs—thus, as if out of dread, it takes refuge at its own feet. In this state, it provides space for the moon of the twenty-elephant array (viṃśatikari-kṛte vaiṣapatte candram), which has been driven away by another woman; and like one who is not a brother, it grants room to the Kāśya [elephant] out of fear of being banished by its extremely harsh egoism.

Becoming minute, as if emerging one by one from a covering of smooth hair, these soft whorls [of his trunk] are like soft coils. And he—this fearless treasury of splendor in places of terror, one who knows his purpose, who has brought his anger under control, brave, wise, virtuous, gentle, delighting in battle, and free from distress—is, through your power, Airāvata, the lord of elephants, descended as it were to earth. Might he not indeed destroy the rival lineage of the world-elephants, and might he not surely shatter the peaks of the rising mountain of enemy elephants?

Then, after that elephant had departed—honored by the King of Men with a stalk of *puṇḍra* sugarcane offered from his own hand—other lords of elephants appeared in succession. Some were *kīpalās*, capable of delighting in battle, their temples darkened by ichor dripping in clusters like swarms of bees, resembling jeweled stone slabs spread over a bed of young *tāla* leaves. Others, with faces veiled in saffron-colored cloths as if being scorched by an unquenchable fire, were as terrible as the world’s destruction, with flickering lightning-flashes for sprouts.

Some were like clouds at the time of universal dissolution; some, as if assuming the playful stance of the Great Boar, were tearing the earth downward with the tips of their eternal tusks; some were roaring toward the mountain ranges whose ridges had been thrown into turmoil by lions, as if summoning them to battle; some wandered about like messengers of Death, ensnaring people with their outstretched hands and feet; and some, as if in vain, were emitting long hisses out of distress, resembling the sighs of people who have entered [the city] bringing tribute.

Some, as if vomiting forth speed, were impetuous in breaking the harsh external bars of the gates with their sluggish trunks; they were being restrained with effort by mahouts whose bodies were bent forward and who, fearing the snapping of their tusks, employed cruel goads against those destined for departure. Others, their forms obscured by clouds of dust raised from the battered walls of the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, appeared as if smoke-greyed by the fire of their own wrath; they brought down temple trees with the broad blows of their frontal globes.

Acting as if they were prepared for an encounter with rival elephants, accompanied by conchs, cymbals, and drums, appearing like golden [mountains], as if composed of beauty, passion, pride, and steadfastness—mostly noble, following the nature of slow-moving elephants, yet possessing the character of wild beasts—even though they were like frost to the great medicinal herb of fame, these lords of the herd, captivating the eyes of the protector of the earth, seemed to contract the entire circle of the quarters with their own height.

And pointing them out, the commander of the forces [described] those born in the forest of the lord of the earth... deeply immersed, their fears dispelled... traveling through waters turbid with mud and otherwise clear at other times; gazing upon the *kāśa* forests on the banks of the Kauśikī; wandering through the lands of Kāla; possessing the fragrance of the bark of *āgaru* trees on the broad banks of the Lauhitya; having the fresh red hue of conch shells; having the eastern ocean turned grey by the spray of sand tossed up during their impetuous play on the riverbanks; and having the water-birds (or "water-leaf-chariots") agitated.

Addicted to the sport of splashing through water and land, they frequent the slopes of the mountain ridges where their tawny monkey-like forms are mirrored; they spend the midday heat of summer crossing the waters of the Gomatī while embracing clusters of lotuses and lilies; they take refuge in the Bhāgīrathī, cooled by the flood of liquid from masses of snow-stones melted by the day’s scorching heat; they tear at the peaks of the mountains that are their kin with their teeth and claws; they roam upon the slopes of those mountains that have been beautifully wedded to the weight of fresh clouds; and they shake the heights of lofty peaks with their repeatedly traversing paws.

The mountains, whose ox-carts were covered in the dust of the [earth] element, extended as far as the lands of Kālida, Kāla, Kīṭaka, Āśi, Kosala, Kirāta, Puṇḍra, Malla, Mala, Magadha, Aṅga, and Vaṅga; by their very nature as forests, they possessed moderate strength and speed, were slightly elevated at the tips, and roared with sudden bursts; their heels, hooves, tusks, flanks, bellies, peaks, lips, and ears were not particularly prominent, yet they exhaled great heat from within and belonged to a noble lineage; they had broad trunks, possessed tails, and were free from the defect of sluggishness due to their physical exertion.

And likewise, there were excellent forest-born elephants brought forth, possessing the valor born of victorious deeds; these were produced in the forests of the Cedis and Karūṣakas, frequenting the waters of the Revā and Śoṇa rivers, roaming between the eastern and western oceans. They raised a tumultuous clamor during their bandha-yuddhas (combat-arrays), and with the tips of their tusks, they scraped the ground at the peaks of the Mālyavat mountain. They shattered the thickets of trees on Mount Dhundhu with their temporal secretions, and their deep thundering served as a master teacher for the wild dancing of peacocks intoxicated by rut. Their flanks were marked by the spray of waterfalls, and the heat of their summer torments was cooled by the moss growing upon those slopes.

Delighting in the mountain regions of Priyanāga, Priyaprasthaka, Caiti, Dīha, Nandina, Kaśika, and Śyāmūka, they were enriched by forests; dwelling on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, they plucked jackfruit from its roots; they were greedy for the taste of the spreading filaments of the Tamālā lotuses; they carried the cries of the forest deer of the Prabhla river-banks; they were fondly fed morsels of parched grain, white seeds, and water-lilies; they caused the clusters of shining Udumbara, Kaṭodumbara, and Kadamba trees to tremble; they longed to drink from the Pampā lake; and they sported in the waters of the Śuktimatī river, which was as bright as a broken pearl.

The excellent elephants have their attachment severed; they are as dark as the color of time, with teeth of minute hue, swift-moving, with lofty faces, fierce, with beautiful feet, and neither too long.

These people of Daśārṇa, born from the forest-tracts [of that land], are like the sons of the Yamunā, possessing a complexion as dark as her waters; they are like husbands of the Vetravatī, never satiated by its enjoyment; they are like friends of the Sukara-chāyā, drawn by its natural flavor; they are like servants of the Citra-mālya-vanī, devoted to constant attendance; and like the inhabitants of Veṇuvatī, they respond to the sound of the flute. Affectionate toward the Vatsa country, they have thick faces and hands, fine and sparse moles, large heads and necks, and broad chests and teeth.

There were rutting elephants with long trunks and webbed toes, accustomed to firm blows, with eyes honey-brown in hue; their temples were moist with the joy born of the flow of ichor, their hindquarters were exceedingly developed, and they were generally the color of lotuses.

(e) These [beings], born in a forest where the ground was studded with mountain peaks shattered by the bodies of fighting gods and asuras, where the essence of living beings had fallen along with their blood, and where the growth of trees, creepers, and grasses increased; there they subsisted on clusters of young shoots from *nālika*, *tīra*, *karṇikāra*, *nāga*, *plakṣa*, and *pravāla* trees, and they were like great-bodied *śalmali* trees, white as the banks of the Indus, with *dhava*, *madhūka*, *nyagrodha*, *gṛdhra*, and *atīra* trees, and *tini* bushes.

In the stalks of the *ekameda*, *modakī*, *ikṣurita*, rough *śirīṣa*, *aśvattha*, white *valāgni*, *bahukrānta*, *tanuvṛndāraka*, and *ikṣupālikā*, they were intent upon the *śṛṅgāṭaka*, its juice, its stalk, the *nāḷikā*, *nalana*, *tāla*, and *nalapotikā*; they were devoted to the *sika*, *kaṭama*, and *anu*, having abandoned their desire for the rice and lotus-roots within the bowers of every grove.

[The elephants] who swallow the *ākacchapā* fruits, who tear apart the *kākaṇḍupatikā* with their tusks, whose trunks grasp the *śyāmāka* grain; who have destroyed the *jambu* forests, who have cut and shattered the excellent *śleṣmātaka* trees on the banks of the Śreṣṭhavatī; who have churned the reeds and *vañjula* trees on the shores of the earth; who, by the force of the wind from their tusks thrusting into the mud-banks, have uprooted the pure *tamāla* trees growing in the thickets of the riverbanks; who break the *piñchā* reeds upon the sandbanks; [these are] those who long for the lovely women of Avantī.

With their bodies and skins made immortal by our favors, they were astonished by inexhaustible enjoyments; they were restless with the intense joy of wandering, smelling the fresh scent of tigresses, tossing playfully like waves of young monkeys, possessing the full expansion of a hundredfold portions, sleeping at will after being warmed by the fierce dust beloved by the wives of others, moving freely among the clusters of Pāriyātra mountains, leading the way in the descent from the Sūpakūṭa mountain, and sporting with the white-flowered Vāsantī trees on the slopes of the snowy mountains and mango groves.

Those elephants possessing a measure of one-sixteenth of a *kalā*, who are skilled in their own eyes, teeth, gait, and bearing; who are endowed with the perfection of size, strength, body, and courage; whose lips, palate, and tongue are red; who resemble great boars or lions; who have swift and long strides; who are not timid; whose hair is glossy; and who are elevated, fortunate, and fit for enjoyment—these are the "fragrant" (*gandha*) elephants.

These [mountains], born in the Kalinga forest, extend as far as the kings of Kaliṅga, Utkala, Mahiṣaka, Andhra, Chakacha, Kuḍumba, Puṇnāḍha, Prāṅkaṇa, Kerala, Cola, and Pāṇḍya; they traverse the Tailā, Ikṣumatī, Laṅkā, Vaitaraṇī, Mahoṣā, Aṣavatī, Nakranavā, Śuṣkanadī, Śvasenā, Veṇā, Kṛṣṇaveṇā, Suprayogā, Godāvarī, Cūrṇī, Sūkarikā, Sannīrā, Praveṇī, Vaisyā, Tāmraparṇī, Kuñjā, Kumārī, and the Agastyatīrtha on the southern ocean.

They have a mind like a lake; their breath is through fine hairs; their heads are well-established; they are superior in the hips and lower parts; they possess great bodies and are full of vigor; their eyes are like those of the *kalaviṅka* bird; their feet, nails, and long staff-like arms are low-set, rounded, well-placed, soft, and long; they have long hair-crests; they are capable of long journeys; they are smooth-skinned; they endure hunger and thirst; they are patient, united, strong, and possess knowledge corresponding to their names; they have shoulders that are firm; their palates, tongues, and lips are copper-colored; and their horns resemble the color of honey.

The lords of elephants possess bows of matching color and excellent lineage, with thick, long, and broad necks; they have small sheaths, beautiful tails, and are free from defects in their movements; they suffer no decline, resemble lotuses, crush the forces of enemies, are naturally fierce, and possess bodies that are a sight to behold.

Furthermore, those enemies of the gods, having found delight in the forests of the western regions—along the Godāvarī and Dāruvarṇa rivers, the Bāṇa and Mūṇa rivers, the Nirā and Abhayamarathyā rivers, the Parā and Madhukranda rivers, and the Damana, Tāpī, and Narmadā rivers, as well as in other great rivers—and having taken pleasure on the plateaus and forest-clad tracts of the Jāṅgala regions belonging to mountains such as Mandara, Kumuda, Kṛṣṇagiri, Sahya, Tuṅgavara, and Matyamārtha, they moved about, carrying market-stalls stocked with ghee, honey, parched grain, oil, and other goods.

Moving about with pride born [of their state], they fed upon *cakrāṭaka*, *vālīka*, and *darbha* grass; they were consumers of *umā*; they observed vows of eating only *markaṭaka* and *muta* seeds, as well as barley, wheat, *śyāmāka*, *priyaṅgu*, *vrata*, *adhika*, *balita*, *utkāla*, *analapalāśikā*, *kaṃdalī*, *vīraṇa*, *marucela*, *votsarṇavāka*, *pārṣṇīkākalā*, and the consumption of the *grāsa* of the wicked *vānīkāśatraputra*; they chewed *śataparvā*; they were the glorious sons established by their father in seven ways; they possessed firm, sharp, long lips and hair, and were thick, joyful, and equal in skin to the lap of the Earth.

Those with the fragrance of lotuses, distinguished by their short necks, possessing excellent and beautiful bamboo-like [limbs], with dark-spotted feet, considering themselves heroes, with beautiful eyes, and dwelling in their own forests... [following] their vow, they have taken refuge in the region where the Sarasvatī disappears, as well as the Sarasvatī, Kaśerumatī, Nyaṅgrumatī, Nīlaguhā, Vṛtraghnī, Pārṣṇimatī, Pūrimaha..., Devataka, Dāśārṇa, Māṇicara, Koñjama, Arbuda, and Ūrjayanta, and other [places] whose inhabitants are not settled among the Marus.

With thin hair, feet, nails, ears, and skin, and with slender bones yet firm... though [they may be] difficult to conquer, they are well-proportioned, very beautiful, fierce, gentle, and of medium stature; they are accomplished in training, distinguished by the perfection of their actions, generally very long-lived, and wanderers through the mountains and forests. They frequent the lovely lakes and rivers—the Irāvatī, Vipāśā, Vitastā, Śatadrū, Candrabhāgā, Sindhu, Devikā, and Sarasvatī—as well as the Himavat.

From the vicinity of the Pādāṅkura field, they have occupied the Kālakavana forest; thereafter, there are herds of elephants characterized by ten-fold limbs, secondary marks, and firm hooves and nails; possessing vital breath, large trunks, well-developed dewlaps, broad shoulders, thick skin, wrinkled bodies, coarse hair, and prominent tusks; dull-witted, performing difficult tasks, brave yet mostly sluggish, with little capacity but great exertion, prone to longing and meditation, skilled in subduing their enemies, excellent for carrying loads, and preeminent through your majesty.

In this regard, some [diseases] arising from the combination of bile, wind, phlegm, and their movements manifest as intoxication (*mada*) in autumn, summer, winter, the rainy season, and spring, and they discharge [their symptoms] at all times.

Today, however, due to fear of fire, fearlessness toward other elephants, the impact of weapons, the certainty of being struck by enemies, the crushing weight of an exceedingly heavy burden, the pressing of the temples against the rut-fluid of rival elephants, or due to excessive pain from the work or from passion during the mating season, having perceived their intoxicated nature, they were driven away from one elephant by another through the application of the goad or other means; and those who consume what is offered by hand—being skilled in the art of casting morsels—were attended to by trainers with mouthfuls of food.

[The mountains] were pierced by the women of Kaṭaka; furthermore, they were set ablaze by various substances such as agnikāśmi, manthāka, citraka, elā, hastiparka, pātīmūla, tirāsī, kandara, marīcipaṇi, jakakapota, paṅkāsaubhañjanaka, and añjana.
