By the excellence of clarity, by the flowing forth of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), by the very nature of the tree, by the abundance of vital energies (*ojas*), by the measure of strength, by the preeminence of mental stability, by the refuge of [the moon], by the birthplace of the *soma*, by the station of speed, by the characteristic of pleasure, by the manifestation of virility, by the mirror of pride, by the sharpening of brilliance, by the encouragement of enthusiasm, by the means for gentleness, by the configuration of loveliness, by the form of majesty, and by the possibility of beauty.

By means of the abundance of forbearance, the very essence of beauty, the splendor of Lakṣmī, and the fragrant qualities of sandalwood, agallochum, jāti, and mango trees—and by Madana, who, filling the earth with the weight of perfumes clinging to priyaṅgu, campaka, uśīra, saptaparṇa, Draviḍa, padma, kuvalaya, utpala, hīra, tālī, and haṅgulukī, made it appear as if composed of flour—he rendered the embodied one radiant in three ways; such that even Death would be overcome by terror and flee, powerless, let alone the faction of his enemies.

Furthermore, these elephants—thirsting for water, covered with the dust of the embankments, their luster appearing faded, with foaming red eyes, breathing fragrant sighs, their flanks well-arched, their trunks held up to their nostrils, addicted to yawning, their faces fully radiant and complete, playing with erections during sexual dalliances, and fixed in passion toward sounds and other objects—bear the signs of those who have approached them.

These elephants of noble lineage, their passion for the eyes already aroused by the first stage of rutting, are now filled with clear joy; with rows of fragrant breaths flowing profusely from the openings of their trunks and rubbing against the temples, these many-tusked beasts shine forth, trumpeting melodiously.
Furthermore, as they enter the second stage of rut, their excessive desire fully unfolds, and they pursue the beauty of their former faces like a most compelling scent.

But these others, overcome by the intoxication of youth, lacking confidence toward others, and bound by their low station, wander about with the arrogant displays of pride; they are like forms of frost due to the nature of their rays, as if from that time forward they were ignorant and deluded in all actions; they are to be pointed out without hesitation because of their state of gradual progression; they are stained by passion despite their outward appearance of nobility; and though subject to anger, they do not transgress the teaching, being intoxicated by the power of their strength as if through the skill of wine, yet fallen into the arrogance of pride.

Thus, emitting a constant brilliance like thundering clouds, they display their agility with supreme speed like the winds; they bear a state of intoxication like a swarm of bees wandering over their temples.
Yet these others, like demons seeking to slay every living creature, being deluded by pride, exhibit a state of furious rage.

These others, as if possessed by madness, here and there discharge a stream of sounds as if it were a flow of pride, emitting a rain of wrath; even fighting with trees, they wander in vain day and night, having abandoned their proper state of conduct.

These others, however, born of noble lineage, do not count themselves as such; they pay no heed to social recognition, nor do they recognize themselves; merely terrifying the world with their incessant, spreading laughter, they are like the seventh [state] of those who have shattered all boundaries.

When the elephant corps had been assigned their respective positions according to the king’s command, Mārjuneya—towering like the bull of Hara, with symmetrical proportions and a body covered in thick, bristling hair—stood at the head of his herd. With a whiteness as bright as froth, he was pursued by the Ocean of Milk, which mistook him for the horse Uccaiḥśravas. Flanked on both sides by two yakṣas of superior strength and stature who clung to his flanks like Mount Kailāsa, he appeared as if he were biting down in a rage to restrain his own momentum.

His two eyes—long, broad, and glossy, drawn wide as if by a sudden surge of speed from the very moment his nails began their scratching, and free from the defect of unevenness common to kinsmen—seemed to be being anointed with a dark-brown, sunken liquid of molten gold possessing the luster of a *karṇikāra* flower in full bloom; while his nose, with its prominent tip like a mature leaf constantly quivering as if in anger at the touch of the sun’s rays, appeared perfectly full, as if its roots were firmly established, with its well-defined features rendered formidable by its upward-turned shape.

With a stream of radiance white as foam emanating from his fangs—which were curved inward toward his lips and reddish-brown in hue—he seemed to be vomiting forth a mass of autumn clouds clinging to him at the moment he leaped into the sky; with a broad, flat, and wide forehead that was upturned like a platform for the martial strides of valor; with ears that were exceedingly dark, rounded and sharp yet hairy, appearing small as if out of modesty, and resembling two pillars of pride or two sprouting shoots on the tree of his prowess.

With a long, tender, and copper-colored tongue, he possessed a face that was smeared with red [lip-stain] yet pure due to its pristine nature; his chin, jaw, and beard were endowed with a long, rounded, and well-proportioned symmetry; his lips were reddish with fine lines, his palate broad, and his mouth—enclosed by smooth, gapless, and free-from-defect lips—was closed and possessed an exceedingly fragrant scent; and because of the mass of his auspiciousness, he displayed a towering height as if having performed a supreme act of ascension.

He shone with his head held steady and pressed down by a garland of soft, pure, and fresh *anuvālaka* flowers, which, together with the lion-maned mane, appeared like a victory-bannered chowrie held by the Lion himself; he was endowed with a neck that, though short, possessed a hanging dewlap free of flesh, and a throat that, being thick, curved, and drawn up from below, formed a hump upon the head; his shoulders were firm, broad, and full of well-knit, solid muscle, and his chest was stable, thick, elevated, full, and wide.

With arms released, gradually tapering, and thick; with knees well-set and covered by flesh; with shanks firm, closely joined, and thick like the cords of a royal elephant; with soft, well-supported, and rounded calves; and separated from other births, he moved with a playful gait at the start, like the dancing matted locks of Śiva adorned with the moon—his deep inner soles being touched by long, sharp hair, and his feet appearing as if fashioned from the dark-blue stone of Vṛtra’s enemy (Indra), with high, rounded, and dense swellings.

He was endowed with circles of hooves that were worthy of being the jewel-caskets for the crowns of every rival king, possessing an exceedingly glossy color like the trembling of milk within, and carrying unprecedented frogs that were as if caskets of dust for the residence of Lakṣmī; his body was round, high, dense, and thick as if from being a mine of auspiciousness (*śiva*), and he was joined to a back that was curved like a bamboo, low, and full, as if from the absence of the conduct of anger found in mountain-climbers, while his flanks were flawlessly covered by a form resembling a mṛdaṅga drum due to his graceful, leaping, and dancing postures.

With a belly that was exceedingly large due to the mass of its internal organs, yet perfectly circular, symmetrical, and without flaw; bearing hindquarters that were not inferior; and carrying a tail that was long and thick at the tip due to its being well-restrained—possessing superior proportions in speed such as the *trivā* and others, yet diminished in ailments such as the *prauḍha*; firm in its shanks and possessing an exceptionally beautiful circular form—he was like an enemy of strength (or a lion), acting according to the commands of his master, and requiring diligent care like a king.

Bearing his burden like a sage, free from anger, and exceedingly gracious, he was like the very other shore of courage and like life itself; he was the sport of the Goddess of War, the birthplace of audacity, the source of splendor, the perfection of sovereignty, the instructor of speed to the Wind-god, the root of beauty for the Moon, pure, lofty, and the progenitor of all that is dear to behold; possessing auspicious conduct, this jewel among horses named Bhadravāhana was like the flow of the Ganges.
Puṇyāvarta, while reciting even with a sense of mastery the majesty of Bhagīratha, fell upon his lord with great respect—a gaze as white as nectar, filling the quarters with wonder.

And that lord of steeds, possessing superhuman power, perceiving his master’s intent, neighed with a sound that was sweet, resonant, deep, and melodious, with a low and pleasant reverberation; his hooves, adorned with golden rings, scratched the surface of the earth, his mane and tail were tossed upward, and his nostrils quivered as he stood there. By that sound, the entire world was filled, as if by the oceanic spray scattered by Hari.

The superintendent of horses, however, replied: "Behold, O Lord, your worthy ally in battle, Bhadravāhana! This horse is exceedingly strong, exceedingly brave, exceedingly formidable, and exceedingly swift; for such is the nature of the breed born of the Tiraścī lineage."

Oh, how wonderful! This mountain, beautiful with its multitude of auspicious, stainless, and right-turning shells and buds, like a mass of milk, and esteemed as a collection of the essence of all jewels, has appeared here together with the goddess Lakṣmī and the Lord Puruṣottama, even without the labor of churning. I believe that by mounting this [mountain], even Mahendra could be conquered; for in the past, he was defeated by the lord of the Dānavas, Bali, even though he was mounted upon Uccaiḥśravas.

Indeed, such qualities as brilliance, color, strength, and speed cannot belong to this creature, whose nature is water and who was distressed within the depths of the ocean agitated by Mount Mandara. And when its speed is mentioned, its gait appears lame; like the Lord of Birds with broken wings, or like the quarters of the sky being obstructed, even the mind seems to move slowly. Furthermore, my friends, this one is capable of devouring Vāsudeva, Bāṇa, Bali, Śatru, and Bhakṣa.

And when that [horse] had been approved by the king and was pleasing to the eyes of the world, other horses also rose up in succession, galloping with speed as if making the very sky ripple. Then, as the military commander pointed them out with his forefinger raised in a gesture of courtesy, he proceeded to describe them in order: "Let favor be shown by casting a glance from this direction."

Indeed, these red horses—with coats like coral trees, with manes and tails as tawny as copper filaments—were bestowed by the Lord of Kamboja, whose pride was humbled by the mere shadow of your arm’s peak and who kisses the pollen of your lotus feet with his crest.

These black-tailed horses, brought here out of fear by Vāyubhūti (the Lord of Wind), who bowed down at the same time as Bāṇāsana, appear like black antimony ore extracted from a cave; they are entirely dark-hued.

Regard these arrows—drawn by the Lord of Gāndhāra as if they were his own life-breath—as being fashioned from refined gold, yet appearing like yellow silk due to their golden hue. With their shafts resembling the skin of the *āmra* tree and their feathers green, they possess hair-like down as green as parrot wings. They were offered as tribute by the King of Sacrifice (*adhvararāja*), who possessed such great pride that he once shattered the single bolt of the city gate with a thunderbolt-like strike against his host of elephants; they appear as if produced from emerald stones.

These white camels, whose coats are as bright as polished copper and whose manes are like tufts of white wool, have been presented by the King of Sindhu—who, through his alliance and the gift of all his possessions, was shaken by the churning of the Mandara mountain that is your staff-like arm—as if they were heaps of glowing charcoal covered by a fine white ash.

Likewise, these black cocks—whose powerful chests were once split open by pride and now serve as door-panels for the gateway of valor, drawn out by the force of their own breaking—have their bellies, thighs, and faces crowded with networks of black spots, while their wide-open crests are stained by bees clinging to them like blossoming *śephālikā* flowers.

These [elephants], sent back like dark-blue sapphire-stones terrified by the falling of your rod, possess manes as white as radiant pearls and skins as blue as the clouds; they are like those Krauñca birds that fled in fear from the banks and marshes agitated by your herd of elephants, with their many-colored hair, manes, and tails, and their unblemished, non-blood-red hides, possessing the color of lions enamored with your prowess.
These, moreover, are the fair ones, released from the heat of your majesty, white as the *kumuda* lilies of the ivory-temple and conch-shells, wearing the pearl-necklaces of the river-banks.

These [flames], possessing the blackness of the hair of the Lord of the Ocean (Keśava) when revealed, imitate the mass of clouds and the heaps of stones on the Mahendra mountain; they are the very hairs upon the head of the Enemy of Añjana (Agni).

These flames, which follow the sequence of colors—resembling the luster of blooming *moca* flowers, the glow of ripe, red *karkandhū* fruits, sprouts as copper-red as coral, and the dark hue of the peacock’s neck—are like the massed crests of the fire at the end of an aeon, acting as the black roots of Time (*kāla*).

Shaken from the battlefield expanded by your warriors on that day, abandoned by the lords of the Yaudheyas, these tawny ones—possessing the luster of earrings made of lotus filaments and the *cakravāka* birds atop polished foreheads, resembling the golden mountain peaks shattered by the winds of universal destruction—bear a hue that rivals the color of Indra’s horses.

These are the yellow-hued [elephants], who—having been deprived of battle by the dust raised by the force of your horses, and having been presented as tribute to the Lord of Vana out of despair—possess the beauty of Indra’s bow, are dark like garlands of *śirīṣa* flowers, radiant with streaks of yellow orpiment dust, the color of golden jasmine, lovely with reddish-brown eyes, and captivating the forest with their green hue; they create a day of celebration fashioned from the color of young lotuses, and are yellow-colored.
These others, whose skin has turned red from being placed upon the hair of the swift antelopes terrified by the tumultuous clash, possess the color of a peacock’s throat.

O Lord, these *pāṭala* trees, sent by you as a remedy for the unbearable force of the poison of your majesty, have become bearers of poison through fear; their hairs are white and red, like the interior of blossoming *pāṭali* flowers.

Behold them, now embraced by the weeping wives of the mountain-dwellers who were torn apart by your stainless sword—appearing like drops of water from Prayāga, consecrated by holy ablutions, dark and white upon their slender bodies.

These [mountains], their retreats blocked by the encirclement of your army, have their variegated black hair (or antelopes) scattered by the fleeing mountain-dwellers, and their feet (bases) are turned blue.

These white *pāṭala* flowers, with their few and sparse hairs, are honored by being scattered as the very remnants spat out from the corners of your eyes; they are covered by clusters that have not been wiped away.
Likewise, these *sumanā-pāṭala* flowers, with their sparse red and abundant white hairs, are offered as a tribute by the form of your thighs visible in the mirror of the jewels of your toenails.

To create those *guñjā-pāṭala* flowers with white and pale hairs, which resound with the brilliance of Kashmiri saffron melted and scorched by the intensity of the sun’s fierce rays, [the Creator] must have drawn them from the cage of his own pride.

These—timisra, pāṭala, and hari-pāṭala horses, with their many white, black, and tawny manes, were captured by you when Śatānīka was arrogant in battle and his forces shattered by a net of hundreds of arrow-heads;

they are those whose long journeys were spared by the extinguishing of the spreading fire of your wrath upon the Pārvateya troops, and who have earned the right to conquer the entire host of kṣatriyas dwelling in the middle of the land of Bhārata.

These—bearing various names produced by their own specific colors and methods, with filaments mixed with the essence of diverse hues, including *aṅgarītis*, *siddhārthakas*, those of the foremost color, those variegated with flowers, *puṇḍras*, and those variegated with circles; resembling elephants, peacocks, frogs, partridges, cranes, swans, lapwings, sparrows, cocks, black antelopes, golden bulls, jasmine, *bhaira*, *raidhera*, and mice; possessing continuations, connections, irregularities, deformities, and flickerings; endowed with yellowness, clarity, oiliness, and breadth; and with eyes like the luster of jewels—were as if streaming forth rivers of vital energy.

Following after the similarity of their qualities, they belong to the fourfold class; they have straight, thin, high, long, and fleshless mouths; they are sharp, possess three circles, and are triple-deep; five of them are soft, while seven possess an excess of sharpness produced by the lightness of ether, fire, and wind; they do not abandon the dullness dependent upon the heaviness of the earth; they bring about auspicious states through the commonality of their qualities; they consist mostly of *sattva*, have little *rajas*, and—due to the absence of *tamas*—are abundant in even flavors and rare in uneven flavors, yet are also characterized by harsh flavors.

On his four cheeks, with two, three, and four [jewels]; on his forehead, with one called Devamaṇi; on his neck, with one named Rocamāna; on his two arms, with two armlets (*aṅgada*); on his two ears, with two called *mekhalā*; and on his chest, with four large, smooth-colored, fixed, and auspicious *noma* jewels arranged clockwise.

Adorned by water-stalls and other facilities, and graced by joyful people born in that land who were delighted by hundreds of paths, they were further embellished by a stable, abundant, and multicolored earth that was neither parched nor overly moist. Avoiding the harshness and thinness found in Kāśī, they were endowed with excellence of body, character, gait, complexion, fragrance, voice, and luster; being four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine years of age, they were well-proportioned, engaged in various activities in all directions, and resembled vast forest expanses.

They were like Śrīvṛkṣakas longed for; they were joined together like celestial palaces featuring svastikas, vardhamānas, and nandyāvartas; they were like the phonemes characterized by vowels and consonants; they were like rainy-season days with visible dark clouds; they possessed a beautiful appearance like the wine of the western ocean shimmering on the banks of rivers; they were like the dark fortnights not yet brightened by the moon; they were like the rising of auspicious omens foretelling welfare; they were like those dressed in auspicious garments, possessing the eight auspicious signs; though originating from regions such as Sindhu, their faces were invisible; they were like the whorls within a pearl oyster shell.

Though accustomed to leaping, these horses do not have emaciated bodies; though possessed of natural cavities, they are free from all defects; and like those fashioned by the surging force of the winds at the end of an aeon, they enjoy every luxury.

Then the king distributed elephants and horses, according to their merit, along with wealth and honors, among the sons of noble families. While his own weapons were being worshipped, his mounts were being honored, heaps of wealth were being distributed, and circles for the drinking of heroes' liquor were being specially established; while the wives of heroes—adorned doubly by the encouragement of their beloveds and resolved to follow them in death—were present; the King himself, having first purified his priest, bathed three times a day at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā with waters sanctified by the presence of the five jewels and consecrated by mantras, and having offered oblations...

Having offered oblations into the Jātavedas fire kindled with fuel, having bestowed his entire possessions along with himself upon the twice-born according to the prescribed rites, and having duly dedicated his honored weapons and vehicles while observing the fast, that day and night passed like a pair of earrings for him as he sat motionless, his face turned toward the sacrificial pit which was ablaze with the gems of the planets and stars.

Desirous of surmounting the peak of sunrise like another Hemakūṭa mountain, the divine sun-god, his form crimsoned with lac-dye, cast off the dark-blue silken garment that was the night and rose up. The night-lotuses shriveled as if from anxiety over the destruction of all kings; the earth opened her eyes through the beds of day-lotuses as if desiring to witness the assembly; and pairs of cakravāka birds were reunited like the long-cherished desires of noble warriors for those of fierce splendor.

As if out of a passion for battle, the arrows, with their feathers fully set, began to fall of their own accord here and there with great force. When the time of dawn arrived, the entire army arose as if awakened by the striking of the sun’s rays and put on its armor. For instance—a terrifying clamor broke forth, resembling the loud trumpeting of a herd of elephants of darkness being struck down by the lion of the day-maker.

And a tremendous roar, as if rending the sharp-sounding drums, seizing the ears and hearts, filled with the swelling pride of the great warriors' defiant "huṃ" cries, resounded through the three worlds like the shriek of the cosmic egg bursting; it wandered through the regions of heaven as if desiring to tear them apart, following the sounds of conchs, cymbals, trumpets, horns, flutes, maddalas, and ānakas, and in an instant, by fanning the fury of the rutting elephants, it seemed to bring together the end of an eon.

And the elephants, their forms rendered exceedingly hard by the dense and formidable arrangement of their massive tusks—which resembled the two outstretched staff-like arms of Death drawn near to their faces—seemed as if they wished to seize the entire multitude of living beings in the world with those ivory-muzzes from which very sharp black-iron sheaths had been cast off; while some were adorned with the fluttering banners of victory fixed upon coils of serpents that were bent with fear, others with [banners] of a different, more formidable kind.

It was occupied by heroic warriors—some from Jālinī, others from Ahaṃsya, and still others from Krauñcapaṭyā—who were further distinguished by their skill in handling various weapons; they carried bows with flower-bud-shaped ends, wore leather finger-guards, and were clad in helmets, armor, and tunics. Fearless, learned in the traditional sciences, and possessing an unfailing back (in battle), they were experts in the employment of many weapons, having surrendered their very lives into the hands of Death.

With their ears adorned with golden ear-rings, bells, gongs, and chowries, and equipped with golden girths, neck-chains, and well-saddled saddles; appearing like bards with their faces turned toward them as they were praised by swarms of bees intoxicated by their ichor; they moved forward with steady and playful strides, carrying all kinds of weapons and merchandise from the city.

The horses, having embraced the surface of the sky through their extreme swiftness as they leaped with impetuosity, had their mouths restrained by bits that seemed to have been dropped out of fear that even their very lives might fall [from their throats] along with their breaths; their chests were secured by leather straps fastened tightly across their flanks, upon which were fixed seats of variegated and excellent wood supported by soft leather straps placed upon their backs, while their bodies were filled to the brim with pride as if fearing the bursting of their frames.

Their bodies were covered by quivers well-fitted with leather and fine feathers, hidden from view; they were adorned with rows of stainless golden hair-like filaments and their limbs were shielded as if by hundreds of fragments of light flashing from the dense masses of clouds shaken by their speed. They were equipped with fifty arrows whose tips were shaped for piercing and cutting, with four full quivers, and with two each of discuses, *tomaras*, iron spears, *kaṇayas*, *khaḍgas*, and *prāsas*, along with two each of lances and bows on both sides, and with four bright [missiles].

They were occupied with two swords, wooden boards, medicinal powders, ointments, and smoke-pipes; they were filled with *mātravrīhi* rice and *mukha* vessels, and were furnished with *vṛddhipatra*, needles, leather bags, threads, cords, conch shells, hollows, and rims. Because they were so full of weapons, they appeared formidable—like the tusks of the elephant Kāla, who had entered and emerged from hundreds of assemblies, broken by the hardness of his body; they resembled the wings of horses cut off by Śālihotra and then restored.

Waving clusters of chowries, adorned primarily with gems, gold, and silver, their horses controlled by well-trained riders; holding firmly in their hands the *vadhra* (reins) and carrying water-vessels; accompanied by those skilled in all weapons who were clad in iron mail, whose devotion to their master was unshakable, who knew the proper place and time for advancing, retreating, and crushing the enemy, and who were tireless, fearless, and mounted on steeds that moved with sweet gait—these [chariots] set forth.

And there were chariots with tinkling bells, their side-panels and walls adorned with various tiger-skin patterns and fragments of gems, and featuring variegated poles; they were like good masters providing comfortable refuge, like lords possessing well-constructed axles, like the powerful with wheels in motion, like the winds of universal dissolution with their undercarriages, and like lions with their neighing—[driven] by those of celebrated prowess, known for their fragrant fame, grateful, whose backs had never been seen [in retreat], and who followed the vows of heroes.
Provided with their protectors and holding the reins by those who possessed every excellence, the [chariots] set forth as if dancing, with their banners fluttering brilliantly.

Some, clad in armor and with girdles fastened, were ruddy like those dwelling in the forest of Aruṇa, appearing as if they had emerged from the fire of wrath; some, dressed in garments of deep blue silk, shone forth like great thunderbolts bursting from the belly of a cloud; some, wearing saffron robes, blazed brilliantly as if seated within the solar disc eclipsed by a planet; and some, arrayed in white silken cloths pale as the inner leaves of a young *rambhā* plantain tree, seemed as if they were being embraced by their own glories incarnate.

Some were clothed in variegated garments, appearing as if born from the sons of Indra and Upendra due to their passion for splendor; all had thickly bound, formidable, and curly locks of hair. They were skilled of hand, with forearms adorned by bracelets, and were equipped with quivers, swords, bows, spears, javelins, mallets, clubs, scimitars, and daggers. Wearing colorful tunics, bright garlands, and various mounts, they moved with diverse gaits, as if swelling with pride and bursting forth with insolence.

As if generating pride, as if inflaming valor, as if rousing wrath, and as if summoning manly prowess, they rose up from all sides, terrifying the entire world with their supreme war-cries, regarding even their own lives as mere blades of grass.

And the lord of the people, having passed that night without sleep as if unable to endure his own internal heat, bathed at dawn with pure waters, recited prayers, and performed the morning twilight worship (*pūrvasandhyā*). Then, having risen, he offered salutations to the Blessed One upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and to Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Varuṇa, Vāsava, Yama, and Dhaneśvara—each of whom was seated upon a red lotus—and received their blessings while intoning the mantras of his preceptor; thereafter, he also [received blessings] from the remaining deities.

Having performed the fire-ritual, having caused the benediction to be recited, and having paid homage to the noble lady Candralekhā—who possesses a lofty form, who is like a streak of the comet that brings about the destruction of the bee-clan (or the lineage of Madhu), and who is intent on removing the distress of those terrified by the fear of [the demon] Nāmaṣabha...

With the courtyards of his palace like verdant meadows from the lattice of rays emanating from emerald bracelets and the protective amulets strung with red thread, wearing white garlands, garments, and unguents, he touched auspicious tawny cows—whose hooves were hidden by tips of horns encased in gold and whose calves were of youthful hue—and having received hundreds of thousands of them, as well as armor and consecrated weapons, he was surrounded by those skilled in the *Atharva-veda* mantras of Jīmūta and other victorious spells that preserve one’s complexion.

With his body dappled by the rays of the jewels from the necklaces, crowns, armlets, earrings, and long pendants adorning his hands, as if his lap were covered by the mass of peacock feathers from his fluttering vehicle, he set forth, accompanied by Brahmins equal to Brahmā who were reciting the *Agnihotra-śastra*, the *Apratiratha*, the *Sāuparṇa* hymn, the *Śakuna-sūkta*, and other victory-mantras, while performing all the prescribed rites for departure.

He had been consecrated with holy waters poured from thousands of golden jars; his head was adorned with fresh garlands, his limbs were smeared with the finest unguents, and fragrant incense was being wafted about him. He sat upon a great red hide, lined with a man and provided with bamboo arm-guards, which was as long as Mount Mandara used during the churning of the ocean by the gods, and which resembled the doubled coils of the serpent Vāsuki, curling to the left and right.

It was covered by a girth-path, its ropes knotted together and concealed beneath a woolen rug spread over it; its back was variegated with the application of mineral pigments, appearing like the King of Mountains himself brought to serve as a mount through royal majesty; and it was bound at the neck with an exceedingly strong, virtuous, and friendly halter, suited for a firm embrace, which acted as a restraining mechanism to suppress pride and maintain total control.

He wore a neck-ornament (*graiveya*) and carried a seat (*bṛsī*) adorned with a pair of coverings fashioned from shimmering gems and gold, which, with its upraised variegated wings, seemed like a wondrous river; his body, covered in golden armor, resembled a mass of clouds embraced by a cluster of yellow lightning; and he was flanked by two swords as dark as black clouds and as terrible as the fall of a thunderbolt, like the months of *Śrāvaṇa* and *Bhādrapada*, or like the oceans striving to protect the boundaries of the entire world.

With eight bowstrings, which were like bows terrifying as venomous serpents and fit to be drawn by the hands of great heroes; with twenty lances, which—due to their superhuman power of striking—had become like the severed staff-like arms of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa cut down by the arrows of the descendant of Kakutstha; with three iron goads, glowing like the sacrificial fires of the Tretā age and resembling elephants themselves; and with a hair-seizing hook that was like a line for burning the forest of enemy-head-lotuses, its turret-work piled up and its leather thongs extended like a pair of tongues.

Adorned with a Vaijayantī garland from the daughter of Śūra, equipped with nooses, darts, slings, plows, axes, knives, drills, razors, and other tools, and with thirty-two quivers—resembling the claw-cages of black tigers—that were filled with fifty sharpened iron-tipped arrows each, capable of piercing and cutting through various formations, he appeared as if made of love. His ear-cavities were decorated, and his chest was marked by the scars of wounds inflicted by the edge of a sword. He seemed truly adorned.

Having taken up incense and collyrium, he ascended Hemakūṭa, which—by its immovable form as it were—was presided over by many various medicinal herbs; which resembled a wondrous cloud descended upon a mountain peak; which was covered by the beautiful chowries and fans held aloft by female attendants, like a pure, cool, fragrant, and well-protected flame; whose coral-stalked pillars were obscured by a mass of clear silk banners; which appeared like an ocean due to the application of footstools; and which was occupied by twelve qualities through the recitation of the mantra of the desired vehicle, as if they were seated upon it. Having worshipped the elephant that served as his mount, he mounted the golden peak.
Surveying his entire self with the excellence of the Niṣāda guards moving along all his flanks, he sat down and remained there;
then, surrounded by a circle of all his equipped feudatories, adorned with the royal parasol and chowries, and having conquered his own mind, he marched against the enemy force.

And he beheld, following him house by house, a ground seized by the army, which—due to the dense masses of rutting scent-elephants forming a continuous line—seemed like a rain-sacrifice (*varṣādhvara*) through the excessive weight of the clouds; and which, due to the circular canopy of the parasols of many thousands of vassal kings, seemed like the white expanse of a sandy beach on the shore of the ocean; and which was adorned with thousands of noble steeds, whose hooves were seemingly skilled in touching the sky because of their constant habit of leaping into the firmament, and who were decorated with golden trappings.

With its massive, formidable, and fierce fangs appearing like the world at the end of an eon, it was as if the forest of *pārijāta* trees had been brought forth by the ocean even before the threat of churning, out of fear; with its tips whitened by dense masses of falling snow that delighted the clusters of peacock-feathered arrows of hundreds of shimmering chariots, it was like a vast forest of heroes, or like the treasury of the universe, endowed with a multitude of banners and horses variegated in blue, white, crimson, and green.

It was as terrifying as the garden of the City of Death (Yama) due to the falling of shimmering sword-leaves; like the cowherd settlement of Nanda, it possessed beautiful elephants formed by the strength of Hari; like the settlement of Vṛndāvana, it was enveloped in dense and variegated darkness; like the Rāmāyaṇa, it was slowed by the agitation caused by the chariot of Paṅkti-ratha; like the battle of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, it caused the expenditure of Śakti-missiles by Karṇa, provoked by the lion-roars of the great warriors Gaja and Ghaṭotkaca; like a state of meditative absorption, it possessed an inner tranquility; and like the stream of the celestial river, it was well-established in various rows.

Like the slope of a breast with well-fashioned, beautiful wings; like an astrologer who has traversed the [zodiacal] signs and discerns the distribution of planetary strengths; like a sovereign whose subjects are brought to prosperity by a protective enclosure on all sides; like a difficult poem (*duṣkarakāvya*) in which the *sarvatobhadra* meter is composed within the arrangement of the inhabited regions (*janapada*); like a treasury where space is assigned according to the distinction between essential and trivial goods; like the pool of the Yamunā (*Kālindī*), from which the serpent has emerged though held back by cowherds... (Note: The text contains several archaic or technical terms related to architecture, astronomy, poetics, and royal administration. The translation attempts to preserve the metaphorical density while rendering the Sanskrit terms into English.)

The enemy host—capable of vomiting forth [destruction] through the application of new spells, yet unable to withstand [the enemy's] counter-spells; possessing winds that blow favorably for itself but acting as adverse gales against the other; emboldened by its own strength yet demoralized by the strength of the foe; urged on by its own generals despite being exhausted; presided over by its own unwearying lord despite being harassed; having magical rites and sorcery proclaimed by its priests and men engaged in recitation and oblations; with the success or failure of its own and the enemy’s maneuvers described by astrologers and others; and appearing most terrible to behold.

And as he danced, terrifying the three worlds with the fierce roars released from his rising passion of wrath stirred by the sight of the enemy host, he calmed the excessive fatigue of his own army; then, having countered the lion-leaping [Haryakṣa] with signs of recognition and having arrayed his forces against the invincible *sarvavyūhabhid* formation, he urged them forward for battle.

Then, from both armies, as if garlands of clouds being shaken by the winds, beautiful golden staffs—resplendent with the graceful patterns of leaf-designs inscribed in molten gold and flashing like momentary lightning—began to discharge, here and there, a profuse rain of arrows that roared terribly, their flight obstructed as they expanded like the longings of love.

The horses, having cast off their harnesses, rushed at one another with great speed like swans emerging from mountain caves with wings white as chowries; they were difficult to behold due to their brilliance, like heroes who have shed their armor and are flashing with the splendor of the sun, plunging into the enemy forces without attachment.

With streams of ichor twice as hot as usual due to the intensity of their mutual gaze, the lordly elephants rushed forward from all sides with the fury of a thunderbolt’s fall and a torrential rain; their dark trunks were like spears falling upon the temples of their rivals, their crimson cloths for facial coverings fluttering in their passion, and they seemed to blaze with the fire of wrath kindled by the incense of black aloe-wood and the flow of their temporal juice.

And the kings, their fury unrestrained by the sight of the enemy's ranks, urged on various mounts by the force of their impetuous wrath; challenging one another with raised weapons and commanding their soldiers, "Kill! Kill!", they assumed a form capable of destroying the entire world—like the sun at the end of an aeon, difficult to behold—and engaged in battle with their equally powerful and heroic adversaries, like lions against lions.

And in that interval, suddenly assuming a form capable of swallowing the entire aggregate of the world... a mass of pollen, turbid as a cluster of the bristles of a great boar, born from the agitation caused by the collision of a vast force, yawned forth, enveloping the sky and obstructing all light. Within it, for a moment, everything stood as if painted, as if carved, as if paralyzed, as if shriveled, and as if its very breath were snatched away, like two banners rendered motionless by a gale.
Furthermore, having suppressed that tamasic transformation through extreme heroism, an exceedingly terrible combat took place for a moment, like the crushing of darkness by light.

And then, as if tearing [the world] with the merciless strikes from the corners of eyes red with weeping; as if splitting the temples with the fierce blows of staffs that made the kettledrums resound; as if rending the hollows of the ears with the terrifying roar of the drums; with the more powerful shrieks of those dancing like the matted-haired Śiva in his fury; and with the trumpeting of those swelling with pride and panting in haste— (Note: The provided text contains several lacunae and scribal errors. The translation above attempts to reconstruct the sense based on the available fragments and standard poetic conventions.)

[The air was filled] with the humming of bees agitated by the fear of the falling of fierce rays from the sun upon the waters of the lotuses that had spread throughout the entire universe; with the resonance of various musical instruments being played, thickened by the chanting of hymns for the propitiation of the deity of Death; and with the throaty cries of the troop of dancing warriors, which increased the longing of the celestial nymphs, mingled with the clinking of sharp bits and the loud noise produced by the striking of the hoofed hooves of the mounts upon the vast surface of the earth.

By the deep, resonant thundering of elephants—uttering playful trumpeting with gurgling and gurgling sounds like a series of rattles, their tusks clashing against rival elephants with a *jhaṭa-jhaṭa* roar as terrifying as a stroke of lightning, their temples being sprayed by swarms of bees frightened by the collision of many falling weapons—and by the massive reverberations following the trumpeting of those beasts, which was interwoven with the sound of kettledrums; and by the unrestrained, robust clattering of chariots whose poles and frames were shattered by mutual impact; and by the [roars] of great warriors pressed down by the towering [elephants]...

A tumultuous clamor was being raised by the exceedingly harsh *huṃ* cries of falling arrows—which, drawn back to the ear and released from bows that caused a fever in the ears, had vanished into the expanse of the sky—mingled with the *paṭapaṭa* sound of the heaps of bones in the bodies of elephants being shattered by their trunks and feet, and intensified by the most fierce warbling of formidable winged creatures such as hawks, vultures, cranes, herons, crows, and ravens, amidst a vast mass of thick dust.

Darkened by smoke and crowded with various nets of weapons incessantly revolving, it resembled the surface of the primordial netherworld (mūlarasātala), where the surface of the earth was struck by the forceful snouts of divine boars, causing the shells of cosmic eggs to burst, while a succession of great serpents writhed about.

Then, as if enraged by the obstruction of their confident and vigorous striking, the mass of dust gradually subsided along with the warm stream of blood flowing from the onset of the heroes' combat. When the dust had settled, like the minds of the wise, the sunbeams—rendered pure by the light of the weapons and striking against the succession of sharp blades—shone a hundredfold like heroes.

Just as a sharp great sword, though its edge be dulled by the recitation of prayers amidst the armor of a warrior, cleaves through the enemy's compact ranks—piercing even those who are most preeminent, illustrious, endowed with diligent virtues, free from flaws, possessed of noble limbs, and whose vital organs are well-guarded; so too, while the fires were blazing and the world was being consumed, the moths, appearing as they descended toward their destruction, fell with swift flight. And the Lord, fearless and armed with his mace, rushed against the hosts of the Asuras.

The claws of the soldiers, following the command of their master, tore asunder the hearts of the enemies—hard as iron though they were—as if they were tender sprouts; these claws, fierce and possessing the form of perfected power, produced a mutual state of indignation that was like the earth’s foundation, established upon many virtues. Even those who were full of longing did not feel contempt for the gracious ones; such is the nature of virtuous men.

In those women who were like whirlpools set in motion by the current of the populace, the executioners—like headless trunks with floating rafts clinging to their outer sides—swiftly protected them; yet, by means of arrows whose harsh wing-sounds fell upon the flowers of their minds, they mercilessly severed those lives sustained by effort, which, though bound to the mouth, remained unblown like young lotuses.

The arms of the kings, with their thick ears and necks, fell on all sides like great mountains hurled by the winds at the end of an aeon—mountains that had begun to discharge rows of weapons to destroy the world of living beings, yet remained unshaken; they made the earth tremble as they fell, their jeweled bracelets flashing like the blazing flames of the fire of calamity, fueled by the intoxication of wine and manifested during the time of universal destruction.

Even when their feet were severed, their gait remained graceful; though their other limbs were afflicted by a multitude of unrelenting pains, their glories did not grow dim. When those of great majesty were overwhelmed by deep blows to their vital parts, their lofty spirits attained a state that was truly embodied.

...with a gait that was disciplined, unerring, protected, straight, not turning toward all directions, with ears neither contracted nor flapping, with the belly held in, bent, yet unshaking, and remaining in the posture of the *arucaka* [necklace]; with the five defects of the armpits known as "smearing" (*pralepana*) avoided; neither too far forward nor too far back, neither too withdrawn nor too extended, like a rutting elephant; raised like a pillar, with eyes released from the blinking and wandering [of distraction], with the corners of the eyes neither squinted nor closed, and with the lips neither too wide open nor too tightly shut.

With his tongue licking his lips, revealing his teeth, and raising his eyebrows; smelling his own nostrils, laughing not too much, and twitching; looking at his seat while his face shone with the concentration of his mind upon what he saw; as if drinking in the target with his eyes—neither too high nor too low—with fingers held in the third position, closely joined like dark bees, and holding a bow whose middle was not grasped; and with an arrow that was neither too high nor too low, its feathers facing the ground, its tip fierce, and its shaft straight, he aimed at the chest, belly, and waist of the deer.

They shot arrows that were level with the palm of their hand, free from defects such as being raised too high, and whose feathers had been trimmed; they released them without trembling, without striking the shaft against the bow, not holding it too high, and without moving the tail-feathers; giving one arrow at a time, they did not waver during the aiming process; they joined the arrow to the notch with the knuckle of the finger and pressed it with both hands; thus, while the bow was being strung and the arrow aimed, they did not tremble, nor did they lift or lower the bow, nor did they fail to wipe or polish the shaft, yet the arrows were severed [by their speed] without being broken.

Like those afflicted by heat seeking shelter, they were radiant with thick water-bearing clouds; like the hosts of Varuṇa, they had performed their evening worship; like noble lineages, they were free from the defect of contact with the tips of wicked swords; like those devoted to Dharma, they avoided falling into miserable states; like a succession of wheels, they were perfectly square even when whirling the sword through the eighteen sword-movements; like the moon in conjunction with the Vaiśākha asterism, their wings were clearly outspread; like the varieties of elegant sayings, their movements were well-executed in the *ālīḍha* posture; and like those greedy for gain, they were ever-striving.

Resplendent with many flickering movements, they were like Malaya breezes causing graceful creepers to dance; beautiful with outward eddies like the currents of rivers, they were like those seeking purity who smear themselves with cow-urine; showing auspicious courses like the doctrines of the Vedas, they were like the winds of universal destruction that are momentary; sweet in their striking like the drums of Mura, and even when their backs were struck as if by their own limbs, they remained unbounded even in their wandering course—even while performing these things...

They were strikers who, though resembling Time itself (*kālakalpa*), could sever the elbows, shoulders, and arms of others yet could not be severed themselves; though they were as if intoxicated by passion (*rāga*), they did not cling to the laps of others; though they were like Death (*kāla*), their feet, raised in fury, cast down the nooses of Yama and the thunderbolt; though they were not slayers of cows, they bore the *gośīrṣa* sandalwood [or the mark of a cow]; though they were not Brahmins, they wore the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); like dancers, their arms moved about as they whirled through many steps; like carpenters, they were skilled in forming auspicious cross-patterns (*svastika*); like lions, they tore at elephants with their sharp claws; and like the proud... [they were].

With their mounts smeared with the dust of their sharp hooves, they set out like tigers intent on returning from a hunt; possessing the dark luster of dried mud, they were like deer adorned with antlers; with their inner turns characterized by incessant splashing like waves upon the shore, they proceeded as if mocking Death itself.

And there were ploughs made of *tugṅgin*, bamboo, cane, *paṭāroha*, *devadāru*, black sandalwood, *spandana*, *apanaka*, *khadira*, and *śiṃśapā* wood; their handles were five, six, or seven cubits long; they were of excellent quality, provided with handles made of *prokṣala*, *ayata*, *krañja*, *ayasaniṣīna*, and *jāyasā* materials, and possessed sharp edges. Their blades were shaped like the uneven scales of a fish, or like the tongues and mouths of serpents, or like the leaves of the *aśoka*, *aśvakarṇa*, *karavīra*, date-palm, and *tāla* trees; they were two, four, or ten finger-breadths wide, and one, one-and-a-half, or two-and-a-half finger-breadths thick.

Polished with a paste of equal parts of *vyāghranakha* and the soot of burnt clay, they were washed until spotlessly clean, their various characteristic marks clearly revealed; with lusters resembling the brilliance of beryl, peacock necks, blue lotuses, and white flowers, they seemed to create a second heaven free from possessiveness, while their chests, radiant with the hue of honey and other such substances, bound together a beauty like that of a lotus-stalk, emitting as it were the fragrance of the Goddess of Prosperity herself, who dwells nearby in her equanimity.

[The army] was equipped with surāsāti-swords carried by those wearing prominent ornaments of silver and coral; with *nālika* spears serving as wings; with many types of vessels such as jars for *pittha* and *āmalaka*; with fifty or sixty *pālī*-measures of equipment; and with tools corresponding to their own dimensions for cutting, splitting, binding, bandaging, scraping, carving, and wrapping. On the ground, there were *alātacakra* (fire-wheels), *aśani* (thunderbolts), *vidyutkṣipta* (lightning-throws), *nāgākrānta* (elephant-attacks), *lātāvarta* (whirling clubs), *bhaṭamusala* (warrior-maces), *vidyuddaṇḍa* (lightning-staves), and *aṃsa-kuraṅga* (shoulder-deer).

Displaying in succession various wonderful maneuvers—such as the *bhujabandhu*, the *ākrānta*, the *parikṣipta*, the *vāraṇa*, the *ullekhya*, the *alekhya*, the *kṛntana*, the *avakṛntana*, the *yamadaṇḍa*, the *bhiṇḍipāla*, the *varāṅgikṣepaka*, the *kārmuka*, the *śroṇiparigata*, the *āsphola*, and the *vāṇa*... [desiring] the *jā...*—they demonstrated these artistic feats and the excellence of their techniques: the *vṛścika*, the *pakṣāvarta*, the *devadaṇḍa*, the *cakradaṇḍāvarta*, the *kāladaṇḍa*, the *nāgākrānta*, the *devākrānta*, the *bhṛtabherī*, the *gūḍhameṇḍa*, the *bhujākrānta*, and the *svastika*.

Performing the lion-leap (*siṃhākrānta*), the cow-penetration (*gavyāviddha*), and the fire-brand-circle (*alātacakra*), they—having struck down the host of Māra’s army—set in motion the deer-warden (*kuraṅgavāraṇa*), the svastika-warden (*svastikavāraṇa*), the scattered-warden (*vikṣiptavāraṇa*), the banner-overpowering-warden (*dhvajākrāntavāraṇa*), the mercury-liquid-warden (*rasaravartavāraṇa*), the immovable-wheel-warden (*acalacakravāraṇa*), the tail-member-warden (*vālaṅgavāraṇa*), the elephant-warden (*vāraṇavāraṇa*), the Yama-given-warden (*yamadattavāraṇa*), the sword-action-warden (*asikarmavāraṇa*), and the toppling-warden (*pātanavāraṇa*), like dancers in their natural attire, they moved about with joined palms.

Holding the reins with one hand, they performed all sixteen modes of galloping—namely, the hawk-attack, the seizing, the belly-turn, the arrow-drag, the root-and-top turn, the upward turn, the shoulder-turn, the scratching, the beautiful-pressed, the hidden-tip, the wing-pressed, the cross, the mark-thrown, the vine-turn, and the scattered—as well as the various maneuvers involving the attachment of the *karkaṭaka* (the curved rein), executing them correctly.

In quadrangular, circular, triangular, and elongated [wounds], those that have gone upward, downward, or sideways, those that are not fully surrounded, those with blood-red ripples, those with thin exudation, and those with upward-turning [edges]—these are the sixteen types of wounds to be recognized by their locations, such as the sides, hips, wrists, seat, cheeks, head, temples, navel, heart, nipples, and eyes; likewise, there are sixteen types of complications arising from the humors (doṣas) when combined, characterized by swelling, discoloration, pain, and the like, including those resulting from improper incision, excessive cutting, or erroneous surgical maneuvers.

He established mechanical devices for chariots and elephants—namely, the *trikalpa-siṃha-niṣpoḍita*, the *adhomukha-śārdūla-parisarpaṇa*, the *ākrānta-kṛntana*, the *parākrāntābhimukha-pārśva-karma-parāvartana*, the one called *kheda-grahaṇa*, the *yojayat*, the *abhāga*, the *akarmamiśra*, as well as the *sāyaka-yaudha-bhūṣaṇa*, the *śastra-vikrama-maya*, the *mantra-uddharaṇa*, the *vajrāvartana*, the *vidyunmaṇḍala*, the *sūcigamana*, the *indravajra*, the *vṛndabhīṣaṇa*, the *bhūtakendra*, and the *śatrughātana*.
