They seem to manifest the pride of a multitude of gods honoring the Sage, as if they were a rosary of seeds from the *muṣkara* plant, which has drunk the entire day’s worth of sunlight and now, out of a desire for intense asceticism, wears the circle of bees around its neck with longing devotion for their recitation.

He was seated upon a seat of black antelope skin and cane, placed upon a smooth pedestal within a bower of mādhavī creepers, resting against the trunk of a young elephant that was neither too large nor shared its station with others; he sat there, having quickly concluded his exposition of the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*), the sound of which had ceased like the deep resonance of a cow that has rested after giving her last drop of nectar.

He was being saluted by sages who, like white lotuses drawn by the sight of the ocean of milk, were imbued with unsurpassed flavor, their bodies bristling with joy and their minds awakened; they gazed upward at him as if he were the moon’s deer, its thirst for ordinary nectar recently quenched, yet now thirsting for the nectar of knowledge, having approached with a longing to drink that nectar of wisdom, his body embraced by them without fear through deep trust—just as a forest deer might be.

He was favoring with compassion a young swan, who, having approached with great eagerness, seemed to have become attached to his feet as if to asceticism itself; the bird was addicted to drinking the radiance spreading from his claws. He was discouraging the young ascetic boy—who was threatening him with a broken lotus stalk—from his persistent questioning, while at the same time encouraging the young parrot, who appeared victorious in its own way, by stroking its breast with his own hand.

He was offering [fruit] with pomegranate seeds—extracted from the interior of split pomegranates and possessing the brilliance of the finest crystal—which had been gathered in leaf-cup vessels placed nearby; he was being attended by a swarm of bees sent, as it were, by the entire host of sacred fords (tīrthas) out of a longing to behold him, following close behind his feet and clinging to their surface like the dust from the flower-offerings on the courtyard of the hermitage, which had turned them a tawny hue like the color of the tips of the ascetics' hair disheveled by prostration; he was dressed in a lower garment and upper robe of reddish-brown washed bark-cloth.

His limbs were veiled by the morning sunlight clinging to him like an embrace from a present and gracious friend; his body was sanctified by a line of sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) that seemed like a flight of swans, which—seeking the path for the entry of internal purity—had formed a circle around his limbs thinned by asceticism, as if peeling off his skin out of a longing to sprinkle them with the waters of holy fords; and his belly was darkened at its surface by the scraping of bundles of sharp *kuśa* grass.

He was resplendent with his right hand—which, with its finger-joints made rough by the turning of the beads of a rosary of *rudrākṣa* seeds, seemed like a mass of rain-clouds from the rising smoke of the fire as it consumed the oblations; which, under the guise of streams of light from the gems on his nails, seemed to pour forth the water of the granting of fearlessness to all beings; and which, like a staff of honey, was the wealth of a delightful assembly for dispelling the intoxication of pride in all the gods—while he was resolving all the doubts of the great sages concerning this entire world composed of the elements.

Because its meaning was so well-ascertained, it did not cut us off by means of [excessive] elaboration; rather, with its spreading rays of light—which resembled a multitude of shimmering nets moving along the paths of arrows struck against mountains—it was like a river of exceedingly cool sandalwood paste, like the primordial streak of the Milky Ocean at the rising tide of the circle of all the senses, and like a row of *sinduvāra* flowers in the grove of Sarasvatī in full bloom, or like the bright fortnight of the month of Śarva for the increase of the moon of the Dharma.

He seemed to display a flight of autumn clouds rising from the depths of his own clear mind; with a beard as white as grey hair, appearing like a mass of foam produced from churning the nectar of all the scriptures, he resembled Śiva, whose stream of the Gaṅgā flows down to the very ends of his head; his hollow cheeks were like whirlpools in the current of tears shed during prayer; and his prominent nose seemed to pacify the loss of the brilliance of his gaze as it was being drawn upward.

As if drinking in the spreading radiance of the sun, those two [the sun and moon] became exceedingly darkened; they rained down, as it were, a shower of nectar born from the *tapas* of the penance groves; they distributed, as it were, the bliss of meditation to the hermitages; they were conduits for the overflowing stream of the essence of friendship exceeding even the mind; and they seemed marked with the *ūrṇā-tilaka* of the sovereign circle of sages, who had applied lines of long life with ashes at the conclusion of their *agnihotra* sacrifices—[those two] whose steady state between the two eyebrows was established through meditative concentration. It was she alone who... bowed.

...possessing a face that acted as an eight-petaled lotus for the play of the clear Sarasvatī, endowed with a mouth that was a jar containing the treasury of all sciences; yet, though possessed of such [beauty], it was not devoid of passion—[a face] whose form was like a messenger sent by the arrival of the clouds, dark-brown like a honey-bee, [yet] flooded with the splendor of the rising moon; [a face] which, like a vessel for increasing all the buds of heroism, was lovely as an Aśoka flower, and possessed ears variegated at their roots like streaks of twilight clouds in a deep embrace.

Though his face was long with the defects [of passion], he was radiant with the nectar of divine compassion; though he repeatedly practiced drinking [liquor], he was never a farmer; though he was the foremost among those looking upward toward the state of the entire universe, he was free from the dust [of worldly attachment]; though he was the strength of the assembly, he was the sole refuge for the fire [of wisdom] on every path; and though his rosary of beads was constantly whirled, his senses were perfectly tranquil.

He beheld the sage Vāmadeva—a mass of asceticism whose fame was renowned, who was intent on the continuous succession of hundreds of virtues, who possessed threads of intense heat yet granted desired boons, who was the sole beloved of Sarasvatī, who was a day for penance, who possessed the rising of great majesty, who was exceedingly long-lived, who followed many unseen compositions, who took sole delight in supporting his own being, who was highly exalted with an uplifted face, worthy of being gazed upon by the world of Brahmā, who had practiced dwelling at Puṣkara, and who had rejected the god of love.

Upon seeing him, his boldness overcome by the power of her asceticism, he became as if terrified; with a certain trepidation bound within his heart, he shrank both in mind and body. As if out of reverence for the thought that "sacred lands are to be approached only with effort," his head was bathed by the tresses of light-rays from his fingernails, which were bent like lotus-buds in the form of folded palms. Thus he stood before that assembly of her attendants, whose excessive curiosity was concealed by the appearance of their guest, whom they had never seen before.

With his body bowed low as if by the excessive weight of his thousand eyes, which were simultaneously turned toward him and rolling with joy, he—his hair standing on end as if plunging into a great pool of merit—performed a salutation with a mental disposition inclined toward the Dharma.

While the king—having performed the salutation of the feet of the great seer as was his custom—considered his head to have achieved its purpose, as if marked by the crest-jewel that is the insignia of sovereignty over the entire three worlds, the sage, delighting him like the sun with its tawny stars in the twilight sky, gazed again and again with wide-open eyes at the king’s downward-turned lotus-like hands folded in a tender *añjali* and closed at the tips of the fingers, and having perceived [the truth], he spoke.

Having grasped the entire account of what had occurred there from its very beginning—like an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of his hand—he, though steadfast, with his eyelashes bedewed by glistening drops of tears of joy, though he had long since cast off the relish for worldly affairs, though his disposition toward affection was as if asleep, and though the bonds of worldly attachment had been shattered like a mass of intensely heated iron, yet as if touched by a certain agitation, rose from his seat and, having gone a few steps with his red lotus-stalk garment trailing behind him, remained free from attachment.

Stretching out his two arms—which resembled aged serpents still clinging to fragments of their slough and were covered with a network of hair white with age—the great sage embraced the king, whose hands were pressed by the weight of the king’s exceedingly burdensome honor. Then, having received the opportunity from the king—who was fearful of transgressing the prescribed rites—after inquiries regarding health and other formalities, the great sage, filled with joy, performed the ritual honored by tradition, concluding with the offering of the *madhuparka* prepared with the *madhumat* mantra.

And when the king had sat down in the place pointed out by him, the assembly of sages—overwhelmed by the constraints of his extreme favor and dependent upon it—perceiving that unprecedented and wonderful excess of respect shown by the monarch toward the great sage, asked: "Who is he? What is his lineage? What indeed is his name? What penance was performed by him in a previous birth? For what purpose has he descended to this earth? And how is it that this high-souled one has such a limited retinue?"

Furthermore, this is another great marvel: not even a sesame seed’s worth of a scar is visible upon the limbs of this Great Soul, which ought to have been adorned by the marks of wounds from heroic combat—marks that are neither divine nor vulgar. How could such a person have endured the crushing impact of blows in a battle devoid of gods, asuras, or Tāraka? Or, if such a thing were possible, how could his life-breaths remain within his limbs, mangled though they were by the tracks of hundreds of weapons, without ever leaking away?
Though she was overcome by the excessive force of her passion, she remained there, unable to speak further due to the weight of her teacher’s severe restraint.

As she stood thus, the sage, observing the assembly of sages, smiled slightly; out of curiosity to hear of the Lunar dynasty, he seemed to bathe their faces—with foreheads already rosy from the application of the heat of the five fires—using the luster of his teeth. "Alas! Your mental dispositions are curious, yet you have understood the situation."

"Listen with curiosity to the life-story of this mass of auspiciousness, which is the ornament of the face of the quarters; it is a tale of wondrous sentiment that captivates the mind from the very beginning of his lineage. Thus he began in due order: "There was a king who was a swan among monarchs, whose voice was as sweet as the three Vedas (Madhu-kānta), who was the sole bearer of the delight of noble character, who delighted in sporting in great lakes, and who, like the golden egg of Brahmā, drew toward himself both gods and demons by the power of his majesty."

Therefore, [he was] the one who amazed the three worlds... the purifier of the world’s sins... the constant friend of the Sacrifice (Agni), the beloved of Ambā (the Earth), the enemy of the lotuses, the life of the sky-dwellers, the smile of the splendor of the sky, the crest-jewel of the Lord of Ambikā (Śiva), the brother of the Kaustubha gem, the foremost of the Kṣatriya lineage, the lord of the gods, the master of medicinal herbs, the unborn one... like a mountain, the ornament for the sake of non-destruction, the one praised by the Śasmarya and Valaka tribes.

The Lord of Stars (the Moon), whose star-like pupils were as beautiful as the petals of a blooming night-lotus bud and served as mirrors for the cheeks of amorous women, had a son named Budha by Tārā, the beloved of Aṅgiras. This preeminent deity, a treasury of wisdom, surpassed Bṛhaspati in intelligence. From Budha, through his union with Ilā at the sacrifice of Manu, where Mitra and Varuṇa were present, Pūru was born, who was equal to Purūravas.

The region named Ilāvṛta, which surrounds the central land of Jambūdvīpa, exists even today as a mountain range comparable to Hiraṇyagarbha; it is a rain-giving land where the people enjoy the drinking of the Jambū river, which carries the golden juice born from the Jambū tree. From Aila, through Urvaśī—the foremost Gandharvī of Mahendra’s lineage and the daughter of Dakṣa, who was like a cluster of Mandāra blossoms on the thigh of Janārdana—Ayu was born.

Nahuṣa, who surpassed the Lord of Heaven through his eightfold sovereign powers of longevity, begot upon Prabhā—the daughter of Svarbhānu, whose radiance was shimmering—a son named Yayāti. This Kāmadeva-like Yayāti, the delight of Nahuṣa, enjoyed all the divine forests, foremost among them the Nandana grove; he subdued the circle of Dānavas by causing his excellent chariot, which had been bestowed by the axe-wielder [Śiva] as a mere mouthful of honey from the lotus-like lips of Viśvācī, to circle the earth exactly six thousand times. His songs served as an instruction in the nature of desire that leads to world-weariness.

From Yayāti was born Pūru, a bull among kings, by Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan; though his youth was veiled by the net-like wrinkles of old age due to the harsh curse inflicted by his father for his dalliance with another’s wife, he remained beautiful and charming. From Pūru came Janamejaya, who, like a thunderbolt, split the mountains of his enemies and delighted the people of both city and countryside. His son was Prācinvān, whose banner was marked by victories in the eastern quarter.

He was a hero who expanded the earth, having spread it out from its original growth; he was renowned for his valor and the destruction of the Śakas. He was a hero who, though transgressing the bounds of righteousness through his prowess, was nevertheless named Namasyu (the one to be revered). He became the bestower of fearlessness to the gods, yet [to others] he was the giver of fear. His lineage was Śundhyu, purified by the destruction of his own impurity through his own splendor. He was "Bahuvidha" (the manifold one), intent on various forms of policy; he was "Bāhuvidhi" (possessing many methods), having placed the burden of the earth upon his arms; he possessed terrible weapons and had crossed over all doubt.

His son, whose splendor surpassed even that of the sun, succeeded him immediately after him. Having established the true path, he was fierce toward his adversaries; he was Rudrāśva. Like a lamp for his lineage in a vessel of clarified butter, he begot of Ghṛtācī a son of fierce luster, the foremost of ten.

In battle, from Takṣakātmajā—who was ablaze with the shaking away of the darkness created by the frowns of enemy warriors—he begot Antināra, whose essence was infinite. From Antināra, Yamasutā obtained a son who was like a forest fire for the destruction of the forest that was the lineage of the Adarīs.

Having been terrified, yet not trembling, and having cast away pride with respect, he whose lotus-like splendor was like a crown and an uṣṇīṣa, who was provoked by his son’s sincere propitiation, [acted] with an arm that was abundant in the enjoyment of your arms, [an arm] born of the fire of his wrath. Like the four great oceans arising from that [fire], the eldest, Bṛhatkṣatra—whose position was unsurpassed, whose conduct was not backward, and whose disposition was favorable—attained the sovereignty of Mahendra.

His burden was borne by a noble elephant named Hastin, whose trunk was like that of Airāvata, the mount of Hari; he who possessed a single auspicious temple and whose face was adorned with a lotus. That city, the capital of heroes, the ornament of the earth, was marked with his name. There arose a lord of the quarters named Ajamīḍha—the first-born among the twice-born [Brahmins] of the cities of Mīḍha and Puramīḍha—whose fame was like sandalwood paste for the world’s impurities and who moved with the grace of a lion.

His wife, like the sky with its shimmering stars and lovely clouds, gave birth to a son, a prince (*ṛkṣa*) who was pleasing due to his association with the circle of kings. His prowess was unassailable; he was protected by the Daughter of the Sun (Savitṛ), who herself was scorched by the heat of penance and tormented by the god of love. From Saṃvaraṇa—who was himself shielded by that protection—he was born Sāṃvaraṇa, a man of preeminent courage, whose long body was dedicated to the protection of living beings... [he whose bow was beautiful] with a terrible *huṃ* sound that struck terror into the lions of the mountain-like Kuru clan, a clan heavy with virtues and the sprout of a lineage protecting its essence.

From Sudhanvan was born the Caidya, who—having removed the enmity with great kings and being a physician for extracting the harsh thorns and spikes that were the enemies of the entire world—was a man of accomplished virtue who brought contentment to the earth bounded by its four quarters. From him was born Bṛhadratha, who was like another Indra; he whose eyes were like those of a peacock, shimmering and variegated as if from a mass of pearls gathered within the shells of oysters.

His brilliance was a transformation of fire, as if it were the very measure of his great-armed strength; his intellect was as sharp as the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass; he was a bull among men. Therefore, he was "Possessor of Flowers" (*Puṣpavān*), for his own fame—blackened by the sighs of the wives of all the quarters—was like a flower. He was "Excellent-Bowed" (*Sudhanvan*), for his variegated bow was fashioned from the gold-leaf of the sun, heated by the lake-like eyes of his enemies' wives which were filled with tears. He was ever-vigilant, possessing a manifest pride, and was a giver (*Darva*).

The son of Gadara was Jarāsandha, who was ever intoxicated with pride and joy; whose throat was scarred by the friction of the earth’s surface as he tossed it about in his longing for battle; who made the city-gates his own playground by dragging them with the tips of his hands; whose iron fetters jingled at his feet like the anklets of a noble matron; and who was the eldest son of the entire Kṣatriya race, skilled in every art of war and true to his word. His son was Sahadeva, who did not fall short of his father’s prowess and was capable of plunging into the ocean of the Bharata war.

From Sahadeva came Somāpi, who drank the Soma juice along with the gods; his son was Śrutaśravas, renowned for slaying Dānavas. From Śrotraśravas came Cakṣuṣaśravas, who was endowed with a life of great vigor. From him was born Niramitra, whose heart was won over by friends through the performance of auspicious rites. From him came Sukṣetra, who enjoyed the entire domain of a universal monarch through the strength of his own arms. From Sukṣetra was born Saukṣetri, whose great deeds for the world were perfected through the path of the Kṣatriyas.

From him, who possessed a digit of nectar amidst worldly existence, was born Mahāsena, named Senajit. He begot a daughter by Śatruñjaya, who had utterly destroyed all his enemies. From Śatruñjaya was born a lord whose name was true to its meaning: Vaibhava. Like Bhava (Śiva), he was pure and reached the secondary limbs of the source of beings; like the clear sky, he was supported by clouds; and like the earth, he gladdened the world, his fame serving as a mantle for the women of all directions, and he was secure.

His son was Suvṛtta, whose conduct was fit to be recited by purified people; from him, like light from the orb of the sun, arose Netra, who became the eye for all subjects. From Netra was born Sunṛpa, who resembled the form of Kāma when it had been tormented by the fire of the wrath of the Three-eyed Lord (Śiva). From Sunṛpa came Suśruta, whose sacred learning was white with compassion for those fallen into the drinking of wine. From Suśruta was born Dṛḍhasena, who was firmly established in the mastery of the Vedic lore (Kāśyapī) relied upon by the followers of Suśruta. His son was Nayana, whose eyes were like the red lotus.

From Naya was born Nayaviśadamati; from Sumati was born Subala, who equalled the strength of his own arm; from Saubali was born Sunetra, whose eyes were reddened by the passion for the lips of beautiful women; his son was Satyajit, who caused the Kali age—fond of flattery—to tremble with fear; and from Satyajit was born Viśvajit, the conqueror of the universe, whose name was Jina.

From that sacrifice of universal conquest (*viśvajit*), which bestowed all as sacrificial fees (*sarvadakṣiṇā*), the Great-Souled Ripuñjaya—having surpassed Sañjaya by his conduct—attained his own self as if it were the Lord Dharma incarnate. Under his guidance, no one ever beheld the face of a beggar; with him as their leader, no one ever entered upon a wrong path or encountered the misfortune of stumbling; and with him as their lord, no one was oppressed by the burden of maintaining a family, for he bore that weight himself.

That teacher did not grant even a dream’s worth of opportunity for any lack of discipline, which is the means for achieving mastery over all lower realms. Indeed, by him were rendered as if humiliated those who discharge the intoxications through many outlets—such as the intoxication of power, family, learning, wealth, and beauty—with a flow that is exceedingly harsh, like scent-elephants shedding their rut through excessive streams.

Once, having reflected upon the Purāṇas and realizing that he was the final descendant of the lineage of Bṛhadratha, he felt as if consumed by fire in his mind, as if destroyed in his reputation, as if seized by pallor, as if eclipsed by dejection, as if smeared with insignificance, as if overwhelmed by despair, and as if asleep in a state of emptiness; letting out a cry of grief, bewildered as to what should be done, and because of his confidence in my appearance, he approached me and, in tears, asked the cause of his lack of fortitude.

Through the grace of the speech of the masters—speech that reveals all tantras, is unartificial, and has been sung by the authoritative ones—he was awakened by me alone, who had acquired inspired eloquence through diligent application.

Indeed, ascetic practice in the presence of the Blessed One is capable of utterly transforming the future of one who is destined for it. For this wife—who gives birth to the lineage of men born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or sprouts; who offers the fleeting glimmer of pleasure in vulgar enjoyments woven together with great effort; and who is devoid of the praise of bestowing true relish—is not to be compared to this [asceticism]. This [asceticism] is a friend that is a ground of trust, independent of servants who perform tasks for hire; it is a teacher whose heart is to be propitiated and who acts for one's welfare; and it is wealth that accomplishes one’s desired goals through effortless action, providing protection from beginningless suffering.

This wondrous means of accomplishment is a great medicine that removes all diseases, produces a lack of enmity, and subjugates all beings through the creeper of karma; it is a wakefulness born from sin that possesses the six qualities and ascends to extraordinary dignity, yet its sovereignty is not difficult to attain nor its practice arduous here, for its requisites consist of horses, chariots, fruits, roots, grass, and shrubs—[the very essence] of asceticism.

In her [the queen], there were ministers’ wives who offered many kinds of seductions, who acted with mutual hostility, whose conduct was characterized by the transgression of prohibitions, and who gave instructions on what ought to be done. However, [there were others] who were naturally simple, free from the impurity of desire, devoid of envy, who had cast out the speech of atheism, and whose purity was sincere; they filled her ears with the means of spiritual attainment. Behold the abundance of fruit resulting from the practice of austerity!

That these two, the sun and the moon; Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Draviṇapā, Savitṛ, and the Aśvins; Vāyu and Agni Śociṣkeśa—exalt themselves in the sky with wondrous majesty; and that the great ṛṣis, headed by the Seven Sages, as well as the deities, abide having surpassed others through their power—all this [is due to him].

Even those pleasures enjoyed by the lords of the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, gods, and Pannagas, as they are described, are merely the occasional manifestations of a slight success in asceticism. Even a mother, while performing penance, becomes angry with her son; yet asceticism is exceedingly gracious. What need is there for more? There is nothing else like it that is effective in all undertakings; or rather, let this [power] be sufficient, having been established by what we have uttered.

Surely even the Blessed Ones—the Moon, Kṛṣṇa, and Brahmā—who are handfuls of seeds for the sprout of the world, though they have not obtained [this power], yet, having attained it, bear this lake-like expanse that produces the progenitor; and by attending upon her with great reverence, they proclaim her majesty. It should certainly not be thought that one who dwells in the forest, desiring the forest, undergoes such exertion and movement out of fear of afflictions (*kleśa*). Indeed, those who know the asceticism (*tapasyā*) of a forest-dweller understand that it is a hundredfold greater than the exertion of one who dwells in a village and desires worldly pleasures.

"No," they replied, "just as householders have ploughed their fields at home, so too must we bear those delusions that move within the heart and the sufferings of arduous ascetic practices; O Tālavali, which is more grievous?"

For a wise man who is tormented by the false accusations of courtiers and members of the assembly, and who suffers from a pervasive fever of anxiety as if he were standing in the midst of five fires—even if he should experience distress from the tears of his own kinsmen and the like, I do not think that the waters of the earth, which bind together the showers of rain, would moisten the body of such a person lying upon a slab of stone cooled by the arrival of a frost-free winter night in the same way that those [tears] do.

But surely this alone is sufficient for dwelling in the forest: that here one enjoys everything with a pure disposition, accompanied by women of pure character and clean breasts, free from all agitation; that one resorts to trees that grant the shadow of pleasure from their wives, which are fragrant and habituated to yielding sweet fruit; and that one does not serve kings whose conduct consists of hands entreated for a succession of taxes and weariness, who bring only torment.

Deer are those whose acquaintance is guileless and whose nature is characterized by an easily accessible disposition toward trust; whereas those who possess the mere scent of kinsmen are killers whose intimacy is scattered and swallowed by the passion for self-interest, whose nature is cruel and distrustful. Therefore, having taken refuge at your feet—which are both nectar and medicine—this person has, through a distant means, accomplished that goal which was to be achieved by a virtuous person.

And in that region on the bank of the Soma-sutā river, there dwells the Lord Parameṣṭhin, residing in a forest hermitage and attended by blessed sages; his feet are marked with the conch and the thunderbolt, and he has the chariot of Vainya standing near him. He is the refuge of Umā, the supreme lord who reclines upon the earth, whose body consists of the wind, fire, forest, mountains, and sky, and who is both the subtle and the gross, the imperishable and the supreme among all things. [He is present] for one who has sought refuge in Him.

When it was said that for those who persist in their own views there is "vomiting" [of what has been learned], he—due to his spiritual fitness (*bhavyatva*), his great learning (*bahuśrutya*), and his conviction based on self-realization (*ātmapratyaya*)—abandoned the royal insignia on that very day and took up the emblems of a sage.

For instance—he bound upon his head, with a loosened cloth, matted locks that shed their redness like the first sprouts of asceticism; with a hand whose passion for touching sword and bow had been dulled, he grasped a water-pot as if it were the very vessel of tranquility; upon his waist, which remained natural after ceasing the habit of wearing fine garments, he fastened a bark garment, bright red like a fire clinging to the impurities of sovereignty;
and with forest-grown herbs, he made his body thin, having lost all hope for other food.

For instance: for some time, though free from the fault of greed, he was satisfied with nothing but husks obtained without delay; for a while, his livelihood was interrupted by the passage of time, so he subsisted on roots, fruits, leaves, flowers, vegetables, and water-moss that were unripe; then again, he consumed only raw things.

There too, he lived with a superior water-channel and a young calf within the enclosure; he was a leader by virtue of his fierce asceticism, remaining submerged in fearlessness, having cast off all impurities such as the husks of grain, and wandering about. Having crushed [his food] himself, he consumed a mere trifle of food at irregular times; naturally self-restrained, he performed the function of a mortar using only his teeth as a mortar.

Free from the sense of "mine," bearing no burden here on earth, having established his *agnihotra* in a single direction, and observing the rules of fasting and conduct, he practiced his vows with the skin of a deer; moving with the same gait as a deer, he lived among the deer. For some period of time, he engaged in the practices of the forest-dwellers and took his meal (*pāraṇā*) in the color of the forest. He drank only a very small amount of water; he drank only the purifying wind.

He lay down upon a bed of moss-covered stones where the withered branches had been broken by wild elephants; a place where the spray from the frothy snorting of boars—provoked by the heat of hundreds of flames fanned by artificial fires—had scorched their lean bodies; and where his head was drenched by the falling drops of pure, cool snow-water that had gathered into thick masses.

And Sūcīpalaka, taking refuge in the *palaka* tree whose thorns were like needles, practiced a supreme meditative absorption (*samādhi*) throughout the nights, his head bowed toward the smoke-crested tips of the *kurusaka* trees; he observed without fail whatever sequence of desired vows was seen in the scriptures, even as he remained amidst rows of [trees] bent down... Having performed circumambulations of the vast earth as if it were the whole world, having bestowed his mind’s misdeeds as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and having completed the duties of his pilgrimage, that king—whose merit was like that of a man-god—dwelt for many years in the hermitage of Badarī. Then, returning once more to this grove of asceticism, I heard from the mouths of sages that at that very time, there arose in that royal sage extraordinary and world-astonishing manifestations, such as diving into the sky and traversing the waters.
