She herself respectfully placed her hip against the side of his retinue; she regarded him as if he were only two years old despite being many years past, for he was embraced by signs of compassion as if he had fallen into a state of helplessness, like a lion cub.

Carrying some rice-pudding obtained by chance, which was cooled by being placed upon broad leaves and flower clusters, she approached and paid homage to the Queen together with her husband. She then spoke: "The maidservant Vindhyasena makes this representation: 'This boy, as if suited to a young servant, has waited for the arrival of the Prince; he is now at our command... [but] your Majesty’s feet are the final authority.'"

"O dear one, tell me, for I am filled with joy! From where did he originate here? Could this be the fulfillment of some *apsaras* who was seducing some *ṛṣi* in this forest? Otherwise, how could such a thing happen to one as delicate as a young *śirīṣa* bud? Is this perhaps the power of the Vedas? Thus, his curiosity having burst forth, the lord of the earth himself questioned that Śabara. He, having bowed, replied: "O King, please listen!"

In another birth, in this very Vindhya forest, there was the husband of my maternal aunt—a second Kalavya as it were, or perhaps an incarnation of a portion of Kali; a creator of tumults, a source of great joy [to his own], one who had seized the chiefs of the forest hamlets, a plunderer of inhabited lands, a protector of thieves, one unacquainted with hunger and thirst, and an expert in the timing of battles—[known as] Abhijña... Like a monkey in climbing tall trees, like an owl in its nocturnal wakefulness, and like an elephant in rut...

There is a leader of the Kirātas named Sārthamardana—a name truly suited to his character—who, like a lion, is a destroyer of all gathered hosts; who, though crying out in hunger, remains unshaken by the afflictions of cold, heat, rain, and wind; who acts with deliberation and is habituated to undertakings within his capability; who distinguishes the cries of wild animals and possesses matted locks that never fail as omens; who is not dilatory in what must be done, does not falter in hardships, and does not turn back in vast enterprises; who is skilled in all weapons and terrifying even by his very form.

May he recognize me as his maternal uncle, named Mālātacakranāman. Having learned from the mouth of an agent that the King of Mithilā was approaching, we—driven by arrogance and without hesitation—encountered him as he was crossing the great forest. Believing him to be a caravan capable of fulfilling our desires because of its vast abundance of provisions, and perceiving him to be within our grasp, we roared, danced with joy, and having seized a man, offered him to the Goddess Vindhyavāsinī on the banks of the Sindhu.

Having established that a hundred [coins] were to be paid for each head, they—whose hands were smeared with the mass of blood flowing from their own forearms as they wielded well-sharpened swords and daggers, whose bow-staffs were strung with bowstrings made from the essence of the vitals of living creatures, who had just now whetted their forest-stones on the tips of fresh peacock-feather arrows whose blunt edges were dulled by the thick coating of dried blood, who had gathered secure provisions such as meat on spits, dried venison, and wild creepers, and who were surrounded by flocks of animals—to inspire confidence...

Having traveled for only a few days, our spirits were uplifted by a multitude of auspicious omens; having made our agreements and being assigned to their respective ambush points by the commander-in-chief, we remained hidden in the thickets, taking refuge among the forest creatures as if we were invisible.

And it proceeded, filled with the appearance of intoxication; its young heroes were distressed by the snares of glances from those who live by their beauty; the womenfolk hung upon it, lured by greed for the fresh shoots of excellent palm trees; one hand of the men held sword and shield while the other was intent on gathering the sweet fruits brought down by the Trijita soldiers; its ranks were broken as they pursued deer rising along the path; and the common folk were busily engaged in various tasks, such as rushing to seize the calves of the cows that had wandered here and there.

He proceeded with great caution, surrounded by a multitude of people who were filled with apprehension as if they were thieves fearing a trap; whose ranks were swelling with those of humble status who were being honored; where the cries of the petty masters, agitated by the sudden striking of sticks and the casting down of oxen and bags, increased to a level unbearable for the ears; which was filled with smiles from within; where the public outcry was being suppressed by the intervention of elders; where the group of weapon-bearers was being rallied back by the apprehension of ill omens reported by astrologers; and where the points of danger were being pointed out by those familiar with the roads.

A great caravan, its supplies gathered by the royal army, arrived at its own territory, accompanied by the blaring sounds of large drums, small drums, and trumpets; with conchs, *piñcholās*, and *kāhaḷas* resounding as they were blown; with circles of horses agitated by the neighing of those who had let out shouts and cries; and with showers of arrows discharged from thick, raised, and formidable bows drawn into circles, crying out, "Kill! Kill!"

Uttering garbled cries, their splendor flickering, their movements turning as they struggled under the weight of their own momentum, like tigers yawning with hunger or as if agitated by the terrible force of a cosmic dissolution, we—our brows and eyes fierce—rushed impetuously toward that army as if to devour it.

Because it was situated within a small camp, because it was on the move, because it was extremely crowded, and because of its lack of confidence and blindness, that region was filled with loud cries of "Hā! Hā! released by the terrified women and attendants of the camp who were fleeing in confusion; it was crowded with carts shattered and scattered in all directions by the roaming herds of fierce elephants, while the brave warriors roared and the armored soldiers were struck with terror by the bristling shafts of formidable archers.

The caravan was instantly rendered helpless—its trees stripped, plundered, and destroyed; its path blocked by blood mired in the merciless trampling of herds of oxen crushed under the impact of the army’s advance; its vanguard beautiful with the outstretched noses of Kirātas, those fierce men who remove fear and act as supreme warriors; its thickets shattered by the sudden, clattering noise of the bowstrings of the soldiers whose backs were broken by the forceful snapping of their bows; and it became a sight of lamentation for our beloved, as the deceitful Śabaras, acting as guides for the fugitives fleeing in all directions, pointed out a path of self-display that had already ravaged and ruined the forest.

But that king, whose majesty was equal to that of the immortals, remained undiminished in his pride even when his entire army was being struck down, like Suyodhana himself. With his bow acting as a cloud raining down showers of arrows with unimpeded force, he seemed to consume them with eyes copper-red from fierce anger. And that haughty destroyer of caravans displayed great prowess against that noble-souled one, performing deeds unworthy of a forest-dweller.

And that great man, being assailed by all of us with our bows ready—like a mountain by clouds—and being cried out against by the chariot-teams as they milked him from above, perceived that his army was difficult to rally, recognized his own vulnerability and the precariousness of his position, and, having largely abandoned his concern for safety, commanded those standing at his side.

In the midst of the confusion, being told that the queen’s carriage had been led away by someone, he set out slowly with his followers, acting with haste as he watched the merchant folk who had taken up their hammers and were seeking safety, along with the women, children, and the elderly. Meanwhile, Sārthamardana, having appointed me to the task of guarding a great store of grain at this roadside station, followed after the king.

Gladdening the Mātaṅgas, Puḷindas, and the Durmukhas, they utterly exterminated the caravan’s insignia; some they slew with sword-strokes, some they captured alive, some they killed like animals, some they drove away with sticks, and some they seized as they fled toward their lives’ end, driving them before the sun’s chariot; while others, who had hidden by entering into thickets, they sought out and, having bound them in a circle, laid them down on their sides, crushing them.

Some, unable to endure [the enemy], were fighting with great effort; [the heroes] dragged them by their hair and, laughing with ease, winked at them. Some they drove like cattle with blows from sticks, herding them into the enclosure of the pen. Some who had fled were destroyed like goats; [the heroes] pulled them back and made them enter the caves by force. Some they addressed with low, mocking words; finding others hidden in bushes, they called out to one another joyfully by name. And likewise, some recounted stories of the Guhyakas.

Releasing showers of curiosity-inducing cries while loudly proclaiming their enjoyment of *āsava*, *surā*, *ariṣṭa*, *sauvīraka*, and *tuṣodaka* liquors; drinking as much as they can hold with roasted meat as a side-dish; grinding camphor—white as crystal—into a fine powder on a stone and scattering it upon their chests with the stench of human blood; wandering through the forest where the elephant-shaped prisoners are kept under guard; and making the *ajikā* dogs, who are otherwise like hungry deer, leap up from their beds every day and run about in pursuit of them as if searching for prey—those men take the greatest delight.

Likewise, as if nourishing their wealth, they were nourished and appeared joyful; though my shoulders were shorn, I felt as if anointed with heavy sandalwood, as if my head were honored by lotuses, as if covered by ornaments for many mouths, as if fragrant with heaps of vessels, as if veiled by heaps of bright-wooled jars, as if in bloom with clusters of chowries, as if budding with groups of jeweled palm-fans, as if starred with the bristling hair on the flanks of horses, and as if [obstructed] by the water-channels broken by wild forest elephants.

It was strewn with severed arms of heroes like the golden pedestals for the self-choice ceremony of Kālarātri; it was covered with the carcasses of horses and elephants like the sandy banks of the Madhurā river; it was filled with the circles of Kaṃsa’s retinue like a heap of golden jars; it was like the lineage of Bṛhadratha where the staffs of the Madhu clan were broken and scattered; it was like a royal court where the world of kings had become bewildered; it was like an anthill crowded with throngs of women whose mouths were streaming with blood; and it was like a multitude of courtesans radiant with jewels, red pearls, and [beautiful] garments.

Having avoided the battlefield—which was guarded by stationed *rakṣas* and strewn with arrows embedded in bloody mud—he approached [the woman] who was tearing at her heart, wandering here and there; whose eyes were closed due to the pain from wounds in many vital organs; who was groaning deeply within for a long time as if her life were fleeing from the friction of Yama’s harsh claws; who was writhing on the ground while blood flowed from her, as if being ground into a paste of gore to serve as a cosmetic ointment by the Night of Doom (*Kālarātri*); and who, like a forest creeper in the heat, was drying up from within due to the lack of water.

I beheld a withering young woman, about eighteen years of age, in the vicinity of that hermitage; and from near her, I heard the sound of weeping like that of a child, yet I did not know from where its origin arose. Then, moved by compassion, I asked, "Is she still living? But she was unable to speak; merely opening her eyes slightly and looking at me with pity, she spoke with great effort: "Noble sir, what is the use of this unfortunate woman being held, whether she be dead or alive?"

"Consider for a moment whether that noble youth, who was hidden behind the sprout-like ears of the elephant calf, will live or not. Having heard this, his curiosity aroused, he approached suddenly and saw the fallen, lifeless man lying as if asleep. He observed that Maṅgala’s limbs were as if covered in glowing embers by the slowly flowing blood; his neck was pinned from below with a *tomara* spear, and he was encircled on all sides by arrows standing in a row, each penetrating three-quarters of its depth.

He observed the petal of his ear, which seemed to enclose within it the entire expanse of the Dharma-lake as if its boundaries were obstructed; which, with upward glances and flickering movements, appeared to be gasping for breath, as if displaying that elephant as still possessing life.

Having lifted and cast aside my weapons, and having touched the elephant’s trunk-like ears with my arrows, I beheld this prince of wondrous life—his body mounted upon spears, lances, and shafts, his back scarred by the dragging of thick neck-ropes, his two arms smeared with splashes of the saffron-hued liquid of elephant blood—and observing that his body remained uninjured, I reflected upon the very marvel of his deed; then, approaching that woman of excellent complexion, I spoke to her.

"O blessed lady! Take heart... who among the beloved of the gods is his father or mother, those wicked ones for whom even such a dispeller of sorrow as he—[who is] like a young lion cub, falling upon the frontal globes of elephants with indistinct cries out of childishness, having by chance fallen from his dwelling and [escaped] into the cage of my ears, filling my entire [heart]—that woman, sighing hot and long breaths with tearful face as if shedding her very misery, [beheld] here the Blessed One, the giver of life?"

"Who else but you deserves to hear this? Thus, restrained by great respect, she spoke slowly, her pain subsiding: "Noble sir! Surely those who have reached the very path of hearing [this] must be possessed of supernatural power and self-restraint—those inhabitants of Videha who are free from malice toward living beings. Their sovereign, the ornament of Janaka’s lineage, is the lord named King Prahāravarma."

He was the friend of the Lord, the King of Magadha—a royal swan who is the sole beloved of the earth bounded by the oceans—and a firm vessel of uncommon affection. And Queen Vasumatī, the ornament of his inner apartments and the birthplace of all virtues, became like a second life to his beloved Priyaṃvadā, possessing an exceeding measure of love for her.

Out of affection for her friend, Queen Priyaṃvadā, desiring to see her who was now carrying a child, went to Magadhā together with her husband. At that very moment, a king named Mānasāra (of Mālava) waged a war against the Lord, the King of Magadha, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā—a conflict equal to the Tārakāmaya war, which caused even the gods to experience horripilation.

There, this King Janaka Prahāravarmā—whose majesty was as unbearable as the radiance of the suns—having brought an end to thousands of Kṣatriyas, lay upon a bed of arrows as if dead, together with his dear friend Siṃhavarman, the lord of Aṅga, in a single chariot; he was then carried away by that king Māgadha from the field of battle.

But that god, his body pulverized by a certain divine sword wielded by an opponent—whose belly was the sacrificial beast for the darkness of the lives of the kṣatriyas, and whose dust-clouds increased the joy of the eyes of the Goddess of War as they ground his volleys of arrows—became such that the limbs of Janaka, the charioteer of the southern region, were like those of a common cowherd, yet remained recognizable as a deity.

Having heard this news, the King of Mālava himself approached, his crown, earrings, long pendants, and other ornaments cast aside; shedding tears like a kinsman for the sake of the Lord of Aṅga, who had lost six elephants, he consoled him and somehow or other steadied him with various accounts of the duties of heroes. Day and night, he personally supervised the healing of the wounds with medicines administered by his own physicians.

That king himself, possessing genuine manliness, was victorious; as for me, however, relying on fate, I am utterly defeated. "What use is this weapon to one such as I, a coward? he thought, and thus he cast away his arms in the midst of all the kshatriyas. Yet, because of such worthy and fitting conduct toward him, my dear friend Pratihāravarmā did not abandon his life even while in exile.

However, regarding the news of his renunciation, the awakened ones took care to ensure the production of offspring, thinking that for those who have not performed sacrifices and have no sons, there is no hope of attaining the world of the ancestors. Thus, when the queen Priyaṃvadā had reached her time for conception, she conceived two embryos at once, like the twin sons of Mādrī.

The delighted Lord of Mālava, having performed the Viśvajit sacrifice in which all one's possessions are given away, and upon its completion, accepted Bhadravāhana—the horse obtained by crushing the Lord of Magadha—from Rati after she had offered him the most excellent honors; he then granted King Janaka permission to return to his own country along with Siṃhavarman.

This king, having departed from the city in due course, arrived at Aṅga; after staying for several days out of friendship with his kinsmen, he set out for Campā. On the very road, hearing from a trusted messenger that the Videhas had been seized by the arrogant sons of his elder brother, Saṃhāravarman—namely Vikaṭavarman and others—he, though having withdrawn all his forces from Māgadha and Mālava, marched forth in a rage to attack them, but was restrained by his ministers.

But his sister’s son, Suhanātha, having heard that the border regions were being subdued, set out from there with a portion of the army to protect himself while intending to march against the enemy; disregarding the hosts of Kirātas, he traveled by this path called Avakra. It is not known in what state he currently finds himself.

But for me, unfortunate as I am, my mother—who was as dear to me as a mother herself—was appointed by the Queen to attend to the growth of the Prince... and she accepted [the task], though it was so beautiful. Then I entered the tent, which was not agitated and offered comfort, without being bewildered; and there, while this youth—holding a fly-whisk with its fringe hanging down...—was treading upon my attendant, he, whose passion was stirred at the sight of me and whose island-like presence was intensified by his impetuous approach, did something... regarding me.

...having emerged from the fever as it were, and having eaten roots and tubers easily found in the forest by the clear waters of some mountain stream, while the orb of the sun was setting and the nocturnal frost was falling like a swarm of locusts, I followed behind Devalikā—who had departed from the house of the Māryā with her face covered by a cloth of snuhī leaves—as if I were a thief, unobserved; and having entered [the place] with someone, I sat down, reflecting deeply.

Then, seizing him by one arm—which was like a young red goat with red garlands and ointments and as hard as an iron bar—while holding a blood-stained, unsheathed dagger in the other, he, who was as dark as the deepest darkness in the high sky, whose shoulder was rubbed by buffaloes, and who was revealed by the flash of a small knife in his palm, was recognized by my voice as that very same old hunter, authorized by the entire village.

Having approached without fear or hesitation, he circumambulated the Blessed Lady, prostrated himself, and—casting aside all mercy—having cast the body of this long-lived one upon the earth, O dweller of the Tinduka grove! O Goddess, family deity of the forest-dwellers! "This is a tender offering of a child for you," thinking thus under the influence of his latent impressions, he raised up a small creature while intending to tear it apart.

I, however, desiring to see his divine nature, and modulating my voice with a deep, resolute tone mixed with feminine inflections, said, "Go! Your fear is gone; the evil is destroyed! and even as I spoke, I seized him by his uninjured limbs. He too, having accomplished his purpose, fled away with a joyful appearance, without looking back.

I too, wishing to avoid being seen by the villagers of that place for this reason, departed from the city after offering prayers to the goddess Saṃbhramadīnī. By that very path, I traversed the road with great speed. Having resolved to entrust these subjects to you, O protector of the people, I have now arrived before you. "How this boy grows, how he attains discipline, and how at the end he will bring joy to his parents—all this you alone shall know, O sole kinsman of all beings," he said, and then fell silent.
Then the lord of the earth, whose policy was born [of wisdom], his eyes wide open like two streams flowing with honey, and radiating splendor, spoke as he triumphed.

O Blessed One! I see that while the night still remains, even a deer has been seen—caught in the snare of a difficult-to-construct trap. Indeed, for one who was devoted to his dear friend and possessed of superior learning, there occurred the dragging away by forest-dwellers, the rescue from that place by this aged hunter, the presentation [of the animal], and its recovery with great difficulty from the army of Nindhya, which was like a mirror of our own pride.

"By the power of our intellect, we were drawn from the house of compassion amidst the tiger... and death; and by both children, though so widely separated, it was as if in a dream that we had once again come here together into the hands of our parents. [Imagine] this prosperity and this state of being experienced with such sovereignty—even for my friend Ratnodbhava and for the two sons of my preceptor, Satyaśarman and Kālapāla—may you convey news of their welfare in this context."

As her husband began to speak, Rājavāhana’s mother, standing nearby, asked him: "Noble son, who are these whose appearance is so worthy of praise, and who even now remain unknown to you by name? Surely they must be your very close kinsmen and virtuous men."

And the lord of the earth said: "Truly, Vāsava, your reasoning is sound. You are both dear to me and virtuous. It was impossible for you to know of that wondrous event which occurred while her ladyship was still unmarried; now, however, let it be heard."

Indeed, this father of mine, the creator of all beings, the conqueror of Madana, who was like an eye [to the world], had three ministers—Matisharma, Dharmapala, and Padmodbhava—who were of radiant splendor. Of these, the first was pure, a master of the Vedas (*anūcāna*), of celebrated fame, a performer of sacrifices, one who delighted in non-accumulation, a ruler of his subjects like a father, and was by lineage of the Angirasas.

The other, however, was named Dharmapāla—a name true to its meaning—for he was a descendant of Viśvāmitra, a treasury of friendship, free from arrogance, compassionate, possessed of steady intellect, skillful in his duties, unanxious for worldly fortune, and eager for glory. The story of the other is extensive: from him [Vaivasvata] was born Manu Sthāṇveya; from that Kṣavatha came Ikṣvāku, the root of the Kṣatriya lineage.

His younger brother was Nābhā (or Nediṣṭha), who by the power of destiny moved at will; while wandering through the regions of Kacaraṃśa, he first initiated a new, passionate, and most noble trade with Maṇibhadra in the mountains, oceans, islands, Aṭalī, Puṭabhedana, and other places. Among his many high-souled descendants were the Mayārjunas, and among the Bhalandanas, the descendants of Bhālandana, there arose the Pivītis. Among those living in Svaryāvarta, there was one named Potapa, the very foundation of their fame.

Once, while staying in a town established along the Ganges, my father—who had attained a lifespan of many hundreds of years through the power of his asceticism—encountered Candragupta, the founder of the Maurya dynasty, who was enjoying the kingdom of Nanda in this forest region. Having presented gifts and performed the proper courtesies, he stood there, filled with joy by the king’s supreme affection, and showed him a single necklace from his own collection of jewels that was worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].

When her value was being appraised, the interior of the house was bathed by the rays of her jewels as if by streams of tears from one who had been slighted. Though astonished by the excellence of the gems, Kautilya, the preceptor’s son-in-law, dismissed the merchant with the words, “Come at dawn with the master’s permission. Having departed from the royal palace, he consumed the fragrant betel-leaf obtained through the king’s favor; yet, even while walking on a path difficult to traverse even for wealth, he was seized. And he fell upon the road, struck down as if by the winds of the sun.

Among the attendants who were incompetent in their duties, a certain courtesan, feeling pity for him as he had fallen into such a state, led him toward her own home which was nearby. She restored his life with thick drops of sandalwood water scattered by her sprout-like hands, by the breeze from clusters of jeweled fans that touched him most gently, and by lotus and lily petals gathered from the palace pond.

And he had her laid down to rest upon a soft couch. But Potaka, seeing no other way to repay his life-saving kindness to her, felt ashamed to offer it openly; so, placing that single-string necklace right on the edge of the bed, he went home to rest. However, that intoxicated woman, having forgotten it, sent it back in the hand of a maidservant, accompanied by other ornaments suited to it, after making her swear an oath to return it.

And Āmuktamālavī entered the royal palace unobserved. Having recognized her arrival and perceiving her approach, the king, touched by emotion, summoned her and said, "Show me the single-string necklace from the Yavana expedition."

"O King! That gift of affection has already been given. Be gracious; I have other jewels. Whatever among them you desire to take, please accept it. To the merchant speaking thus, Candragupta, as if provoked to anger, rebuked him like one who had been insulted: "Since you, though following the bounds of propriety, did not honor me and instead gave this gift of affection to Dhanamada, you are indeed not barren [in your efforts]. The ship-owner, however, remained unperturbed; by virtue of his great courage, he replied with a slight smile:

"O King, this gift of life is but a small token of my affection; rather, it is the excessive burning [of my heart] that I feel toward him. Since the duty of the virtuous is not to mention again what has been given, I shall not speak of it. To this, the King, who had been bound by his own forgetfulness, replied: "O Lord, please listen!"

Once, as I was crossing the Andhakaccha region on the shore of the great ocean, I beheld a man who had emerged from the waters. His waist-cloth was bound with golden chains, and a large gem was fastened upon his loins. He held a long sword firmly pressed against his chest, and he was afflicted by the exhaustion of a great struggle with Mahendra. With eight tusks, his bonds loosened and his mouth agape, he was barely remaining alive, gasping for breath. Immediately taking pity on him, I cut through [the bonds] with my sword, comforted him, and asked the cause of his distress.

And it was said by that Great Soul: "For those seized by the fever of poverty, death resulting from persistence [in seeking wealth] is a festival. Having learned this, I drew him away from my own lap and, with half of my vast riches—consisting of hundreds of thousands of diamonds, pearls, rubies, and emeralds—I shared them with him after he had sworn an oath. Then, perceiving me to be born of the Bhālandana lineage and named Potapa, he embraced me as if in great joy and [provided me with] whatever I desired.

He went to his own country. As for me, having gone to the city of Dramila, from that time forward I have attended upon you with heaps of wealth acquired through the successful completion of many sea voyages. This great sin of proclaiming [your deeds] was committed out of fear of you, not out of pride. Upon hearing this, Candragupta was exceedingly delighted yet filled with shame; embracing the merchant, he said, "You are a true man."

And with a conduct indistinguishable from his own, he followed him as if he had formed a bond with him; throughout the entire earth, for that purpose, he appointed eighteen excellent officials over all the merchants.

For example: like a merchant leader, there is equality with all caravans by day and by night; success in whatever is given, whether small or large; mastery over goods reached in foreign lands; immunity from punishment in all matters concerning one's own interests; success in performing actions at the proper or improper time; no seizure of property that has come of its own accord or whose enjoyment has ceased; entry even into the houses of others; and during the day, [freedom] regarding buying, selling, trade, adultery, and thieves—even when the treasury is depleted—as if it were one's own country.

Even when suffering from the extreme pain of separation, he does not manifest through his limbs even the slightest sign of distress, such as trembling of the hands or head, down to the mere act of commanding female servants or even women of the outer quarters. Likewise, whether in the case of an offense against his most beloved or against all others, he is seen to treat royal officers like sons—whether they have sons or are sonless—by refraining from violating their bodies or property and by releasing them like sons, even when they are to be executed, provided it is not for treason. This applies even in the cities, where he permits the use of horse-carriages. And [he acts] except in the case of the execution of those who have betrayed him.

After reporting the types of fraudulent acts and seizures to the King, there follows instruction regarding the restraint of the wicked; the collection of excellent ornaments, garments, and other articles of luxury; the yellow and white emblems of royalty—such as charcoal, conch shells, and drums—used during auspicious rites; and the performance of desired services for messengers and laborers on roads and in cities, whether in their presence or absence, as well as the inheritance of the wealth of those who have died while serving, according to guild custom; and finally, the commendable life of a sea-faring merchant, whose mind is fixed upon the hardships of the voyage at sea.
Longing for his own lineage, he began to give away all his possessions.

While he was in such a state, one day a certain person in the guise of a Brahmin approached him and said: "I have been sent by the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), the master of the Guhyakas, through his divine mind. Listen to this: Indeed, today, due to the turn of time, Ripuñjaya—the son of Bṛhadratha, who has cast aside both kingdom and fame, and whose husbandhood over this city of Kusumapura is such that he seeks to conquer even Fate through penance—having donned the black antelope skin, purified himself with water, and become a crusher of the pride of the god of love in the Kali age, is performing austerities in a forest of asceticism."

While he was in that state, Viśālā’s husband, having slain his master Vītihotra out of greed for wealth, consecrated his own son Prahota as king. He—who possessed sixteen thousand women in his harem and was known as Puṣpārāmavibhramabhramaracaṇḍa—was spared by the subjects because of his harshness in wielding the rod of punishment.

And his daughter was Vāsavadattā, whose fortune was worthy of being the source for the creation of the most beautiful woman in all the world, and who was like the Goddess Lakṣmī herself residing upon the lotus-like chest of King Vatsa. When he had reached the end of twenty-three autumns and departed from the world of mortals, he left behind as the protector of the subjects his son, then twenty-eight years of age. After him, Viśākhayūpa reigned for fifty years; after him, Mālyaka for twenty-one; and then Antivardhana for thirty more.

Furthermore, having cast out that son of a corrupt lineage and having occupied the city of Vārāṇasī himself, Śiśunāga—whose power was as unbearable as the Sahya mountain—ruled this earth for forty years while serving it with equanimity. Śaiśunābhi Kākavarṇa ruled for thirty-six years; Kṣemavarman for twenty-six; Kṣatraujas for forty; Bimbisāra for thirty-eight; Ajātaśatru for thirty-seven; and Darśaka for twenty-five.
Udāyin enjoyed sovereignty for thirty-three years, Nandivardhana for forty-three, and Mahānandin, his successor, enjoyed the glory of that lineage for exactly as long.

While he was ruling, a magnificent performance of a great drama, delightful with its abundance of aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and emotional states (*bhāva*), commenced in this city. By chance, the two treasures Śaṅkha and Padma—possessing human forms and having arrived there—beheld it, having manifested their presence out of interest in the aesthetic flavors. Among them, Padma was bound by the fetters of spells by some mantra-practitioner of great power who had recognized him.

He was released by his vow, which bound him for a distance of one *yojana* from the city in every direction; he was also questioned by Candrāvṛṣṭi and Jasubandhu. And thus, while being tormented and desiring to withdraw what remained of his body, from that very king of men, Nanda—known as Mahāpadma—was born to a low-caste woman who was [in fact] a woman of excellent complexion. He, moreover, withdrew the entire collection of gold along with the life-span of all the *kṣatriyas*.

At that very time, there was a twice-born man named Kalāpin in Utkala who, being childless, obtained through the grace of Kātyāyanī a maiden named Kātyāyanī who could grant all desires; he then appointed her to the service of the sacred fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*). And she, by the very path of the wind, became pregnant.

But her father, having become deluded, abandoned her and left her in the Vindhya forest; there, by the power of destiny, as she was about to enter a forest fire, the god Agni appeared in person and directed her to dwell on the Godāvarī. She went to that agrahāra and, entering like one preceded by a great comet, she became a sharer in the status of a twice-born through her own vow of asceticism, and gave birth to a son named Vararuci, an ornament of the world, who was like the very essence of Vaiśvānara.

When Vararuci was about five years old, both of those wandering mendicants came to his house. One of them was named Myāli (the other was Indradatta). Of the two, Kātyāyana said: "O Blessed One, listen attentively. I am the son of Bhānubhartṛ, a descendant of Bhṛgu and a native of Parāntaka. Although I was cherished by my mother as her only son, my father seized me and did not have me educated."

Having married a Brahmin woman named Brahmadā, who was intoxicated with passion, a certain wandering mendicant (*maskarī*) entered for alms and was slightly delayed by her foot-adorning (*pādarañjana*). She rose, bowed to him with a smile, and gave him alms. Out of curiosity, I asked her the reason for her smile; she, however, directed me toward that very sage as the one to be questioned. But because it was impossible due to shame, she herself, being importuned, spoke with great difficulty: [The rest of the passage follows: "This mendicant is the son of a certain Brahmin from the city of Kāmpilya. He has mastered all the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and he is well-versed in the six systems of philosophy (*ṣaḍdarśana*). He knows the secret doctrines of the *Pāśupata* and *Kāpālika* sects, and he is skilled in the arts of sorcery (*kārmaṇa*), incantations (*mantra*), and the subjugation of others (*vaśīkaraṇa*). He is a master of the *Śākuna*, *Vāstuvidyā*, *Svapna*, and *Aṅgavidyā* [sciences]. He knows the *Jyotiṣa*, *Nimitta*, *Arthaśāstra*, and *Rājanīti*. He is an expert in the *Dhanurveda*, *Gandharvaveda*, and *Āyurveda*. He knows the *Māyāvidyā*, *Yogavidyā*, and *Mantravidyā*. He is proficient in the *Citravidyā*, *Vaiśika*, and *Kāmasūtra*. He knows the *Śilpaśāstra*, *Gajaśikṣā*, and *Aśvaśikṣā*. He is skilled in the *Tarkavidyā*, *Vyākaraṇa*, and *Chandas*. He knows the *Nirukta*, *Kalpa*, and *Jyotiṣa*. He is an expert in the *Sāmudrika*, *Lakṣaṇa*, and *Vaidyaka*. He knows the *Mīmāṃsā*, *Nyāya*, and *Vaiśeṣika*. He is proficient in the *Sāṃkhya*, *Yoga*, and *Pātañjala*. He knows the *Bhagavadgītā*, *Mahābhārata*, and *Rāmāyaṇa*. He is skilled in the *Purāṇas*, *Itihāsas*, and *Upapurāṇas*. He knows the *Tantras*, *Āgamas*, and *Mantras*. He is an expert in the *Yantras*, *Maṇḍalas*, and *Mudrās*. He knows the *Dhātuvāda*, *Rasāyana*, and *Vajrakriyā*. He is skilled in the *Khaḍgavidyā*, *Cakravidyā*, and *Golakavidyā*. He knows the *Vetālasādhana*, *Śavāsādhana*, and *Piśācasādhana*. He is proficient in the *Bhūtasādhana*, *Grahasādhana*, and *Rākṣasasādhana*. He knows the *Nāgasādhana*, *Sarpasādhana*, and *Viṣasādhana*. He is skilled in the *Agnyutpādana*, *Vāyusādhana*, and *Jalasādhana*. He knows the *Pṛthivīsādhana*, *Ākāśasādhana*, and *Digbandhana*. He is proficient in the *Khecaratva*, *Antardhāna*, and *Vaśīkaraṇa*. He knows the *Uccāṭana*, *Stambhana*, and *Mohana*. He is skilled in the *Vidveṣaṇa*, *Māraṇa*, and *Ākarṣaṇa*. He knows the *Yakṣasādhana*, *Gandharvasādhana*, and *Devatāsādhana*. He is proficient in the

"I was raised by this sage as a female mouse. When he was about to set out on a pilgrimage, I entered his luggage unperceived even though my mother tried to stop me, because I was distraught at the prospect of separation. Seeing him... when the disciple began to bathe, I was cast aside due to my animal nature; falling headlong into the mouth of a hawk, I landed again in the waters of the Bhāgīrathī before being fully submerged. By that death at the sacred ford and by her devotion to the Blessed One, supreme [merit] was produced... and she now possesses the favor of her husband. Seeing this very thing, a smile arose upon the sage."

"Even for me, who remembers my previous birth, this sequence of her passing away is certainly true; for as she fell into a swoon, Madaya... [intended to] lead me into delusion, the Blessed One, wishing to dispel that confusion, entered her physical body and, delighting me with teachings on the Dharma, caused me to take up the life of a renunciant."

"Because the syllables did not emerge from his mouth, he cast aside the extensive treatises... and while wandering in that assembly of mendicants, he was mocked as a 'foolish yogi' by those addicted to various scriptures. Out of agitation, he returned to my master’s house and maintained his meditative flow (dhārā). Then my master commanded me: 'Take Śrutadhara and attend upon him. This very person, who has been difficult to encounter at any time, has finally been seen today after a long interval. Now, hear from me how his arrival came about. Thus he spoke, pointing toward the second [person].

He also related: "In the city named Kāmpilya, I was a disciple of my teacher Gopālaka, and my name was Indradatta. He had a daughter whose contrary name was Virūpā. My teacher, finding her devoid of knowledge of the four Vedas and the six auxiliary sciences, ordained her as a slave-girl. But she, having conceived a passion of love for me due to my appearance, remained intent on death if she were married to anyone other than me."

Desirous of seeing the full bloom of youth in this dark-eyed maiden, I maintained the status of a *subrahmaṇya* priest in my master’s house for the sake of acquiring the knowledge of Brahman. And the King, having been commanded, went to the side of Bodhāyana, placing this friend of mine at the forefront; and this matter was not in vain. This long-lived one is a fit vessel for divine study. Therefore, let us cast aside this timidity born of affection, which is common among other women, and let this jewel of a man be entrusted to us.

"When the purpose has been accomplished, we shall indeed restore [the child] to your very hands. But she, having already been awakened to this matter by the venerable Agni and steadied, was nonetheless deeply despondent due to her agitation from the separation from her beloved son; yet, through the effort of the Sage and by her own power, she produced a state of meditative composure and somehow or other consented. Then, taking him—who had undergone the initiatory rites—upon his shoulder, they both settled in Vidarbha with the head of the household.

And when it was asked, "In whose house [is this]? the great multitude laughed, saying: "This lodging belongs to the venerable Upavarṣa, whose teacher’s lineage has flourished, and whose house has been reduced to such a state that its outer walls have collapsed and the roof-panels have fallen away."

"This is strange! thought [Upavarṣa]. Then, having approached by the path indicated by someone who said "some seeker is here," and being asked "Where is the teacher? by the preceptor's wife—who was weeping and crying out, "This is mockery!"—Upavarṣa returned from the field with the yoke and traces of his plow still resting on his shoulder. Having favored them by returning their salutation, that learned man, once they had prostrated themselves, asked, "Which among you, dear children, is Śrutadhara? When Vararuci was pointed out, he rejoiced exceedingly.

Having rested in that secluded place, he spoke to them: "In this city, two sons of Bhaṭṭas are observing the *varṣā* rains-retreat; Varṣa is the more resolute of the two, while the other does not even listen."

Once, having been invited by his senior wife to observe the "Fool’s Vow" (*mūrkhavrata*)—a rite involving the gift of a bedding-cover (*kaśipu*) performed on behalf of some fool, with the prayer, "May I not be born as a fool even in another life"—he ate and set out on the road. Being weary from the journey and dissatisfied because his garment was worn out, he was greatly distressed by his weeping wife. Overcome by shame, he went to the house of his master and stayed there while the cooking was underway. When the food was cooked, he intended to offer the oblation (*havya*) to the deity, but at that moment, a certain bull...

He saw that the grain had been eaten. Furthermore, this very same sequence occurred twice. Then, having scraped his tongue with a chisel from his mouth—which was dripping with saliva—the Lord cast something into it. And He commanded: "The vomiting of the Veda must not be performed until one joint has been obtained. I am that Upavarṣa. This [Veda] has been obtained; what else remains to be undertaken?

Having successively extolled the divine and imperishable [Veda], Kātyāyana mastered the entire body of sacred literature with one [verse], Vyāli with two, and Indradatta with three. When he was commanded by them to request a teacher’s fee (*guru-dakṣiṇā*) and informed that it was for the purpose of giving his daughter in marriage, he desired only a very small amount of gold that had been brought. However, because the entire earth was devoid of gold, all of them approached Mahāpadma, the lord of the earth.

Mahāpadma honored them and others whose greatness was renowned in the scriptures; among them he declared: "Having established my daughter as the prize for the assembly, she is given to whoever gives even a mere *lava* of gold. When the king had spoken thus, a certain young brahmin went with speed, returned with a certain measure of gold, and requested the maiden.

When questioned, he related his arrival to the king: "Out of greed for the maiden, my mother, driven by persistence, wept for a long time and said to me: 'O madman, do you not know that your father, the discoverer of the treasure, was imprisoned by the king right there and gave up his dear life? Therefore, how could there be even a mere *karṣa* of gold for us?'"

Terrified by the prospect of losing her life, she stirred up the ashes from her father’s funeral pyre and, upon hearing that this was the very piece of gold she had found, she was overcome by a swoon of joy at the thought, "I have made the earth my own, free of rivals. Then Indradatta, having mastered the yoga taught by Vyāḷi, entered her body; being that same king once more, he caused Kātyāyana to accept ten million gold pieces for the sake of his preceptor.

Having assumed a fabricated body for the sake of benefiting the people by means of the minister named Āryaka—who was perceived as the ultimate reality—he remained presiding over that very circle of ministers through the mouth of Vararuci, and took his pleasure within those same royal harems. And Virūpā, having become a yakṣī whose form inflamed the fever of love, attended upon him.

But Upavarṣa, having rejected that ten million gold pieces—his own disciple [Bhartṛhari] suspecting them to be sprouts from the shafts of arrows, and [Upavarṣa himself] because of the skull-bowl [he carried], saying "What need have I for ten million?"—thereby acquired the title "Koṭi. That heap of wealth went just as it was to Kubera. But when Padma appeared, the Lord of Treasures addressed him: "O Brahman-sage, since you did not fulfill the desire of Kātyāyana... [the wealth] has been acquired by unjust means."

Therefore, you shall once again be born in this very city as the son of the merchant lord Potapa, named Padmodbhava. Having served as the minister of righteousness to the royal seer Ripuñjaya upon his return from the forest, and having had the earth entrusted to him, you shall abandon the mortal world along with your husband in the former cities; then, having long resided there with Asita, you must dwell for a time in the realm of the gods, free from all desire for worldly existence.

Indeed, now that eighty-eight years have passed since the conclusion of the Mahāpadma [Nanda] dynasty, his eight sons were each uprooted over ten years by the noble Cāṇakya, whose mind was provoked by the theft of Āryā Kāpī’s earrings; thus was Candragupta Maurya established. Under this very king, the Maurya sovereignty shall endure for twenty-four years. After him, Vindusāra, whose essence is inconceivable intelligence, shall rule the kingdom for twenty-five years.

Furthermore, Aśoka, the remover of the grief of embodied beings, [ruled] thirty-six autumns; Suyasas, our instructor, protected the earth for seven years; Daśaratha for nine; Saṃyuta for eight years; Śāliśūka for thirteen; Devaśarman for two; Daśadhanvan for six; and Bṛhadratha for seven.

Furthermore, having once again uprooted [the Mauryas], a Śuṅga named Puṣyamitra—whose general was the Brāhmaṇāyana Bhartṛlakṣmī, a minister intoxicated by passion and evil counsel—he will slay Mūladeva, the destroyer of Vītabhaya and the blazing Maurya dynasty, in battle and shall rule the earth for thirty-six years. Then [there will be] Agnimitra for eight years; Viśākha for seven; Vasumitra for ten; Pṛthuka for two; Pulinda for three; Yoṣavasu for exactly three; and Vajramitra for one year.

Mahābhoga [will rule] for thirty-two years; Devabhūti for ten. After having exterminated him, Vasudeva, the minister of the Kāṇvāyana lineage, will occupy the earth for nine years. Bhūmimitra [will rule] for fourteen years; Nārāyaṇa, son of Sumitra, for twelve; and Suvarmā for ten. Having destroyed that dynasty as well, one named Sumukha will become the sovereign for thirteen years; his younger brother Kṛṣṇa for eighteen; and Sātakaṇṭaki [for the same].

Lambodara had eighteen [sons], and Pilaka twelve. Meghasvāti had exactly eighteen, and Śātasvāti the same number. Skandasvāti had seven; Mṛgendrasāta-kaṇṭhi had three; Kuntalasāta-kaṇṭhi had eight; Svātiptena had one; Pulomāpi had thirty-six; Garikṛṣṇa had twenty-five, Hāla five, Māntalaka five, and Puḷindasena had twenty-one.

(One) Sundarasātakaṇṭhi, twenty-eight Śivasvāti, thirty-one Gautameya, [one] Rujā Pulomāpi, thirty-eight Śivaśrī; Cāri Śivaskandasātakaṇṭhi, twenty-nine Yajñaśrī Sātakaṇṭhi, six Vijaya, three Caṇḍaśrīsātakaṇṭhi, and seven Pulomāpi.

Thus, when six Śuṣṭikas, ten Śaiśunāgas, nine Nandas, ten Mauryas, ten Śuṅgas, four Kāṇvāyanas, and twenty-nine Sātavāhanas—known as the Āndhras—had passed away; and when other [dynasties] had arisen among their servants, namely seven Āndhras, the Ābhīras, ten Garbhis, seven Śakas, eighteen Yavanas, eight Turuṣkas, and fourteen Mukuṇḍas.

While King Ripuñjaya—belonging to a lineage obtained through the grace of Nārāyaṇa—is ruling over Magadha from his hermitage of renunciation, in order to wash away the stains of the intense Kali age during these thirteen [years] and eleven [months], you shall become the follower of the Blessed Lord, the Master of Wealth, having placed that son of yours, a great treasure, in the hands of Padmodbhava. This life-prolonging emerald, set in a ring, must be worn by you. Furthermore, when you wish to cast it off, it should be thrown into water, for that is its proper field.

*Mati*, *Śarmadharmapāla*, and *Padmodbhava*—these three were the ministers of my father-in-law. Having entrusted me to them as soon as I was born, my father went forth into the religious life (*pravrajita*). Thereupon, Padmodbhava, for the sake of preserving the family traditions, appointed his eldest son, named Ratnodbhava, to the business of trade; he then committed these two other sons, Suśruta and Sumantra, to my friendship. Having completed the rites pertaining to the next world and having relinquished his circle of servants, he meditated upon his own deity and passed away.

And Matiśarman, having secured Sumati and my other son Satyaśarman as his companions, sought to ascend to heaven while embraced by a great fever of burning, like the sacrificial fire itself, which had long been gratified by his worship.

But another Dharmapāla, not associating himself with this son Sumitra and others of the Ma...ḍaka clan, and having agitated the circle of kings solely through the power of his mantras, entrusted the burden [of the kingdom] to us upon our birth; then, having departed together with his eldest wife, while his younger wife—who had been abandoned for the sake of pleasure—was pregnant, that wife of Dharmapāla also gave birth to a son, Kāpapāla.

That Sundarasubhaṭa, who was handsome, munificent, and naturally skillful, though learned, became through fate addicted to the vices born of the science of love. Having been rebuked by his brother Sumitra, who behaved toward him like a father, he was forced by shame to leave his own country; and because he has long been lost to sorrow, even news of him cannot be obtained today—while he was speaking thus with eyes filled with tears, a certain young hermit approached the prince.

Bearing the color of a lotus, he arrived at that very place. Honored by the husband and wife with rising to meet him, prostration, and other marks of respect, he sat comfortably and spoke: "The Great King surely knows me, Somaśarman, as one of the disciples of the venerable Vāmadeva."

Having frequented Rāmatīrtha in the Deccan, I am returning; while traveling along the Vartanī road toward Kaliṅga, I reached a certain beautiful temple of Śaṅkara in a vast forest of lofty timber. Having performed my ablutions there, I filled my flower-vessel with blossoms, set it down at the foot of a tree, and approached at dawn a certain mountain torrent refreshed by the streams of fresh rain-clouds for the purpose of bathing.

And I heard a cry: "O Mother, has a place with fire been found by the Blessed One here? Following that sound, I cast my gaze and saw a woman of some piteous appearance with this child held in her hands. Feeling compassion for her, I said: "Take heart, Mother! There is fire-making material; I shall produce fire and give it to you. And as for this [child], out of regard for you, I shall set aside his mere wealth and report it."

I am Duhitṛvardhanī, the daughter of Kālagupta, the chief of the guild, who dwells on the island of Kālayavana. When that maiden had reached the first bloom of youth, a hatred for men arose within her; wishing to remedy this, we attended upon you, noble lady, in a certain grove. There, having seen someone she had not seen for days, she was repeatedly overwhelmed with emotion. Rising up, she cried out, "O dear Samudradatta, where are you? and casting aside all her attendants, when questioned by me, she spoke with great difficulty.

I am that very person, born here on this same island as the daughter of a poor merchant named Kṛṣṇagupta, and my name is Suvratā. Now, while I was listening from behind a wall, someone addressed me in a secluded spot: "I am Samudradatta, the son of a caravan leader from Ujjayinī. I have a friendship with Mūladeva, the son of Karṇīputra, who is skilled in the art of stealing."

And by the power of fate, he developed an irresistible attachment to his heart for a courtesan’s daughter named Madanasenā during their association. This matter was accomplished [by me] through wealth. Enraged, he spoke thus to me: "Even though you are a sinner, because of the favor of the word 'friend' [bestowed upon you], my life is safe; however, if you bring her here, there will be no such safety."

Out of fear of that, being one who had not yet taken a wife, desiring progeny, and being fearful, he wished to marry in secret your daughter whom you gave [to him]. He said, "This is your Hiraṇyaskandha. And having been given by his father, he placed her secretly in a chest, declaring it to be "precious goods," and having brought her to his own home, he settled her in private within a well-furnished residence equipped with all necessities, and lived his life there in concealment.

Then one day, I perceived myself being attended by another man with joined palms. When asked, "What is this?", he replied: "O noble lady! I am that very Karṇīputra. Having made a promise to Samudradatta, who had done me a service, I vowed to violate his wife. Having tracked you down through my spies while you were living in concealment here, I entered your house by means of a tunnel."

Having seen that you were beyond remedy due to your virtuous marks, I deluded you with a certain mantra-deity and brought you under my control. Then, having abducted the daughter of a dice-player from a foreign merchant who was disguised as such, I took her in the presence of all the citizens under the name [of your wife]. I established you in your position as a caravan leader... exactly where you belong. And, withdrawing my disguise in the presence of your friends, I showed you your companion, saying, "Look, here is your friend."

Suspicious, he went to his own house and, not seeing [his wife] in her usual place, was thus deluded by himself; then, for the sake of resuming their legal affairs, he was joined with him [the husband], who had been defeated and made to realize that the marriage was without witnesses and had been performed as a sham, and having been duly punished, he was sent back to his own home. Having conceived a grudge... [and] having returned... [he thought: "When you entered the tunnel and were shown to the king's men, you were accused of being a thief of another's wife; therefore, after first seizing your own self..."

"O noble one, this country must not be abandoned. But you, having realized that I have been violated by you, thinking 'you shall not live,' and seeing it as unrighteousness, desired to die; thus, having thrown yourself into the waters of the Ganges and being carried away by the current, you were rescued to the shore by someone. That person became my husband, Samudradatta. And because of the sight of him, desiring death once again, I was restrained by shame. He said to me: 'Take heart, lady! I know that you have been possessed by some demon named Jālika.'"

"Otherwise, how could you have acted so cruelly, transgressing your own character? You have now regained your life. Previously, however, due to the agony of not finding you, I threw myself into a river with a water-pot tied to my neck; when the pot was broken by a log, I was somehow swept toward a bank by the force of the current even against my will, yet I remained intent on death. So come, let us go."

But I, feeling ashamed, thinking "if you desire me as one who would act thus for you, I remain obedient to your command," having honored that [wish], was brought here to this very island of Kālayavana by my kinsmen, along with a mass of wealth increased by the value of my ornaments.

And here, having been made to abandon her life-breaths by merely hearing of the death of that husband whose name she had once uttered with great effort, she now arose, filled with intense malice toward men; yet, existing even as an ascetic through that very longing for him, she gazed upon this grove where he had once enjoyed himself, and realizing her former birth, said, "I shall give up my life," and while speaking thus, she fell into a swoon upon my lap.

While we were thus distressed and crying out, a certain youth emerged fearlessly from a bower of forest creepers and approached my daughter. With water from a large pond held in folded lotus leaves, and with tears shed from the hollows of his lotus-eyes, he sprinkled her limbs—which were as tender as fading lotus stalks—while stroking them with a hand marked by a fish, its palm bearing the likeness of a lotus.

As if longing for the nectar of a touch so sublime that it transcends all asceticism, she began to blossom with a multitude of hair-tips, like a *kandalī* plant refreshed by a fresh rain after the summer heat. With a sweet glance emerging very slowly from the opening of her curved eyelashes, she beheld a youth who was like a son of the gods. Overcome by both joy and trepidation, he comforted her and said: "O fair-limbed one! Cast off this agitation. Here am I, Samudradatta, to whom you are as dear as life itself."

Those two, having found one another after their separation—now like a pair of swans at Lake Bindusaras, which was speckled with moon-like drops of nectar from *indranīla* sapphire-blue water-lilies—were there cursed by the indignant Nārada. "Since you have dried up that cluster of golden lotuses used for the worship of Acyuta with the fickleness of your beaks, you shall remain separated for many years."

Out of delusion, however, failing to heed that [warning], while we two were still drinking honey from the filaments [of the lotuses] in the pavilion, Nalakūbara—the prince who was sporting in the Santānaka grove on the nearby shore—beheld Rambhā’s face and took pity, saying, "How is it that even animals, whose sensory faculties are indistinct, are cursed by pitiless sages? Such was his compassion. Yet, O lady of the future, in a later birth you shall become the daughter of these very two; thus the great sage, his wrath provoked by the fetters, cursed him as well.

Furthermore, being propitiated by him who was distressed at the thought of human existence, he bestowed upon that virtuous man—who had remembered his former association through supernormal knowledge—the friendship of a universal monarch as soon as he was born, and ordained celestial enjoyments beyond this earth for him, even though he was destined to remain separated from us for sixteen years.

But at the conclusion of my life, O long-lived one, I became the son named Ratnodbhava of Padmodbhava—the crest-jewel of the circle of merchants and a porter for the burden of sovereignty—in Pāṭaliputra. My younger brothers were named Suśruta and Sumantra; having given them as companions to Prince Rājahaṃsa, my father appointed me to continue the traditional duties of our family.

Furthermore, while wandering alone upon this earth by chance with my life-breaths barely sustained and my mind agitated by an unwell wind, I reached this place from the abode of sea-monsters. And by fate, which moves in concealment, I have been shown this flower-grove where the memory of my former birth is clearly manifest. Indeed, on this island, I obtained Suvratā, who moved with a playful gait like a forest-lady of the Yavana islands, and whose vow of devotion to her husband was well-guarded.

Among the twice-born who had performed their morning rites, he [bestowed] perfumed oils, bathing powders, myrobalan, fragrant garments, scented flowers, ointments, delicious drinks, supreme foods, fine cloths, perfumed betel, and so forth; and for that one [brahmin], a pair of silken garments bearing a painted ruddy goose couple, a floral ear-ornament whose filaments were stirred by the breath released from his nostrils, and betel sprouts upon which playful drops of water rested like breasts placed upon the surface of the earth with the forefinger touching it.

And Kāmapāla, the lover, having caused his side-glances to move slowly like a stream of liquid lac, as if they were the very essence of the interior of the minds of women— glances that were like long ponds of blue water-lilies with petals slightly opened by the practice of inscribing letters upon the inner surface of a single nail, and which, being darkened by their own depth, acted like a bold thief or a silent robber sent on a secret mission to plunder all the wealth of the heart— he gazed at Kāmalatā, whose face was revealed through a single petal-like opening, her true nature manifest through the purity of her yoga-like vision.
A charming female swan in a cage, gazing at the moon with the thought that it is a white lotus,
utters various indistinct sounds, compelled by the power of her longing.

Thus it was said. Having experienced that [moment] as if it were composed of honey, her gaze became languid; she placed her hand, which was adorned with dangling curls at the root of her ear, against his ear, and having herself leaned there, she departed a short distance away, her excellent letter being read by someone hanging from the branch of a red *aśoka* tree, whose belly was distended by the bursting forth of a row of tender sprouts and whose tips were raised upward. Kāntimatī also, under the pretext of gathering flowers, [moved] several steps toward the direction of the wind...

...he brought them together at the proper time. And he trained them—following the sequence of the *puṣpagarbha* [method]—gradually over time with a diet of wholesome food, milk, and ghee, and by means of the application of hoof-trimming and other treatments. After six months, having begun the training with small amounts of butter, and after three years, having further tempered them through the use of firewood, *utkārikā* cakes, enemas, and ointments, they were perfected in the five senses such as sound, in the five lineages (*gotra*), in the five streams (*dhārā*), and in all three circles of action (*karmamaṇḍala*).

He ordained those who had received initiation within the circles of the Vinaya and possessed the [proper] limbs, having trained them in various rites through one hundred and eight types of binding—including the *kapāla*, *kaveṇi*, *rābhi*, the eighty *avasthāpanās*, and the hundred *muṣṭis* and so forth—and their fathers likewise attained that same abode once they were freed from the curse.

And the king won over that lord of elephants, Hemakūṭa, even as he remained in the sixth stage of rut, by means of words mixed with conciliation. His followers, who had followed him along with attendants and the like, became invincible through his son's power; and seeing them, the lord of the Aniruddhas addressed his queen: "O Queen! Behold the prowess of your son!"

From the Lord Brahmā—who dwells within all beings as their inner essence—there arose eight husbands of female elephants, born from the touch of the Grandfather’s lotus hand. These were begotten by Sadaṇḍa together with Āsaptaka, by Rocya and the other six [sons] along with the seven *Sāman* chants beginning with the *Rathantara*, and by the eight female elephants beginning with Abhramukā, Kapilā, Tāmraparṇī, Añjanāvatī, Śubhradantī, and Piṅgalā. These lords of the elephants are Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Puṣpadanta, and so forth.

"Vāmana, Supratīka, Añjana, Sārvabhauma, and Kumuda—these are the names of the elephants stationed upon the chests of the Asuras. Among these young elephants, who are like actors in the performance of sporting upon the slopes of the breasts of those mountain-like beings, this one cub appears distinguished from all the others by his stature and his greatness of spirit, as if he were emulating their noble characteristics through his speed, energy, and strength."

Then, on an auspicious day, having performed the rites for the deities and having secured [the elephant] by means of bonds appropriate to the task, they approached it with suitable *pārāvata* (restraining) measures. It was established that the terrestrial [elephant] should be brought under control through the threefold action (*trikriya*). There is attendance, maintenance, and training through the sevenfold equipment consisting of the *damya* (tameable), the *aupavāhya* (mounting), and the *cārin* (roaming)—namely, the non-elephant mount, the water-crossing mount, the staff-mounted, the hymn-mounted, and the battle-mounted—along with the war-equipment and the *nāgarāyaṇa*. Thus, there is the roaming [elephant], the non-elephant mount, the water-crossing mount, the staff-mounted, the hymn-mounted, and so forth.

He appointed Śuddhopavāhya as the one destined for the path, having provided him with all the perfection of requisites and attendants divided into seven types; and toward those who had correctly entered the path, he felt no resentment toward their conduct.

Then those boys also, having become more capable, were brought out from the house in the fourth month; they were given their first solid food (*annaprāśana*) in the sixth month; their tonsure ceremony (*caulakarma*) was performed in the first or third year; and they were invested with the sacred thread (*upanīta*) according to their respective castes in the eighth, eleventh, or twelfth year from conception, or in the fifth, seventh, sixth, or eighth year. They wore garments made of *kārpāsa*, *raurava*, or *vāta* skins, as well as *śāṇa*, *kṣauma*, or *āvika* fabrics; and they were equipped with girdles of *maurvī*, *śoṇika*, *kauśya*, *āntaka*, *balvaja*, or *mesvala* grass, all accompanied by the recitation of mantras.

Wearing garments of cotton, hemp, or flax, with their sacred threads suspended over the right shoulder, they carry staffs made of *vailva*, *apāmārga*, *vaidala*, *pālāśa*, *khādira*, *udumbara*, or *aśvattha* wood, adorned with hair from the forehead or the nose, or with knots, fragments, or thorns. Having previously practiced the middle and later rounds of begging for alms, they do not emerge from their dwelling until the appearance of the sun or the stars; during both the morning and evening twilights, they remain standing, sitting, or moving about, reciting the *Sāvitrī* with fuel-sticks brought from afar and placed in the open air.

Kindling the sacred fire at dawn and dusk, serving their gurus without envy and with steadfast devotion, rising before them and retiring after them, following them when they depart and returning when they come, not speaking in the hearing of others, not expressing satisfaction during meals, sleep, anger, or in the presence of women, nor in matters of divine worship or excellence; avoiding stone slabs and various types of alms-bowls, and subsisting on pure alms-food permitted by their gurus.

He avoided the odors of honey, meat, and liquor, as well as fermented acids, raw meat, and harmful substances; he refrained from wearing unguents, shoes, and carrying umbrellas. He was free from desire, anger, greed, dancing, singing, instrumental music, gambling, slander, and worldly distractions, and he did not look at women or accept gifts from them. Through various Vedic vows, he mastered all the Vedas, all the Prātiśākhyas, the entire *Dhanurveda-saṃhitā*, the whole of the Itihāsa-Veda, and all the Āyurveda and other sciences, having thoroughly studied the Vedas and their branches.
And likewise, on Mount Śikṣātantra-mantranirvacana-śabdānuśāsana-yajñavidyā-yojya-jñāna-chandovibhāga, he attained supreme proficiency.

Moreover, Rājavāhana attained the highest mastery in the *dharmaśāstras* such as those of Manu, Vasiṣṭha, and Gautama; in the *arthaśāstras* such as those of Uśanas, Bṛhaspati, Vaiśālākṣa, and Bāhudantaka; in the legal codes (*smṛtis*) of Bābhravya, Ānādi, and others; in the *kāmasūtras*; in the extensive treatises on the arts (*vārtā*); in the science of logic (*ānvīkṣikī*) in its entirety; and in all the sciences of elephants and horses. Having mastered all these branches of knowledge, he surpassed everyone everywhere by virtue of his manifold qualities.

But out of affection, he remained exactly the same. Thus, when the residence at the holy ford was completed, and the children had grown into youths, having reached the full measure of sixteen years, Rājavāhana—dispelling the joy of his parents as it were—having consulted with his wife Rājahaṃsī, made this representation: "Your Majesty, at the very time of Your Majesty’s departure for victory, there exists a destiny ordained by the gods for Prince Rājavāhana. Affection ought not to obstruct what is intended here."

Even that which is beneficial does not lead to ultimate welfare if it is like bitter medicine made sweet by sugar; therefore, let the anxiety of separation—dense with darkness—cease, cease now, for he is the treasury of splendors. Let him now bestow his daughter upon the prince, who is as broad-chested as a slab of precious stone, so that she may not be lost to the boundless royal fortune. For she, failing to reach this deep abyss, would only lead to long-lasting grief.

"May this [prince] go forth from the forest like the Great Boar, uplifting the earth; may the world rejoice, finding its protector, beholding that Supreme Person who bestows the fruit of vision upon our eyes—He whose form is a great mass of unsurpassed and wondrous splendor. Even as he was departing, Queen Vasumatī, her complexion instantly distressed by the separation from her son, fell into utter agitation.

The King as well, having announced his own separation from bliss, though casting off his superhuman composure, fell to the ground, overwhelmed by grief; his gaze was dejected due to his support failing him, his face withered like one whose merit is exhausted. Even Sumantra and the others, seeing the power of Daśaratha’s [sorrow] and fearing for their own sons, were overcome with agitation. Just then, the venerable Vāmadeva arrived, accompanied by a host of sages, shaking the very foundations of the mountain.

The circle of ministers rose up in agitation, their forms possessing the beauty of full-blown lotuses whose loud humming was interrupted by royal swans drenched in spray from the snowy waters; with these seekers of form, they all, like the sun, seemed to fill the world with their own essence. Then the king, bowed down by the heavy burden of his son’s departure, breathed no sigh of relief for himself, as he had previously done when his son was born.

The divine King Hamsa, surrounded by Arthapāla and his attendants, approached the venerable sage like Harivāhana approaching his grandfather, and stood before him with his head bowed in salutation with joined palms. And as the king stood at the sage’s feet like a tree beneath a rain-cloud, the wise one, emitting a shower of nectar-like words in a gentle voice, gladdened him with these very firm words:

It is true, O royal swan, that you are bewildered by various rumors; are you perhaps deluded by a great longing for Lake Mānasa? Has this season arrived unexpectedly as a foul day, since you—by means of those playful lotus-eyes of yours which resemble auspicious signs—desire to experience all alone, and by yourself, this wealth of the Lord that is to be enjoyed by the three worlds?

"Within this circle of the seven continents, illuminated by the excellence of your own splendor, you are like a lamp within a hall; even though you may be staying anywhere, whom will you leave fatherless today? O King of Kings, you who surpass the assembly of gods and the royal sages, you who possess unwavering fortitude—surely this jewel-like ornament of the earth is capable of providing a firm support for stability, like a mountain-king made of gems. Thus he spoke, as the sky became radiant.

“O Blessed One, in the past, my life was restored by the Blessed One Āmardaka after it had been severed by a divine sword. Now, once again, when my life was seized by grief for my son, I have been sustained by you through the power of consciousness. Now that I have regained it, the paths of both the virtuous and the wicked are clearly visible; today, the anxious thought of separation—the enemy of happiness—is at last stilled. May I remain in the presence of the Blessed One, O Blessed One, while I am well; let the Blessed One instruct me regarding what must be done. Having thus steadied his mind with effort, he stood with palms joined in reverence.

Then the Guru, gazing intently at the prince’s face—steadfast as the host of gods—directed these words toward him for his victory: "Since you have performed the initiation of even a single person like yourself—one who possesses the specific qualities of action inherent to that caste, who is a substantial entity sharing the nature of the great elements, and who is the source from which the entire world's experience arises—this entire world is thereby consecrated by you. Therefore, we have bestowed upon you with our whole soul these treasures of knowledge, which we have guarded with great effort."

Like a sword polished on a whetstone, your intellect has now been refined by learning; it is ready for this youth to achieve his goals. Furthermore, for teachers who are insatiable in instilling virtues in their own disciples, there is no fault of redundancy in their beneficial instructions. Thus, this detailed exposition of my counsel has begun.

For one who has practiced the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and reached the culmination of the stages of life (*pāramāgama*), yet has ascended to youth and is engaged in the duties of the householder stage (*gārhasthya*), this [life] is likewise rooted in the exhaustion of labor. For by that [stage], the wealth of the field-bound man becomes dependent on a single source. Indeed, when men unite their resources against those who are unattainable and hostile to their interests, the sixfold forces of desire and the rest stand before them; and for one fallen into the midst of these, even the senses—which are capable of destroying the objects of the senses and which, though being released, carry away one's own vital breaths as if they were their own—[are overcome].

And thus, in this group functioning as a collective, if one were to neglect even a single member, the wrath of the others would become incurable, just as when the chest of Tārkṣya was struck... the collection of his senses was instantly pacified; and just as by a favorable wind, the thirst arising from the womb of one's own mother-in-law ceases, so too do they indeed turn back toward the cowherd in a state free from affliction.

With their vision obscured by the spreading of rising dust, their minds deluded by false errors, and following the path of the black-trailed fire (Kṛṣṇavartman), whose exhaustion from the enjoyment of the three worlds does not end in itself? It is the Brahman-sages who, as if having reached this very village of sense-objects within you, are now withering it away.

Royal sages, self-controlled, having conquered the earth, given away wealth, or having enjoyed pleasures with propriety, performed great sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees for the sake of infinity; yet, becoming free from attachment, they renounced them. These [sacrifices], beginning with the mantras, and you as well—like a musk deer in a forest thicket, you are the enjoyer of the three worlds; however, the fruits of past actions, even as they are being spoken of, do not ripen without time.

For the performance of a funeral procession depends upon both divine and human action; neither of these two is capable of accomplishing it by itself, independent of the other. Indeed, even when the blessed Parjanya rains at the proper time, he cannot cause seeds to sprout in saline soil or upon stones. Nor does rain poured down upon a field of good deeds yield its desired fruit if the seed is corrupt. Because the attainment of results depends on these visible causes, that which is called "human" [action] is as essential as the other.

Since the accomplishment or failure of security (*yogakṣema*) is brought about by this [human] deliberation, it is not the case that the attainment of desired or undesired results is granted through prayer, because they are produced by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Thus, the term "deity" (*deva*) is not applied [to such a cause].

Even while contemplating how to attract prosperity, those desiring victory enter the circle of the twelve kings according to rule; yet, like those skilled in mantras, they do not hope for success unless the king’s counsel is well-guarded. For a mountain-like ruler who raises up the hidden splendor of his own majesty has his supreme foundation in these three: counsel, energy, and protection of the subjects. If even these three are united, they accomplish this triple world very quickly, as if for the purpose of manifesting their own portions, and they remain endowed with power.

For one desiring to ascend the palace of spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*), the various virtues serve as the steps; here, decline, stability, and growth—which are to be sought through patience—are established by means of these six primary qualities that constitute the very head of the edifice. Thus, one’s own sovereignty is achieved.

Just as one who has acquired strength might overcome a superior foe by employing the six qualities like flavors, at the appropriate moment and place, through the three means of oppression, destruction, and emaciation—which strike without distinction—so too does he possess a splendor like that of the Lord’s body with its three blazing eyes. Furthermore, for a conqueror whose nature is to exercise the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), all these kings, endowed with the characteristics of allies, enemies, neutrals, and those in between, serve as the very instruments of his play.

But by your father—this man who has completed his studies, who perceives the elderly, whose senses are subdued, who is a friend to pure ministers, counselors, and domestic priests; who employs spies at the eighteen points of vulnerability; who is intent on winning over the citizens and the circle of constituent elements; who is skilled in the means of concealing counsel and knowledge; who understands the application of the three types of envoys; who is habitually industrious; who blocks all doors to misfortune; who is expert in the performance of every kind of duty; and who, in accordance with power and purity, has appointed all the superintendents—[he governed].
