By one who does not withhold even a trifle that ought to be taken, who does not desire to take even a vast fortune that ought not to be taken, who supervises legal affairs, who inflicts punishment as deserved, who maintains social order, who has uprooted the thorns of enemy kings and their fortresses, who is skilled in the distribution of the circle of states (*maṇḍala*), who delights in the application of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), who is capable of determining the entire range of calamities, who is expert in the deployment of the components of a military expedition, who is proficient in the rules of warfare, and who employs a variety of means through combination and alternation— [The remainder of the sentence is implied by the context of the preceding description.]

This earth, possessing a single umbrella and extending over vast distances, was enjoyed by him—who was powerful, skilled in the application of all resources, possessed of marvelous deeds, and devoted to the three aims of life—just as the land of Bhārata was enjoyed by Bharata.

Thus, for the most part, being of such a disposition and by nature intolerant, King Mānasāra—the Ikṣvāku ruler whose name was truly unfailing—hurried to the city of Avanti; yet, having been cast down from there by the blessed Āmardaka for his sake, and having lost his pride in protecting the earth, he was eventually conquered by Your Majesty, he whose heroic vows are beyond reproach.

Thinking, "Therefore, I am the victor," he immediately laid down his weapons and, having consecrated his son Darpasāra in sovereignty, became intent on providing a worthy bridegroom for Udayavantisundarī. Because that was impossible, Darpasāra—though his essence of hope had now vanished and he was filled with no small agitation—out of pride and a sense of humiliation, entrusted the lordship to his brother-in-law Caṇḍavarmā, who was of a fierce disposition. Then, propitiating the Destroyer of Andhaka (Śiva) through most rigorous meditation, he dwells upon Mount Kāla.

In this interval, together with your friends... [the mountain] must be cut by you. Namely, Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmali, Gomeda, Puṣkara, and Ucava (or Audāra)—these seven continents are situated like a wheel, each encircling the one preceding it, with their size increasing twofold successively from one hundred thousand *yojanas* onwards, and possessing the greatness of lifespan, enjoyments, and majesty that progressively excel one another. Of this very Jambūdvīpa, which has an extent of two thousand [yojanas], there are six mountain ranges [dividing] the six regions (*varṣa*).

And there, Mount Vicitrakūṭa is eternally situated; though its base extends far, it is always beautiful in form; though it is not dissolved, it shines with triangular and quadrangular splendor; it is eighty-four thousand yojanas in height and sixteen thousand in width; it is golden, like the playful *tāṇḍava* dance of Nīlakaṇṭha; it is the abode of the bamboo-flute and the vessel; it is Meru... its depth is thirty-four thousand [yojanas] and its breadth is [thirty-four] thousand; Mandara is likewise [extending] toward the eastern mountain, Nīla.

Mālyavat, Hiraṇmaya, Kiṃpuruṣa, Harivarṣa, Ilāvṛta, Ramyaka, Hiraṇvān, and Kuru—these are the regions (varṣas) equal in number [to the mountains]. In the middle, however, is Hiraṇyagarbha... These regions are inhabited by Nīla, Śveta, Śṛṅgin, Āṣāḍha, Bhadraśva, and Madhyama. Furthermore, like a great garment, there is the region of Kṛṣṇa-dhanus, resembling a vast mantle. To the south of that is the land of Mahāmeru, which is like the eye of the Cakravartin-like Bhārata-varṣa. Indradvīpa, Varuṇadvīpa, Somadvīpa, Gandharvadvīpa, and Nāgadvīpa are its [sub-]islands; and furthermore, Kumāri is nine thousand yojanas from this island. Again, it is exactly nine thousand [yojanas].

...the grove-lands and the principal mountain ranges. On the back of the Himalaya, the mountain that bounds the [rain] zone, there is a lake named Acchoda, its waters clear as crystal; from it flows a stream of pure water. There, on the southern-eastern side, stands a place where the darkness of the forest is deepened by the thickets growing along the banks of the Añjana river—darkness intensified by the tears shed by lovers angered by their trysts in the grief-free forest being forgotten by yakṣas drawn into assemblies of dharma with the Māṇicaras.

May [the merit] go to the lotus-stamp adorned upon the broad lap of the feet of Paśupati; to the Muñjavaṇa forest, where the minds of those whose possessions were taken away by Brahmā-rākṣasīs were agitated by the tossing of their breasts, and where the cool waters of the mountain lakes were offered for bathing by throngs of spirits wandering in intense devotion to the essence of music; and further to the Bindusaras and Hiraṇyaśṛṅga, where the lineages of the Brahmā-rākṣasas were destroyed by the sacrifices performed by Agastya, who dwelt there in incalculable numbers.

There, the purifying celestial river (Gaṅgā), whose current was slowed by compassion for Bhagīratha who was emaciated by asceticism, and whose crest-jewel-like intellect was restrained and released [by Śiva], desiring to flow southward as a favor to Bhagīratha, entered the Himavat from the north—she who, though divided by her distinctness, was like the Vindhya range; she entered the groves of the two trees, the Vanaspati and Jyotiṣmatī, which had long been delayed in the supreme battle, where the rows of herds of deer were glancing at the lotus-pollen-laden Cakravāka birds whose joy was surpassed by the splendor of the sacred groves along the banks.

Because of their attachment to the enjoyment of milk and curds, the hosts of gods who have partaken of ambrosia descend again among human beings. There is a Jambū tree named Sudarśana, beautiful with its clusters of fruit hanging down for the distance of a *krośa*, which is the dwelling place of the foremost venomous serpents such as Vāsuki and Takṣaka, whose bodies are like fresh [flames of] love; it is the source of the Viṣṇupadī river and the fountainhead of the Gandharvas’ youth. From there, [the mountain] manifests itself as a vast expanse of jeweled stone, solely to provide an unbroken means of self-satisfaction.

And where the birthplace of Jāmbūnada gold—the splendor of which is like a mass of light from the enemy of Vṛtra—is situated; where, because the surface of the sky is as if screened by Mount Meru acting as its parasol, the curiosity of those desiring to behold the darkness [of the underworld], though shaken off by the words of the Pitṛs and Mānavas, has not ceased even today; thus is Mount Meru well-known, surrounded by the gods of the earth with their splendors, and purified by the limbs of Siddhas, Brahman-sages, and those bound in yogic postures through oblations at sacrifices, and by Vaiḍūrya stones...

It displays, as it were, a flow of nectar; it is the abode of the seven classes of ancestors, where the expansion of Rati is cultivated by the enjoyment of honey from the blooming *rohimaṇa* flowers on lovely trees; it possesses the splendor of the moon’s nectar-like beauty; it is established upon a foundation of gems and all kinds of jewels; its sands are like those of the Rudraka lake, which, though fierce, is naturally gentle; its lakes are filled with lotuses that are inherently mild even in the heat; it is simultaneously a heap of honey, a burden of venerable and blameless love, and a place where the luster of blue water-lilies arises from the consumption of the juice of jackfruit.

The seven mountain ranges of the Varṣas are: Karī, Kiṃpuruṣa, Ayoṣ, Varṣāyu, Indravajraprabha, Ṛṣabha, Dhūmra, Dundubhi, Trayavagā, Mālī, Jalāśana, Jātavedas, Saṃvartaka, Paścimataka, Somaka, Varāha, Nādarāśi, Candrameru, Candra, Jaladhara, Raivata, Nārada, Śyāma, Dundubhi, Asta, Somaka, and Sumanas. These are the seven mountain ranges of the Varṣas. Their lifespan is ten thousand years; they possess the splendor of Indra’s thunderbolt; and they are [named after] the Ṛṣabha, Dhūmra, Dundubhi, Trayavagā, Mālī, Jalāśana, Jātavedas, Saṃvartaka, Paścimataka, Somaka, Varāha, Nādarāśi, Candrameru, Candra, Jaladhara, Raivata, Nārada, Śyāma, Dundubhi, Asta, Somaka, and Sumanas. These are the seven mountain ranges of the Varṣas.

Therein, the commencement of clouds from Mount Meru; water taken by Indra from the moon; [the waters] seized by the Aśvins... two Ṛtavas were produced; Śyāma attained a state of extreme blackness; Dundubhi and Surāsu were free from passion... he destroyed Akṣa in the days smeared with the hair of Arci; on the days of Loma, Mātariśvan blew... named Dhruva, thus the arrangement of the hermitages of Asthikī; Satya, Śauca, Śāli, Khini, and Nitya—these are the Tretā Yugas; Arada... Dhenukā, Sukṛtā, Garbhagarbhasvinī—these are the rivers that are branches of the Gaṅgā.

In Kuśadvīpa, however, there are seven mountain ranges that serve as boundary mountains (*varṣaparvata*), namely Kumuda, Vidruma, Hari, Mandara, Kakudmat, Citrasena, and Trasa. [There are also] Unnata made of yellow orpiment, Varāhaka made of collyrium, Puṣpavān, Mṛtasañjīvanī, Viśalyakaraṇī, and the heap of jewels (*ratnarāśi*) known as Mahendra-saṅgraha.

Their seven regions are: Śveta (the white and elevated), which bestows the knowledge of the Vedas; Lohita (the red); Veṇumaṇḍalaka (the bamboo-circled); Jīmūta (the cloud-like), which has the form of a chariot at will; Harita (the green), which is salty; Kakudvat (the humped); Mānasa (the mental), which is preeminent; and Kapila (the tawny), which is full of longing—these seven are possessed of great splendor. And there are likewise seven rivers: Dhūtapāpā (the sin-washing), Yonitoyā (the womb-watered), Śivā (the auspicious), Pavitrā (the purifying), Vitṛṣṇā (the thirst-quenching), Candrāhlādinī (the moon-gladdening), Vidyuccandrakā (the lightning-mooned), and Vibhāvarīpuṇḍrādhṛti (the night-marked sustenance)—these seven.

In Krauñcadvīpa, there are seven mountain ranges that serve as the boundaries between the regions: Krauñca, Vāmana, Andhakāra, Devāvṛti, Devendra, Govinda, and Puṇḍarīka. They say that Dvivida and Pāvaka are the names for Govinda and Vāmana respectively. There are exactly seven regions: Kuśala, Manonuga, Uṣṇa, Pāvana, Andhakāraka, Munideśa, and Dundubhisvara. There are an equal number of rivers:
Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Sandhyā, Rātri, Khyāti, Puṇḍarīkā, and Manojava; these are the branches of the Gaṅgā.

In Śālmala-dvīpa, however, there are three circular mountain ranges known as Suramanas, Pitṛbhrama, and Putrānīta; and there are exactly three regions (varṣas), namely Kuśala, Pāpaka, and Andhakāraka.

On the island of Gomedadvīpa, there are two mountain ranges, one made of *surakumuda* and the other of *añjana* and *śātakumbha* (gold), situated in the east and west. There are also two regions (*varṣa*). Encircling these regions is the Mānasottara mountain; and on that jewel-mountain, in the directions of the elephants of the quarters—namely the east, south, west, and north—stand the cities of Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Soma, known as Amarāvatī, Saṃyamanī, Sukhā, and Vibhāvarī. This is the festival of the mountains and islands. Beyond that lies the Svādu ocean, circular in shape, which supports prosperity and destroys sin.

The mountain Cakravāḍa, ten thousand *yojanas* in extent and height, is both luminous and dark, encompassing the world and the non-world. Below it lies the region named Pātāla, a realm of black darkness... [where] Annamuci resided, along with Nārada, Śarabha, Śaṅkukarṇa, Kabandha, Kiṣkindha, and other fearsome Dānava lords such as Bhīmaladatta and Śvāpada, as well as the serpent kings Kālayakṣa, Kalaśa, Jaya, and others; a path frequented by thousands of powerful beings leads to this region known as Talātala.

It shines with glorious cities belonging to the lords of the Asuras, headed by Pāṇḍu, Bhauma, Jambha, Mahājambha, Śambara, Śigrīva, Suvaśa, Khaja, and Gomukha; and to the lords of the Rākṣasas, such as Nīlamegha and Krathana; and to the lords of the Nagas, such as Takṣaka, Aśvataraka, and Prabhala.

The third level, named Tritala, is composed of red earth; it shines with the throngs of prosperous citizens and the sight of the lords of the Daityas—Triśiras, Śiṃśumāra, Tārākṣa, Prahrāda, Hradoda, Agnimukha, and others—as well as Cyavana, Khara, Virādha, Kumbhika, Ulkāmukha, and the like, along with Darśanaśrava, Amṛddha, Paura, Vṛnda, Udyota, Maṇidatta, Pāṇḍaraka, Kapila, Viśā, and Viśrāṇa.

The fourth [level] is named Gabhastitala, consisting of yellow earth. It belongs to Kālanemi, Gajakarṇa, Kuñjara, and other enemies of the gods; to Sukumāli, Muñja... and other night-rangers; and to the lord of fourteen thousand species of birds, Kaśyapa. It is the domain of the venerable Vainateya, who has attained friendship with Mahendra through the power of his asceticism and the marvelous majesty of the moon... [and] whose vehicle is the sacrificial Puruṣa. Thus it is to be contemplated.

The city, with its magnificent splendor and ornaments, was being celebrated by the Vedas. Vitala is the fifth [subterranean realm]. This power belongs to Virocana and the other Dānavas, who possess great clouds, double-tongued serpents, and lightning. That lion-king has been slain. The ministers, along with the queen, went to the Vindhya forest to perform service to the Goddess dwelling in the Vindhyas; due to this tragic news, they have abandoned their bodies right there.

And she, this virtuous woman, having returned from the brink of death, was once again consoled by him in this way: "The comprehension of the gods is difficult to fathom, and the paths of their power are immeasurable. For instance—Kaca, the son of the preceptor of the immortals, though crushed by the Asuras and struck down in secret, was manifested from within the belly of the Lord Bhārgava, even after he had been torn apart."

At her gate, Dāmodara withdrew the reed-weapon (*eṣīkāstra*) discharged by Bhīma, which had overwhelmed the son of Bharadvāja and was about to seize Uttara; and Nāciketa, though struck down by his father’s curse, returned from the city of the dead. And Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, restored his mother Sāvitrī to life through the grace of his preceptor, after she had severed her own head in obedience to the command of an enraged teacher. And Sāvitrī, by virtue of her devotion to her husband, rescued her husband from the hands of Yama, the lord of the departed.

And Rāghava obtained a son of the twice-born from Dharmarāja by means of the offering of Śūdraśami Śambuka; and Bhīmaratha, the king of Gāndhāra, having conquered Nagnabala, attained the status of a Nagnaja.

"O you whose form is divided by manifold colors... even for those [who are] not liberated... yet you, having become a delicate woman dwelling within [the body], have crossed the great ocean; in all circumstances, you alone are the authority regarding the sight of immortality for the long-lived ones. Therefore, apart from her who is the cause of consolation, even that which is called the non-existence of King Rājahaṃsa—not being perceived in the slightest—is also an unobstructed path to death."

And so, while that goddess... and her other [features], her face indeed moved forward before her; she relied upon her fortitude, and somewhere in a hermitage of ascetics, closing her eyes for a moment as if to experience the fruit of her past actions, that seeker of knowledge—having somehow been released by her kinsmen—departed toward his desired direction.

And this aged female ascetic, wearing matted hair and bark garments, devoted to her vows, who was serving the Lord of the Gaṇas while her belly was being scorched by the fire of hunger—while she was saying, "She has been protected in this moment by the King," that washerwoman wept. Having heard this, and perceiving his kinswoman lamenting with incessant tears, and having determined [the situation], that most wise one, out of compassion for me whose breath was failing and whose throat was choked with joy, spoke these words to the Brahmin.
That divine royal swan, together with his wife Vasumatī, grew up alongside his two fathers, Suśruta and Sumantra, and his mothers, as well as with Viśrutamantra and Uptā, and other sons of ministers.

Having been brought up and disciplined in the sixteen sciences, at the command of the sage Vāmadeva—who was equal to Vālmīki—he set out on his journey of victory. For the sake of favoring the one who had suffered humiliation from the Asuras, the Lord descended even without being requested; yet, because he was difficult to perceive, the path of those who had departed was lost. Seeking him here and there, [he saw] his father and mother, whose bodies were as if entering the jaws of death, having emerged [from it]. Then, by means of the tender and moist disposition of my father’s heart and that of my mother, I grasped this very purpose.

He was already made known by her breasts, which were overflowing with love; yet he has been told again by me, or perhaps even more so. However, the incoherent ravings characterized by endless finality, being devoid of purposeful action, cannot be fully discerned; therefore, enough of this excessive prolixity.

We, having gone to our mother’s residence... we spent the night. On the following day... having ascertained the treasure of that person and its utility for the people, accompanied by a few selected men for the purification of their sins, [we visited] the cities sixteen *hasta*s in extent, made of various jewels, belonging to the enemies of the gods (*surāri*) who possess golden peaks, and the abode of Vāsuki, the friend of Śakra, the night-stalker who increases joy with his resonant cries, which is composed of *maṇi* gems.

The seventh, however, named Pātāla, is made of gold; it is filled with the cities of Bali Vairocana—the lord of the Dānavas who was gazed upon by the three steps of the illusory Vāmana; of Mucukunda, who was no different from Indra; of the lord of the Viṣaghara serpents Indranīlāmbara, who is as white as the orb of the moon... of Arcimālin, who possesses two thousand tongues and eyes... together with others, including the lords of the Nāga kings, the lords of the Danujas, and the lords of the night-stalkers (Rākṣasas).

The light consisting of radiance, which upholds the abodes of jewels belonging to those with moon-like faces—abodes eternally delightful through dance and song—sustains the circle of waters ten times the size of the terrestrial mandala on all sides. The great elements, having successively enveloped one another from the beginning, bestow stability upon the world.

Within the unmanifest space of the cosmic egg (*bhuvanakośa*), which is supreme, without beginning, middle, or end, and immeasurable, those [lights] which are intensely active within the cities of the worlds exist right above Mount Meru. By your grace, O God and Brahmin, this shall become obedient to your command.

"Indeed, a certain portion of the splendor of the Vaiṣṇavas has arisen and remains embodied in you; therefore, O best of all sages, everyone must endure your slighting for no more than a month. You are like the constellation Śravaṇa, which presides over all islands and portends victory in every direction; by following a favorable course, you shall set forth just as Pṛthu did to take possession of the earth. Having said this much, he ceased speaking.

Thus revealed by the sage-guru, that supreme Indra-like sovereign, having seized all [his] pride... as if seizing a garment, first brought about the state of his ears being reached by [the king’s] hands upon his limbs; and Sumati, hearing of her son’s power, considered herself to have achieved her purpose. The Lord Śaṅkara also accepted Sarasvatī, like timely rain.

And the venerable Vāmadeva, having dismissed the king—who was following him, humble with discipline and accompanied by his retinue—went to his own penance grove. The royal couple also went to the hermitage.

Rejoicing at times with thoughts of their daughter’s prosperity, suffering at times from the longing of separation, performing at times the auspicious rites for the journey, [fostering] at times... [favoring] at times by recollecting the deeds they had performed since birth, weeping at times, instructing them at times in heedfulness, praying at times for safety to the deities, and [listening to] at times the sages who had arrived to see them, they passed the remainder of the day.

Vyāghradamana, having learned of this news, his heart melted with affection; he suppressed his tears with great effort, and with a voice faltering from the sobbing that choked him, he offered words of consolation. Then, as the river-like darkness arose—greying the sky like incense used for self-purification by the quarters of the world, who were like brides eager for union with their lord, their cheeks stained by the friction of the mass of the universal monarch’s splendor against the mountain ranges—the crest-jewel and fly-whisk appeared like a female elephant.

Having attended upon the night, at the time of its departure, he—exerting himself with great effort, disciplined according to his station, emaciated, and possessing a frail constitution—sat upon the sandy bank of the Āpramāṇa river, which was soft as linen; there, surrounded by a circle of attendants, he waited upon the king. After standing for a long while with unblinking eyes, as if lost in some deep meditation, and having let out a long sigh, he addressed his son.

"Father! In this world-order where mothers always grieve for their sons, especially when they are away on travel, I shall surely be unable to find peace even while desiring to see you. My heart is filled with various intended moments; what more could another advise? This effort is seen to be urged upon me, thinking that the circle of venerable friends should not be neglected by playing with companions—though one who is naturally bound to happiness might ask: 'What have I to do with the welfare of the world?'"

They wander about before you. If that were so by necessity, then why—by you who are vessels for a mass of steadfastness worthy of enduring the torments of a mountain of adamant; by you whose eyelashes are excessively moistened by a continuous stream of rising teardrops; by you whose mouth is parched...; by you who lie prostrate; by you who, though young and vigorous, run after the fawns of the hermitage deer; if you have now become one who has known what is to be known, yet remain amidst every worldly whirlpool, you are indeed equal to one devoid of discernment who has cast away affection.

...of a woman’s heart—this nectar-like food, now brought to you, will delight you during your journey abroad. Even while she reflects thus, and even though she has heard such words, O Viṣahyadatta, she endures this departure as if it were the departure of her very life-breaths; for her, the separation from her elder brother is unbearable. Her limbs, as if undergoing a bursting *puṭapāka* treatment due to the curse of grief, have suddenly been drained by both you and your friends through the forceful extraction of their mutual happiness.

Although her heart was melted by following after him and she had no desire to cause him harm, she—though visible yet [seeming] distant—permitted him to depart with the hope of seeing him again; and as for his life-breaths, whose desires must never be thwarted, she, with a tearful face, wishing to fall at his feet, was restrained by him as he firmly grasped both her hands, and with a voice choked with tears, he spoke thus.

O friend, what is the fruit of this despondency? This is the nature of ordinary people that they fall into such distress; for even when there is room for fortitude, they take refuge in grief. Remember Pṛthā, who remained in meditative concentration for thirteen years even after we had departed for the forest, staying thus for the sake of the city of her enemies. Enough with the fear of misfortune here as well; for how many [are] these fathers and mothers of mine, surrounded by a circle of friends, in this very garden named Udyānavihāravarnapuṣpodbhava?

O you who dwell within the sphere of the sky, tell me how much time has passed; for she has come here repeatedly before us. O Lord, become the husband of these wives who have performed all rites, who are infinite, who move everywhere, and who fall into the shoreless ocean, for the sake of their venerable elders.

Even for him whose foremost attendant has been carried off by the disguised swan, there is indeed a festival of sight as we wander... If you intend this very matter thus: that while we are away, there shall be the joy of serving the feet of the Blessed One; that we shall be entertained by assemblies of sages’ sons and discussions on the *Kuśāstra*; that there shall be the essence of service at the feet of our father and yourself; and that there shall be the nectar of instructions day and night from our father, his sons, ministers, and others—there will be delight in the repeated sight of Vyāghra and Damana, even though [this opportunity] may be difficult to obtain for but a few days.

"None of this excites me. And since Siṃhadamana has arrived right here for the purpose of counteracting our anxiety regarding our separation... [elsewhere] Vyāghradamana went along with his sons and wife. He said: 'From birth until now, Siṃhadamana has acknowledged no one other than the pair of Your Majesty’s lotus feet—neither mother nor father, nor any other kinsman, nor any other deity.'"

And by the grace of his very footsteps, she—having become as pure as a cloud that has shed its water—remained free from blemish. Even though he had been commanded to go to the penance grove and other places, wherever your Majesty’s lotus-feet were present, there she was the first to arrive. She was like a female elephant restrained by the lion-taming *madhukara* [elephant-driver]. Just as her husband had spoken, saying, "If anyone should attempt to cross over the thorns while digging for roots and tubers for the sake of the penance grove's sustenance," even before he had finished speaking, she became as if agitated.

Vindhyasena said something: "Where is my lord’s partiality for the family of ten clans today, and where is this [favor]...? By whom has the side of those worthy of favor been won by the lotuses of the Ajāni lineage, which subsist on water? To his mother, who stood there with a tearful face, Siṃhadamana replied:

"Why do you weep, mother? ... misfortunes pursue one who is masterless, and our animal-like nature is indeed distressed by anxiety; [our] birth is surely for the sake of leading us to the forefront of danger. When they were thus agitated, King Rājavāhana, as if touched by shame, remained silent for a moment; then, as if washing Siṃhadamana’s face with an eye moist with affection, he spoke, his agitation and turbidity having subsided.
"Friend! Do not have heard this otherwise from anywhere... for the elders tell a wonderful story: that Caṇḍakṛṣṇa was once unable to endure my grandfather, Trika, and so forth."

His son, named Kāladaṇḍa, who was like another Kāla (the God of Death), having taken refuge with Caṇḍavarman among the Mālavas and obtained the fierce army of the eleven younger brothers of that king—Ugravarman—to crush the forest-dwellers, has found a path for his exit... For those desiring to thrive do not disregard their enemies; if that enemy force should surrender, then, because they have surrendered and touched our weapons, there will be an end to the fear of the great Gurjara lord, and the subjugation of Vyāghradamana will come to pass.

And while we are present for such a matter, if the elders must exert themselves, what is the use of these arms that are like long pillars of iron? There are likely no others on this earth who are so strong, skilled with the bow, vigilant, and possessed of such courage as you. While you are here, it is possible to proceed without fear.

"Even though I have departed, there is no fear of misfortune for me, as I am enclosed within the vajra-cage of the arms of my circle of friends. Therefore, even if my words are unpleasant, you should reflect upon them; do not again lead me astray," he said, making that his final resolve. Thus, with various timely conversations, having first prepared the ground for the matter at hand, they all retired to their beds at nightfall.

On the following day, when the sun—the ornament of the world—had risen from the waters, dispelling the play of darkness with its radiant glow, its light like that of a ripe, intoxicated, and plump *cīraṇḍiga* fruit; when it had stolen the splendor of the forest of night-lilies (*kumuda*) and was emitting the soft warmth of its rays; when the world was filled with the cries of ruddy geese eager for the earth; at that time, the lion among men [the King], together with his domestic priest, who was like a bull-elephant, [performed the rites] with drops of clarified butter as bright as the moon, which were drawn forth by the tips of the horns of the *rohiṇī* cow.

Having sprinkled his head with water marked by honey and *veśalā*, having approached and worshipped the god Savitṛ, having honored the venerable Lord of Speech and other deities, and having muttered prayers and offered oblations with great concentration as an Atharvan priest, he—like a bee—circumambulated [the fire] clockwise; his mass of matted hair was coiled like a swarm of bees, and it seemed to indicate the ripening of his merit through the very rising of smoke, as if for the satisfaction of the emblems of sovereignty.

With incomparable devotion, he circumambulated the fire-god Hiraṇyaretas—who displayed the forms of horses, elephants, banners, and parasols, who was white and slightly marred by sparks—and, adorned with white garlands, unguents, and garments, together with friends similarly attired, he partook of that milk which was as fragrant as nectar produced by the breaking of moonbeams, which was experienced as abundant and unsurpassed, which delighted the sense of taste, which possessed pure and unblemished qualities, and which appeared like a mass of white conch-shells.

Having consumed the supreme elixir (*pararasa*), sipped the smoke from the incense-stick, and rinsed his mouth, he took up perfumed betel; having paid homage to the Lord Vāmadeva, as well as the other ascetics, the presiding deities of the hermitage, and his own elders, he received their blessings intended to bring about future prosperity. Surrounded by Devarakṣita, Pramati, Mitragupta, and others of his own age—all of whom were reciting the *Apratiratha* hymn—he was accompanied by the sons of sages, and seemed to purify the land of Ilā, which had been defiled by the enjoyment of other wicked kings.

With the placement of his lotus-feet moving slowly in the graceful gait of a lordly elephant, and resonating with the sound of auspicious proclamations (*puṇyāha*) that were smooth and deep, he emerged from his own palace through the main gate—which was filled with pairs of jewel-filled jars placed at the side entrances—and, generating a sense of joy, set out toward the northern direction.

Then, as they were setting out, a certain young Brahmin student (*brahmacārin*) from the right side [of the road] sang aloud this *vasantatilaka* verse, his gaze drawn by the autumnal splendor that graces the three worlds: "In a lake whose water is the color of a fragment of emerald, charming with white, blue, and red lotuses, and adorned with cranes; in which a young swan—nurtured on wild food offered by his own hand—is being filled with lotus-milk (the sap of lotus-stalks) dripping from his beak as he presses it against the tip of his trunk, while filling a leaf-cup of a fresh lotus grown upon the bank."
Shaking the chowries of the clusters of *saptacchada* flowers, this wind has become a parasol for the sky whitened by the clouds;
it sports with the grace of the waters of the rivers that serve as necklaces and the waters of the lakes.
This is the season in which the royal swans rejoice.

Thus it was said. Having reached this place, they heard the lowing of a bull that had obtained its fodder at their feet, its horns smeared with red earth from digging at the riverbank; they heard the joyful cries of peacocks as if they were the dharma of righteousness beginning a reign of good governance, and the sweet warbling of birds like auspicious songs of bards emerging in white robes to proclaim victory. Having traveled for about a *gavyūti*, they arrived at a level hermitage belonging to forest-dwellers, where the water was pure, and which was lined with beautiful trees abundant in flowers and fruit.

In the dwelling of those accompanied by their wives, with the twice-born receiving him at the entrance amidst a clamor as they held *triphalā* in their hands, garlands of *mallikā* flowers, and full water-jars, and were chanting Aindra verses, auspicious *sāmans*, victorious *yajus* formulas, and holy *atharvan* hymns; the King also spent that day there, being entertained by various conversations—both pleasant and delightful—with the ascetics, his own attendants, and his friends.

On that day, Rājavāhana, in private, instructed his two sons, Sumati and Devarakṣita, who were well-established, saying: "Dear children, the one named King is the aggregate of attributes that are entirely concordant with Indra, Varuṇa, Yama, Kubera, the Sun, the Moon, and Vāyu, whose births are for the benefit of all people.

For indeed, it is fitting that he rains [upon the earth], protects the boundaries, instructs those who require instruction, rules over his own, shines at the proper time, gladdens those who are distressed, purifies the unripened, and impels others toward the commencement of their tasks."

If this [Dharma] did not exist, dharma would not be remembered; the Vedas would not be undertaken; the Lord would not be worshipped; the deities would not be propitiated; the social classes (varṇas) would not be respected; the stages of life (āśramas) would not function; those who are distressed or childless would not be cared for; servants would not follow their masters; sons would not honor their fathers; students would not attend upon their teachers; tax-payers would not pay their taxes; and the medicinal herbs and forest trees would not bear fruit in due season.

For his worldly course proceeds unbrokenly through the power of punishment; since he, having risen at dawn, [regulates] by means of the conduct of dharma: the seizure of the son of an enemy, the recovery of a deposit, the sale of goods by those who are not the owners, partnership (sambhūya-samutthāna), the violation of agreements, rescission of purchase and sale, the sale by one who is not the owner or by a keeper, disputes between partners, and the improper application of verbal and corporal punishments.

Among the eighteen titles of legal dispute—namely, verbal abuse, [physical assault], the duties of husband and wife, the partition of inheritance, gambling, and betting—the king, by perceiving the truth through the influence of place, destiny, and other factors, establishes the practice of dharma; and for the sake of the subjects... immediately following that, there is the title of dispute in which we abide.

And by that minister—who was thoroughly trained in the four branches of knowledge, namely the three Vedas, economics, statecraft, and metaphysics; who possessed all the qualities of a subject in their entirety; who was not deficient in...; who was never at any time given over to fear; whose speech was naturally learned, elegant, and free from the defects of arrogance, fickleness, and indolence; who was friendly, pure, highly energetic, devoted to what is good, courageous, possessed of presence of mind in times of distress, free from duplicity, non-hostile, and self-controlled toward both his master and himself—[he governed].

One should strive for the sake of dharma and artha. Furthermore, when the ground has been prepared and permission granted, while seated comfortably with the [king] under one's influence, one should speak of matters that are consistent with the questions at hand, predominantly pleasant and beneficial, with eyes and eyebrows unaltered. One should explain tasks that are possible, not devoid of dharma and artha, and extremely clear. Having entered properly into his conduct, one should encourage him, restrain him moderately in lapses, and avoid both siding with others or creating discord.

One who does not shrink from those who are hateful and so forth, who always and everywhere acts with discernment, and who should be approached without deceit like a deity—such a lord (svāmī) [is to be served] with all virtues... you are those whose nature has arisen together [with him], yet that fault which exists because of playing in the dust and being struck in childhood, arising from great longing and grasping at the perception of conduct—that both are terrifying; [therefore], this youth should be attended by all of us as if he were our own self.

On account of his noble lineage and other future qualities, as well as his complete personal excellence, he was regarded by these ministers as their very master; and thus, out of affection for him, they [entrusted] their own sons to his virtues... how could the prince—on the very first day, having dismissed his father’s retinue; on the second, his familiar young ascetics; on the third, Vyāghradamana, who was to be won over; and on the fourth, Siṃhadamana along with his escort—be able to turn back? For a month he performed the wheel... indeed, the splendor of his side-born [attendants]... was like that of the sun.

[He saw] mercury that pierces a thousand [times], its edges not empty of herbs possessing the colors of asafoetida, rukapuṇḍarīka, Lakṣmī-muṣa, honey, turmeric, bhaṅga, and green haritāla leaves; copper-colored ores; kṛsara [rice-and-pulse mixtures], mudga beans, māṣa beans, and... [along with] apalāśa, śaivala, niśā, hayānava, vardhaka, and plīhan; ores of gold that drip from the ladle like drops, possessing many colors such as lotus, pāṭalī, crystal, pigeon-neck, and sugar-candy.

Though he was well-acquainted with silver mines sought after by other kings, he gazed upon them without curiosity; for he was tall, with a majestic lineage of ancestors firmly established in fortitude, and he beheld a mountain cave that was exceedingly vast, enchanting with its following trees, filled with the cries of *jīvañjīvaka* birds, resounding with warbling cuckoos, noisy with flocks of *koyaṣṭika* birds, and humming with swarms of bees; its base was starry with a garland of droplets rising from rocks pierced by gems fallen from its lofty peaks, while its slopes were strewn with flower-stalks scattered upon the stone slabs of its banks.

He beheld a certain man clad in rags, seated facing the east at the foot of a solitary tree on a sandy bank, surrounded by a river whose roar was amplified by the echoes from mountain caves; he had occupied that space for a very long time and remained there in solitude. He was muttering something while counting his beads upon a rosary; his eyes were veiled by a tattered deerskin made harsh by many scars and calluses; the corners of his eyes were marked by the impressions of his mind’s refinement; his hair was dark blue-black and unkempt; his complexion was as dark as time itself, made coarse by the practice of fierce austerities; his status as a twice-born could be inferred from the white hair on his prominent face;
and he was dressed in garments of bark.

And having seen him, he rose and offered water for the feet and the guest-offering (*arghya*) in a lotus-leaf cup, beginning with words of welcome. He invited him with delicious fruits and roots easily found in the forest. And the princes, whose masterful nature remained unimpaired even as they did not disregard his affection, gazed at Devarakṣita for a long time, assuming the guise of servants.

And he spoke thus: "O ascetic! This is that very power which, even in the case of a beast, produces such supreme [transformation] that it causes one to be seen for a long time, yet not experienced elsewhere—even a tree seen for a moment becomes known as 'Nirviśaṅkamārgadruma' (the tree on the path free from fear), a place of vanguard for the village boundary-lady; and by her, a man is rendered invincible and subject to her own will. For this body of yours, O worthy sir, still possesses a heart moist with curiosity, following the sequence of the world's course."

Born of a pure lineage, he had never before encountered such things as Yakṣas; yet, when his body was cut by weapons, there was a wondrous reconnection [of the limbs] and a certain duration of stability. Indeed, whatever cause one might take as a basis for this is a source of wonder for all transitory beings. Furthermore, at this age—capable of bearing the weight of the enjoyment of sense-objects—he, who had established himself in the householder’s life according to the injunctions of the Smṛtis, now wanders alone in the forest as a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), tormented by his teacher with the cause of world-weariness (*nirveda*).

You ought to understand this: when examined, death is clearly an endless state of misfortune. Who would embrace the suffering of hell while awaiting the fall of the body—a suffering that is like a spell or a medicinal poison, invisible yet burning with heat, a coating of impurity, a treasury of humiliation, a protracted abode of reproach, a banner of despair, a firmly embedded arrowhead of life? It is well-placed [within].

Poverty is indeed a treasure-house of loathing, the very essence held in the hand of Misfortune, the entirety of wretchedness shrouded in impurity; it is the most terrible disease of sin, which has forgotten its instruction because the threads of the hands of all the Daityas have been severed by it. It is ever-vigilant in its curse-like search for a single chink through which to crush the lineage of every person in the world. Yet, there is indeed a remedy close at hand for it: namely, that these [arrows], made of polished *udumbara* wood, are seen to be exceedingly sharp, capable of piercing a hundred and even a thousand targets.

And those of the colors of gold-dust, red lead, butter, pigeon, *gomeda* stone, *vamaśulyaka*, *dhāyākṣauma*, *umākusuma*, and variegated hues—run toward those who lack virtue, O you who are filled with the splendor of many worlds!

Thus, having failed to cast even a glance toward objects that had presented themselves—objects capable of securing welfare in both worlds—that Brahmin, emaciated by harsh asceticism, replied: "Gentle sir, even the virtuous perceive a certain dignity in others that is not the ultimate truth; the dispositions of the noble are wondrous. Thus, your favor in questioning me is a kindness, though you yourself have committed an offense against your own self. For you are one who has forgotten the Vedas and their recitation, and who has not heard of the purpose of the sacrifices."

[He was born] among those who call themselves Brahmins—outcasts dwelling on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains, whose conduct is like that of forest-dwellers, who have not smelled the scent of Dharma, who are unacquainted with the purification of substances, who pay no heed to the consideration of what is fit or unfit to be eaten, who are experts only in what they have never understood, who possess a tradition of merely recollecting their birth through strenuous effort, and who are possessed by savage dispositions as if following the taste for the Śavara funeral offerings and rice-balls.

Mother, I am a twice-born man who bears the name of an old Kirāta, having become a village headman of a fabricated village. Once, while wandering through the forest with bow in hand, I encountered on the path a certain twice-born man, white-haired and grey, moving along supported by a staff suited to his own age; he was about eighty years old, his slow gait burdened by a bundle of handfuls of wild grain tied within the hem of his tattered rag.

But a certain man of ours, seeing him, was thrilled as if he had been asked for a reward; raising his staff, he rushed forward to strike him. Distressed, with his staff held fast at its tip by both hands pressed against his chest, his leather garment hanging loosely, his eyes rolling upward in terror, his head raised in exhaustion, his shanks covered by a jingling chain of bells, and somehow steadying himself on his feet—he cried out, "Son! Do not strike him! Seize him!"

Having himself untied his own bundle of wild grain that was stuck to him, he cried out with words broken by gasping, "A handful of forest produce! Even as he spoke, he was struck down by a merciless blow; though his rags were being forcibly dragged away, I felt compassion for him and restrained [the assailant]. "Step aside! What is the use of this old, ragged fellow who has seized these venerable and aged brahmins? We seek a large quantity."

Having rebuked me, he said: "It is true that Brahminhood is unfit for action in every circumstance, since even this so-called 'elephant-hand' (*mātaṅgaka-hasta*), though afflicted by loathing... wishes to cause [me] to fall. And during a quarrel at its base, I slew him and four other archers (*ātatāyin*). The survivors, however, having torn me limb from limb in their fury, departed."

I beheld the city of the Nāgas, with its high archways that lick the clouds, its radiant golden ramparts, and rows of palaces made of jewels; it was filled with divine flowers visible and invisible, and with flocks of beautiful maidens whose youth was sanctified by their sporting in the waters of the Puṣpodaka river. Furthermore, I saw the Blessed Lord Dharmarāja seated upon a great throne, his divine form [surrounded] on one side by those attending him, appearing as if he were the very embodiment of the discernment between righteousness and unrighteousness.

Out of fear, he raised me up with gentle words as I touched the ground with my knees and held my hands together in a trembling gesture; he said: "This is that very Kṛṣṇa, who has crossed to the further shore of all torments... he who was formerly commanded and disciplined by the royal seer Ripuñjaya. Having become a mass for those whose sins are exhausted, he has come into my presence with his life spared for the sake of the virtuous Śāntipāla, a performer of the Vasantayajña, who is now eighty years old and near his end... where families of evildoers [are not worthy]."

Having shown him these great hells—namely Avīci, Padma, Mahāpadma, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Saptatālaka, Kālasūtra, and Andhakāra—in their distinct divisions, Citragupta said: "Release this one as 'Ever-Terrible' (*nityograpadma*) because of his constant cruel deeds. Having been brought there by Citragupta, I cast down those who are self-indulgent, of unsteady mind, and who deny the state of existence after death, into this incomparable mass of accumulated suffering belonging to the Blessed One.

This is the place of torment for the King of Dharma; for here, amidst the "Kill! Kill! cries of the servants who have become enraged, there is the sound of lamentation—augmented by the shrieks from the breaking of limbs as bodies are writhing within binding machines—that is terrifying like the roar of a cataclysmic wind, and which arises from the crushing of bones, the burning of flesh, and the gnashing of teeth, even as those who were previously unyielding are struck down by weapons and thunderbolts.

Of those being split along the Brahma-sūtra from the crown of the head to the joint of the hips by a stream of sharp-edged axes; of those whose chests were pinned down by the left foot of the executioner’s right hand, which was intent on plucking out their eyes, while their necks were struck and severed by the left hand, resulting in a continuous, gurgling sound like that of a shattered cage of bones as they were being hewn apart; and of those whose heads were trembling and shaking with hands folded in supplication for a channel leading to a fountain of cool water.

With the clamor of falling bodies—intensified by the cries of the hordes of heads as they were scattered by the flinging of iron clubs, maces, and bludgeons from the enraged Kharadūṣaṇa’s downward gaze; with the tumult of their collapse, where the snapping of shins and knees produced a sharp *jhaṭ-jhaṭ* sound amidst the thick air, which was itself choked by the rush of the scent of pure-scented rice-offerings and *siddhavardhitaka* cakes; and with the emergence of those whose throats were forced open by the extraction of tongues that were harsh from false cooking and crooked from deceit.

By the sound of the crushing of the five vital breaths—disturbed by the agitation of the *rakṣas* who resembled leather bags of evil deeds pressed against their waists; by the roar of the grinding of bones at twilight, which was like the laughter of those arrogant in inflicting deformities upon living beings, fueled by the harshness of hurling lumps of raw flesh from their hands, and intensified by the hunger of those voracious with petty greed; and by the sound of the pounding of hands and feet against the sides of the jars of saffron robes as hard as joints of bone, a practice continued for many hundreds of years along that path.

[He was] one who, with his speech—which pierced the vital organs, tormented [others], and revealed through the expansion of painted scrolls of former deeds the workings of Love; which manifested the sequence of affectionate anger and appeasement; which pursued adulteresses fleeing in fear of an embrace; which took the form of hidden wives that were actually glowing iron dolls; and which consisted of much talk by a man whose wicked words touched the most sensitive parts—was like those who have risen after eating glowing iron balls and fruits that follow the taste of molten copper.

[The sound] of those who, having stolen the fire from its hearth, were yawning while lying on their left sides upon beds made of straw mats; of those whose bodies were being torn limb from limb by wolves, boars, lions, tigers, rhinoceroses, buffaloes, and *kurukoṣṇikas* amidst a mass of thick smoke rising from the abundance of fat, marrow, and oil; of those forest-dwelling lionesses who had begun an unbearable [roaring] as they sported in the deer-forest; and of those accustomed to setting forest fires, whose bellies were distended with masses of flames and who let out a thundering roar. Of those who were skillful in various maneuvers...

[He was] one who had been cast into the dark caverns of hell for thousands of years, enduring unbearable suffering; who was skilled in inflicting torment upon others, being repeatedly tossed up and down by the rising green serpents; who was marked with the scars of having his limbs cut off like the leaves of the *asitāla* forest, amidst the terrifying clamor of the *khaja-mathana* and the fierce *arañjara* liquor-distillers; and who was made to wander like a madman by the executioners (*tailika*) who were as fearsome as men of the sword, destroying the reservoirs of Dharma and cutting away the very essence of the sacred monuments (*caitya*).

The world was filled with men who were never free from the deliberations of purity and impurity; it was crowded with the tumultuous sound of the ocean-like roar of the multitude of waves—waves thick with masses of moss and tangled with clusters of betel-nut trees tossed by the force of the pure river’s crossing; it was as if the very limits of the cosmic pillar (Brahmāṇḍa) were being shattered by the sound of hand-clapping and drums, and by the resonance of the mṛdaṅga drums beaten upon bellies that were like blind wells wishing to burn with the fire of hunger kindled by the noise of eating, while the throats of those intent on devouring were choked by needles, and the sound of the mṛdaṅgas struck against bellies was heard everywhere.

Even our ears have become harsh from constant hearing. Furthermore, it is well known that the five great sins (*mahāpātaka*) are: the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s bed, and associating with those who have fallen [from their caste]. Among these, the killer of a Brāhmaṇa must dwell for twelve years in a forest hut, at the village boundary, in a deserted place, in a cow-pen, or at the foot of a tree; with his head shaved, bearing the skull of a corpse as a banner, he must subsist on alms-food purified by the *gosava* sacrifice.

Those who have sacrificed with the *R̥jīṣin*, *Abhijit*, *Viśvajit*, and *Aśvamedha* rites, or with the *Trivṛt-stoma*, having offered their wealth along with its appurtenances, or whatever is necessary for life, or even their entire property to a learned Brahmin; those who do not overcome [their enemies] through [mere] knowledge; those who follow the Sarasvatī river upstream; those who have not thrice recited the Vedic *Saṃhitā*; those who, with heads hanging downward, fall before the sun of most wondrous light; and those who are not [merely] targets of the bow for archers according to the rules—[these are the ones who attain this state].

Those of evil mind who, having acted with violence for the sake of cows or Brahmins, are deluded in many ways, do not go to the assembly of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas even if they have died; nor do they go to the final bath of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; rather, at the end, they undergo all manner of torments.

For thus it is: their bodies are shattered by the net of scorching flames and stinging gnats; their backs are bruised by being dragged over the rough surfaces of sharp, upward-pointing thorny shrubs; they are crushed and torn apart by desert winds that are themselves unable to endure the heat, as those winds carry the dust of parched earth and heaps of glowing embers tossed up by palms striking against hard stones. Devoid of any news of trees or shrubs providing shade, and with hunger and thirst beyond remedy, they somehow catch sight from afar of waters beautiful with blooming blue, red, and white lotuses.

Like two water-pools, these [women] again cause the waters of their own passion to overflow; driven by the force of thirst for sexual union, they become like the manifestations of darkness—incapable of providing utility, requiring constant guarding, and causing distant agitation. In them, there are the violent constraints and false importunities of the wardens of hell; such are the consequences even for those who are defiled by the failure to fulfill the vows as previously described.

Thus, due to the provocation of their guru, the destruction of an unborn fetus, the killing of an Ātreyī woman, the forcible entry into the dwellings of elder kṣatriyas or vaiśyas, false testimony, the misappropriation of deposits, and the killing of women, these evil-minded men suffer great misery.

Furthermore, these drinkers of *surā* have not merely drunk that [liquor] while it was fire-colored; nor have they, by drinking heated cow's urine, the juice of cow dung, milk, clarified butter, or even water, become those with protruding lips, bearing banners, and clad in hair-cloth (*bālavāsas*), who then proceed like Brahmins after having spent the night consuming a single grain of dregs or oil-cake.

Those who are like wine-drinkers, deceitful, false witnesses, betrayers of friends, revilers of the Vedas, and those who eat forbidden food—such wicked people are born here in this very world for a long time because of their evil conduct. Furthermore, those who are makers of counterfeit gold, and those who have caused pain to men, horses, elephants, diamonds, jewels, or palaces, or who have committed the murder of a Brahmin or told a lie—even if they have not been overtly submerged [in punishment], observe what they experience as a result.

Having approached the wives of their gurus, the wives of their friends, the wives of their sons, women of the lowest castes, virgins, and even their own wives, they—having themselves severed their lingas and offered handfuls of blood-stained seeds—remained facing the direction of Nirṛti until the fall of their bodies, lying mostly on thorns, having firmly embraced a radiant form like a beloved wife; yet they were not clad in bark garments nor did they carry skull-topped staffs, and though they remained for one year in a desolate forest, subsisting on wild food and uttering mostly lamentations, they were not [true ascetics].

For three months, they shall subsist on barley; these [penances] such as the Cāndrāyaṇa are for those who have killed cattle. These killers of cows must drink buttermilk and cow-urine, their limbs covered with the hide of a slain cow. For one month, eating barley that is neither alkaline nor salty, they shall sleep in a cow-pen, remaining lying down when the cows lie down, standing when they stand, and following them with all their might as they move about. At the end of the three months, [they shall perform the rite] with eleven bulls.

Having propitiated the twice-born with cows, they desire to purify themselves through delightful rites; yet they are unable to complete even this very vow for killing a cow, or the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. All those who defile the assembly are here distributed among their corresponding deeds.

These [beings], though they are not scattered [with dust], nor are they the attendants of Nirṛti such as the donkey-faced ones; though their splendor has not been restored by offerings of clarified butter poured into the fires of Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Pāvaka; and though they do not perform ablutions at the three periods of the day, nor do they subsist on alms from seven houses while proclaiming their own deeds—even so, they become terrifying to the stars (or to those who observe the stars).

And likewise, just as a woman’s conduct toward a man who causes pain to the twice-born is characterized by constant crookedness, so too, because they do not perform the *sāntapana* and *prājāpatya* penances among those acts causing loss of caste (*jāti-bhraṃśakara*), and because they consume hot barley-gruel for three days among those acts called "defiling" (*malinīkaraṇa*) such as the killing of birds and other creatures, these people wander about in great calamity.

And for the killing of well-behaved Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, those who—being unable to give one thousand, one hundred, or ten cows respectively, with a bull as the foremost—are able to perform the Brahmavrata for one year or six months, they cross over those respective [sins].

For killing a blue jay, a cat, a mongoose, a frog, a female osprey, a crow, an owl, or a lizard, a Śūdra shall observe a three-night vow or drink milk; or, having touched water in flowing rivers, he shall mutter the *Āpohiṣṭhā* hymns or walk a distance of one *yojana*. For killing a eunuch, [he shall give] a *māṣa* of lead; for a boar, a load of straw; for a rhinoceros, an iron spade; for a ram, a goat, or a bull one year old; for a donkey, a cow; for carnivorous wild animals, a milch-cow; and for non-carnivorous animals, a heifer.

Having given to the Brahmins for the destruction of sin—a *kṛṣṇala* of gold for a camel, a jar of clarified butter for a pig, a *droṇa* of sesame seeds for a partridge, a two-year-old calf for a parrot, a three-year-old [calf] for a curlew, a red cow for a peacock, a pheasant, a hawk, and a monkey, a garment or a deerskin, and five dark-colored bulls for an elephant—and having performed penances (*kṛcchra*).

When a multitude of thousands of living beings—sufficient to fill cart after cart—had been slaughtered, those cruel servants, having failed to perform the purification rites for the killing of Śūdras, fell into the hands of weapon-wielding artisans of many deceitful types, including washermen, goldsmiths, blacksmiths, potters, butchers, and others led by these; as well as all the overseers of the workshops and their apprentices, along with cattle-herders, calf-herders, guards, milkers, and churners of butter.

The droṇas, māyagāḍhas, grāhakas, ghaṭikācchedakas, peyālas, māleyakas, śalāgrāhakas, udgrāhakas, lakṣakas, āśāsakas, niryāmakas, adarśanāvīrakas, kārtikas, tarukas, kāratantras, cāpadevatas, ṭakas, kauśeyavāyakas, dukūlavāyakas, śauṇḍakas, āsavikas, apayātakas, kariṇas, anyakaras, kanakadhamakas, ....r̤akapūtakas, vyāghātakas, dhātudarśakas, viśikhas, utpathikas, śuṣkādāyakas, māyakas, and umāyakas—these and countless other cruel functionaries experience their respective fates.

Furthermore, due to the particularity of its origin from the finest trees, the wine-sellers—having conquered the mildness [of other drinks]—proclaim: "This is a fruit-liquor (*phalāsava*) of many flavors; this is an abundant flower-liquor (*puṣpāsava*); this is a fragrant spirit-liquor (*surāsava*); this is a sweet honey-liquor (*madhvāsava*); this is a desirable astringent liquor (*kaṣāyāsava*); this is a *kāśa*-grass liquor that produces health; drink this root-liquor (*mūlāsava*), which is like nectar; this is broken by the fear of the blunt-headed arrow (*bhagnakuṇṭha*); it is immeasurable excellence when boiled with *bhallātaka* and *kākathī*; they call this the nectar of the *kapittha* fruit-pulp."

"This *rājapeya* [liquor] comes from the *sthūmala-kaśakalī* tree; this strength-giving *puṣpāsava* comes from the *kadamba-kaśakalī*; it is fragrant and should be drunk by those free from clouds of disease; it is an opener of the doors of all ailments when applied with *palāśa* twigs—who is capable of describing its qualities? It is an opener of the doors of the *kapittha* fruits!"—having thus enticed them repeatedly, O wicked ones... having made them drink... they boil here in agitation; what flowers [are these]?

Furthermore, those who are like iron caskets for the entire treasury of Kāli’s transformations—mere parodies of the word "kṣatriya," deluded from afar by the greed for even a trace of the poison of sense-objects, hearing whispered advice from well-wishers yet remaining embraced by the long sleep of ignorance despite repeated awakenings by mantras; though their bodies have been washed by the consecration of the water-pitcher, they remain impure and objects of pity; their ears are agitated by the sound of the dreadful war-drum, they become causes for the world’s reproach, and they instill despondency in awakened men.

Appearing terrifying, accustomed to wandering through various regions, with the brilliance of their own burning bodies placed before them, wearing artificial veils, their natural gait constrained by being bound with iron shackles, having entered into a state of servitude, their senses impaired by being mounted upon wooden stocks, their conduct reduced to the mere act of carrying [loads], utterly dependent on others, not even knowing themselves when they have fallen, not looking back even at those familiar to them, and [disregarding] their own kinsmen—headed by their parents—who are subject to a succession of miseries...

Consoling [the attendants] and unable to endure the words of the embodied beings, he said, "I too am worthy of your favor; may this person, who has no other refuge, be graced by the gift of a glance even once. While listening to the circle of servants—who stood with disheveled hair, palms joined in a gesture of supplication without cause, whose hopes were shattered, who were emaciated and of soiled complexion, whose movements were restricted, whose bodies were cast into a state of despondency, and whose very essence had perished—he remained there.

Those whose heat is falsely kindled by burning, who are comets following in the wake of their own lineage, who persist only for the duration of a few sprinklings, yet blaze with arrogance—having turned hostile toward even the three [worlds] that were devoted and loyal to them; with joints falling apart and inner hearts shattered; having become mere dross flowing forth from their limbs without restraint; existing only as a semblance of prosperity; longing to receive handfuls of offerings from nearby people; and subsisting on the funeral cakes offered by subjects weeping in grief.

Even while in the state of being alive, these wretched kṣatriyas—who lack self-control and are no different from the dead—possessing the aforementioned qualities, shall dwell for thousands of years, measured by the numbers *samudra*, *śaṅkha*, *padma*, *śaṅku*, *parva*, *nikharva*, *nyarbuda*, and *arbuda*, in great hells filled with boundless floods of suffering along with those merciless teachers of deceitful doctrines who perform all manner of difficult deeds; and having dwelt there, they consider their birth again in this *Padma* hell to be distinct from the human condition.

And here, the servants of Yama—those who cause coughing, honey-colored expectoration, and catarrh; those born of the lower regions who are deaf and mute; those whose mouths are diseases of the anus; and those great ailments of the rectum—all these, along with the fever that destroys all living beings and the terrible *rakṣas* demons, cause [the world] to tremble.

"Even you have experienced these torments thousands of times; therefore, act now in such a way that you shall not fall here again. When he was thus addressed, I became terrified, my hair standing on end, and thought: "Ah, today I am truly favored! Since the Lord Dharmarāja, who is ever-terrible, has shown such compassion toward me... [I am] instructed once more. Then, as I joined my palms in reverence, he spoke to me: "By the grace of the Blessed One, my heart—which had long been granted solace through easily accessible compassion—now desires to descend [from its state of severity]."

It so happened that the son of Kolāhalika, named Hālābhali (or Kanaka), the lord of the Pulindas dwelling in Vidarbha, was stolen by thieves. Once, while performing his own religious duties, he, together with his attendants and his wife, intercepted a certain noble widow on the road. She, being helpless, cried out: "Alas, my protector! Why is this wife of mine, fallen into such distress, not seen by Your Majesty, who is wise and virtuous?"

"Alas, my son! O Nityograpa! Having obtained such a child as this, why do you not experience such joy? Alas, my little son! O Mahogra! Protect your wife along with your mother! Thus she uttered a cry of distress. Immediately thereafter, like a tiger blazing with rage, a certain youth with his bow strung rushed toward that group of people.

Unable to distinguish that tumultuous scene from the mere appearance of things, she was, as it were, momentarily bewildered. But the Pulinda chief, having comforted the woman along with her son and daughter-in-law, asked her with a compassionate heart and a voice choked with involuntary tears: "Who is this man named Dīrghadarśin? Who is that Nityogra? And who are you, and how have you come to such a state?"

With her breasts slightly overflowing with milk, as if drinking him in with an insatiable gaze, she replied: "O child! He is the preeminent minister of Kuṇḍinapati, the lord of Jālandhara; he is truly named Dīrghadarśin (the Far-sighted). Know me to be the unfortunate wife of that illustrious man. To us were born twin sons, Nityogra and Mahogra."

"This master here is some Ājīvika ascetic who has taken possession of Śravaṇa by his own power; he has been possessed for eight years, and during these days he has perished due to the fault of not being protected. Having restrained those who had begun to wail, I was thus instructed by my husband: 'O blessed lady, let us not uproot our entire family for the sake of one person. We shall cause the King to grant us the grain-offerings and the sovereignty over our sons, hoping for the fulfillment of his commands. Out of fear of you, he protects this man, but not out of a desire to kill him.'"

"That would lead to the ruin of our great family; that noble house must not be led to destruction this very day by him. Therefore, let us spread the report that the two boys were taken away out of affection by their grandfather, who acts for their welfare. Having with difficulty persuaded me and made me agree, he remained... [the text is fragmentary]. Then, a great and fierce elephant-keeper named Aya-sundara, having been informed in a state of agitation that a wild elephant was attacking a man, rushed out in haste. After a long time, having managed to capture it, he returned dejected. Upon my questioning, he spoke while on his bed:

Having now departed into the darkness, with my attendants scattered by a rutting elephant, I entered a certain house; there, out of fear, I pressed close against a wall and overheard a voice speaking at midnight. "O noble lady! Do not think that my delayed arrival was due to some other cause. Hearing this, though the reason was indeed real, the King rebuked me today at night, saying: 'I know you to be self-controlled, wise, and devoted to me.'"

But your maternal uncle Dīrghadarśin, being virtuous like you, has been increasing your prosperity and maintaining proper conduct toward you. However, that son of his, Udvr̥tta, having deceived even many, is said to be destined to become king; he has now begun to protect him. If you so think, abandon him and secretly eliminate that ever-cruel man, uprooting his very portion of power.

"Therefore, supreme joy shall arise from the vengeance upon the enemy, and both dharma and wealth shall be abundant through the accomplishment of my master’s purpose; thus they will turn toward you. Having heard his command, I have come here as if filled with joy. But surely that must be carried out, even if it be commanded by the gods—to slay one's own kinsman. Even when taking wealth from their own kin, which is so difficult to obtain, virtuous men indeed boast of it. For the warm blood of his brother Duḥśāsana was drunk by Bhīma.

To his wife who was speaking thus, Acyuta replied with agitation: "Why are you so distressed? Is it some calamity, or are you under the sway of a great misfortune? Or is it that a reversal of character has occurred, or perhaps you, who act with forbearance, are deluding me by acting contrary to what is dear to me?"

"Who indeed among the elders would be an offender? Yet, that which was committed by the Kṣatriya Bhīma against the lowly sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—who were full of sin, capable of taking many lives, and base—is truly [inappropriate]. Since my maternal uncle Śukla, who is like a mother to me, is pure and of virtuous conduct, and possesses wealth sought after by the whole world, why has he acted thus toward me—someone separated from him for some reason, of low birth, and standing at a slight distance? Do not act so as to destroy both worlds through a calamity sent by fate! Thus she was rebuked by her husband, and with a voice faltering due to trembling, she spoke.

The bride replied: "O cruel one of sinful deeds, you should not urge your husband toward such an act merely for the sake of pleasing him; rather, as if delighted that I have come, you should act while trembling incessantly from fear of his anger, and then, for the sake of inquiry, you should fall at his feet after having set aside all pretense of modesty."

Having entered, I rose from my place; questioned by him—who was armed with a weapon and filled with suspicion—"Who are you, child?"—I replied with shame: "He who was that wicked man on the other side of you, a child lacking foresight and now grown old, has come to conciliate you. Then, having recognized me by my voice and [other] signs, he led me inside and made me prostrate at his feet.

Having been thus exhorted by me on account of my being his sister’s son, he said: "Those kings must never be provoked to anger; for they are quick to wrath, difficult to appease, and the fruit of their abundant anger ripens instantly. Once they have departed, their goodwill is long-lasting. Then, acting according to what was said, he went there and returned. His brother had also returned, having lived among the people with a sense of wonder, constantly filling his head with [wisdom] as if it were a vessel, and unobserved by anyone out of shame. "If you do not take this away, then this misfortune will be repaid from all sides."

"It might be so. Having turned back that man who had followed him once he was convinced, and having caused the elephant to be led back, I have returned. In every way, because of this [man]—through the censure of one whose life is ill-spent, through praise, and through the accumulated merit of his service—the night passed while we were still awake. And in that very manner, by fulfilling the family duty at the proper time for his sake, that virtuous man has honored us, his master, and his own fame.

My husband, having observed my untrustworthy appearance through my deceptive gestures, thought, "He has likely not understood what was done by me. Then the king—having conquered [me] with his intellect, energy, and majesty—gave me a staff as a token of recognition and dispatched a certain trusted chamberlain at an unusual hour, saying: "You must come this very moment in an attire suitable for a night-walker; there is such business to attend to."

Indeed, like a whirlwind tossing straw, even those of refined intellect and mature understanding—having declared to me, "This great purpose shall not be so; such is the outcome for me"—and though bound by my prohibition, they do not consider that the orders for the distribution of rations to the servants are matters fit for deliberation, [as they are dressed] in blue garments and lower tunics...

In its midst, she was visible like a single sapphire in a necklace fashioned from thin gold, with her mass of hips moving slowly in the grace of playful intoxication; appearing as if touched by the lingering rays of the morning sun due to her dark braided hair, she seemed like Rāhu approaching the moon born from her face; and as she moved through the water, she appeared as if preceded by a swarm of bees wandering in the hope of kissing a forest of lotuses, led by the rays of her eyes spreading upward.
